title: Nobody Is the Problem
subtitle: Why Nigeria’s Future Depends on Institutions, Not Saviours
author: Lincoln Matthew
blurb: We keep changing leaders. We keep getting the same results. For more than six decades, Nigerians have tried changing everything: governments, parties, regions, religions, generations. Nobody Is the Problem argues that the search has been pointed in the wrong direction. The deeper challenge is the persistence of systems—rules, incentives, procedures, and habits—that reward poor outcomes and weaken accountability, whoever happens to be in charge.
about: Lincoln Matthew is the Programme Manager of Zeeb Healthcare Development Initiative (ZHDI), a non-governmental organization in Nigeria working to improve health outcomes and accountability in public services. A graduate of Medical Laboratory Science from Niger Delta University (B.MLS, 2023), he began university studies in Computer Science at Benson Idahosa University before circumstances forced a change of course. Much of the author’s adult life has been spent navigating the same institutions this book examines—from the education system to the health system—most painfully while caring for a mother through chronic kidney disease until her death in 2022. Nobody Is the Problem grew out of those experiences and out of a question the author kept asking without finding an answer: why do hardworking Nigerians keep meeting the same disappointing outcomes, whoever is in charge? He lives and works in Yenagoa, Bayelsa State. Readers can reach him through the book’s website.
dedication:
For my mother, who carried our family through systems that should have carried her—
and for every Nigerian still standing in line, waiting for an institution to work.

sections.markdown:
I did not set out to write a book about institutions. I set out, for most of my adult life, simply to survive them.

My childhood was not what it ought to have been, and I did not enjoy many of the benefits that children often take for granted. What I did have was a solid primary and secondary education, and I held on to it as the one thing that might carry me further.

I began my university studies in Computer Science at Benson Idahosa University. I did not finish there. At the end of my second year, I was told I had failed to meet the requirement of 75 per cent attendance in two first-year courses—CSC 101 and CSC 102—and in a physics practical. I attended every one of those classes. But attendance in those courses was signed on a personal computer, and I did not have one. A rule designed to measure whether students were present had, in my case, measured whether a student could afford a laptop. I was not expelled for being absent. I was excluded by the design of a system that did not imagine someone like me.

I did not understand it in those terms then. I only knew that I had lost my place.

I started again. I enrolled at Niger Delta University and, years later, in 2023, graduated with a Bachelor of Medical Laboratory Science. Between the two, I was caught between fending for myself and paying for my education. Every day was a negotiation with circumstances: how to eat, how to pay fees, how to keep going.

Then my mother was diagnosed with chronic kidney disease.

In the time that followed, I learned what Nigeria’s health system looks like from the inside of a family’s budget. Dialysis three times a week. Bills paid one by one, day after day, in a system with gaps everywhere you turned. I paid for as long as I could, largely on my own, until I could not anymore without help that never came. I lost her in 2022.

During those years, I could not think about patriotism, or national development, or what it means to be a good citizen. There was no room for it. When you are fighting every day for things that should be basic—care for a sick parent, a chance to finish your education, a way to earn a living—the nation feels less like a home than an obstacle course. My own struggles began when I was barely twenty-five, and I spent the years that followed fighting tooth and nail for amenities that no one provided.

Much later, while researching this book, I found the numbers behind what I had lived. In 2022, Nigerian households paid for about 72 per cent of all health spending out of their own pockets. Nearly two Nigerians in three were poor by the measure that counts not only income but access to health, education, and a decent life. My story was not unusual. It was typical.

There is a lesson that many young Nigerians learn early: *nobody is coming to save* *you.* No one will pay the hospital bill, provide the computer, or find you the job. You have to find a way. And when you have to find a way in a country whose institutions claim to protect you but too often serve narrower interests, the ways you find are not always good ones. Some young people turn to whatever will help them make ends meet, even for a while, because the honest path seems closed. I do not excuse that. But I understand how it happens, and I believe a nation should ask why so many of its young people are pushed to that edge.

This book began as my own questions without answers. Why does a hardworking person struggle so much for so little? Why does the hospital fail the patient, the university fail the student, the state fail the citizen—whoever is in charge? Why do we keep changing leaders and keep getting the same results?

Over time, I came to a conclusion that surprised me. *Nobody is coming to save us*—and that is true. But it is equally true that *nobody is the problem*. Not one president, governor, party, tribe, or religion. The problem is the set of arrangements we all live inside: rules that exclude, systems that do not work, incentives that reward the wrong things, and institutions that are not held to account. Those arrangements outlast every leader we elect, which is why changing leaders alone has never been enough.

That conclusion is not an excuse for anyone. People who steal, neglect their duties, or abuse power are responsible for what they do, and this book says so plainly. But if we want different results, we must look past the faces to the systems—and demand that the systems change.

Today I work as Programme Manager at Zeeb Healthcare Development Initiative. My aim is to do my part in bringing accountability to the sectors I can reach, within my capacity. This book is part of that work.

It is also written for a particular moment. As I finish it, Nigeria is approaching another general election. Many of us are tired, and many of us are angry, and we have reason to be. But anger that asks only *who* to blame will lead us, once again, to the same place. I hope this book helps readers ask a better question—*what* must change, and how—so that we can begin to change the way we think about our country, and then change the country itself.

I have tried to write honestly about failure without becoming cynical, and to write hopefully without becoming naive. Every chapter rests on evidence, cited in the notes. Where the evidence is uncertain, I have said so. Where reasonable people disagree, I have tried to be fair.

*Lincoln Matthew*  
*Yenagoa, October 2026*

sections.markdown:
Nigeria’s greatest obstacle is not one politician.

It is not one party, one region, one tribe, one religion, or one generation.

For more than six decades, Nigerians have tried changing all of these. Civilian governments have replaced military ones, and military ones civilian. Parties have risen and fallen. Presidents have come from the north and the south, from different faiths and backgrounds. Each change has been greeted with hope. Many have ended in disappointment.

The disappointments share a pattern. Roads are planned and not finished. Laws are passed and not enforced. Money is budgeted and not delivered. Reforms begin with energy and fade when their champions leave. And each time, the search begins again for someone to blame.

This book suggests that the search has been pointed in the wrong direction.

The deeper challenge is the persistence of systems—rules, incentives, procedures, and habits—that too often reward poor outcomes and weaken accountability, whoever happens to be in charge. Those systems were not created by any one person, and they will not be repaired by any one person either.

That is the meaning of the title.

It is not an excuse for wrongdoing. It is an invitation to look further—past the faces in the headlines, to the arrangements that shape what every face can do.

Which leaves a question that the rest of this book sets out to answer.

**If nobody is the problem, then what is?**

sections.markdown:
> “When the same outcome survives different leaders, different governments, and different generations, wisdom asks not only who failed, but what endures.” ## The Morning Nigeria Wakes Every morning, millions of Nigerians wake before sunrise. Farmers step into their fields before the heat of the day. Traders arrange their stalls in crowded markets. Teachers prepare lesson notes before the first school bell rings. Doctors begin hospital rounds. Engineers inspect construction sites. Drivers navigate busy roads. Entrepreneurs unlock shop doors with the hope that today’s sales will be better than yesterday’s. Civil servants report to ministries. Students gather in classrooms and lecture halls carrying dreams larger than the communities in which they were born. Across the country, millions of ordinary acts of diligence, sacrifice, intelligence, and resilience unfold every day. ![Balogun Market, Lagos Island, 2017. Photo: Yellowcrunchy / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.](/static/book/fig-012-01.jpg)

Balogun Market, Lagos Island, 2017. Photo: Yellowcrunchy / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Parents work tirelessly so their children might have opportunities they never had. Young graduates search for meaningful employment. Small business owners take risks despite uncertain conditions. Professionals in both the public and private sectors strive to perform their duties with competence and integrity. Taken individually, these stories inspire confidence. Taken collectively, they present a puzzle. In 2022, the National Bureau of Statistics measured not only income but also access to health, education, decent living standards, and protection from economic shocks. By that measure, about 63 per cent of Nigerians—roughly 133 million people—were multidimensionally poor. Among children, the figure was higher still: about two in every three.1 Those numbers do not describe a lazy nation. They describe a hardworking nation whose effort is not reliably converting into collective well-being. If so many citizens are hardworking, capable, and determined, why do national outcomes so often fall short of national aspirations? Why do societies blessed with talented people sometimes struggle to build institutions that consistently deliver security, justice, prosperity, quality education, effective healthcare, and accountable governance? This book begins with that question. It does not begin by accusing a generation, a region, a political party, or a single leader. It begins with curiosity. Because before we prescribe solutions, we must first understand the problem. ## The Question We Keep Asking When a bridge collapses, we ask who built it. When a business fails, we ask who managed it. When a football team loses repeatedly, we ask who coached it. When a government struggles, we ask who is in power. This instinct is deeply human. We search for names because names are easier to remember than systems. It is simpler to point to one individual than to untangle the web of institutions, incentives, laws, culture, and history that shape outcomes over time. Psychologists have studied this habit for decades. One of the most consistent findings in social psychology is that people tend to explain outcomes by the character of the individuals involved, while underestimating the power of the situations and systems surrounding them—a tendency researchers call the *fundamental attribution error*.2 Studies of organizations have found a related pattern: observers credit leaders for success, and blame them for failure, far beyond what those leaders can actually control, especially when results are unusually good or unusually bad.3 The search for a single cause gives us emotional satisfaction. It gives us someone to praise when things go well and someone to blame when they do not. But simplicity is not always truth. Some problems are indeed caused by individuals. A dishonest official can steal public funds. An incompetent manager can destroy a company. A reckless driver can cause an accident. Personal responsibility is real, and no serious discussion of governance should deny it. Yet there is another category of problems—problems that return even after the individuals involved have changed. These are the problems that demand a different kind of thinking. ## The Habit of Looking for Someone to Blame When nations experience disappointment, public debate often follows a familiar pattern. Some blame politicians. Others blame citizens. Some point to colonial history. Others point to corruption, ethnicity, religion, geography, foreign influence, or culture. Each explanation may contain an element of truth. Yet each also risks reducing a complex national story to a single cause. Nigeria’s history gives the habit particular force. Of the first thirty-nine years after independence in 1960, roughly twenty-nine were spent under military rule—from January 1966 to October 1979, and again from December 1983 to May 1999.4 For most of a generation, authority was concentrated in a single command. It is hardly surprising that many citizens learned to look upward, to one office, for the solution to every problem. That expectation has outlived the system that produced it. Under the Constitution, local government councils share responsibility with state governments for “the provision and maintenance of primary, adult and vocational education” and of health services.5 Since 2023, constitutional amendments have also allowed states to generate, transmit, and distribute electricity, and have moved railways from the Exclusive to the Concurrent Legislative List.6 Yet public frustration over schools, clinics, power, and transport is still directed overwhelmingly at one person: the President. Blame has an important role. Without accountability, institutions decay. But blame becomes insufficient when it becomes our only explanation—and misleading when it is aimed at an office that does not hold the responsibility. If every election is described as the arrival of a saviour, every disappointment becomes a search for a new saviour. The result is an endless cycle of expectation and frustration. The deeper questions remain unasked. What incentives shaped the decisions that were made? Which institutions encouraged or constrained those decisions? Which rules rewarded competence? Which rules rewarded something else? These questions are less dramatic than political slogans. They are also more useful. ## The Cycle of Replacement Imagine a school where every principal is replaced every four years. The first principal promises better examination results. The second promises stricter discipline. The third promises modern classrooms. The fourth promises digital learning. Each arrives with energy and new ideas. Yet after twenty years, the school still suffers from poorly trained teachers, outdated curricula, weak accountability, and inadequate funding. Would it be reasonable to conclude that every principal was uniquely incapable? Perhaps. But another possibility deserves attention. Perhaps the school’s governing structure, incentive system, and institutional culture make lasting improvement extraordinarily difficult. Replacing principals may change the face of leadership without changing the conditions under which leadership operates. The same logic applies far beyond schools. It applies to hospitals, ministries, courts, corporations, and nations. Nigeria offers its own evidence. ### Evidence Box: Same Outcomes, Different Leaders - **Government effectiveness.** The World Bank’s Worldwide Governance Indicators assess how well governments formulate and implement policy and deliver public services. From 2004 to 2025—across the Obasanjo, Yar’Adua, Jonathan, Buhari, and Tinubu administrations—Nigeria’s score remained between roughly 29 and 37 out of 100.7 - **Electricity.** In the last quarter of 2025, the plants connected to Nigeria’s grid had a combined installed capacity of 13,625 megawatts, yet average hourly generation was only about 4,450 megawatts—roughly a third of capacity, according to the electricity regulator.8 That output is close to the country’s entire installed capacity as reported in 1988, when the population was well under half its present size.9 •**Corruption perceptions.** In Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index, Nigeria scored 26 out of 100 in both 2024 and 2025, ranking 142nd of 182 countries in 2025.10 *These indicators do not prove that leadership is irrelevant. They show that,* *across very different administrations, the outcomes most citizens care about* *have proved remarkably resistant to change.* ![Figure 1.1. Installed capacity and average hourly generation of Nigeria’s grid- connected power plants, October–December 2025. Source: Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission, Fourth Quarter 2025 Report.](/static/book/fig-017-02.jpg)

Figure 1.1. Installed capacity and average hourly generation of Nigeria’s grid- connected power plants, October–December 2025. Source: Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission, Fourth Quarter 2025 Report.

Complex societies rarely fail for one reason alone. Likewise, they rarely succeed because of one extraordinary individual. If this is true, then perhaps the most important question is not **Who is the problem?** Perhaps the better question is: **What enables a nation to convert the talents of millions of individuals into consistent collective success?** ## Looking Beyond Individuals Every society depends on people of ability and character. Leadership matters. Citizenship matters. Culture matters. History matters. This book does not deny any of these realities. It argues something different. It argues that these forces achieve their greatest impact through institutions—what the economist Douglass North famously called “the rules of the game in a society.”11 Institutions shape incentives. They establish expectations. They reward certain behaviours and discourage others. They create continuity when governments change. They determine whether good intentions become public outcomes or remain private ambitions. A capable teacher can inspire students. A strong education system can transform generations. An honest judge can deliver justice in one courtroom. A trusted judicial system can strengthen confidence across an entire nation. A visionary entrepreneur can build a successful company. An enabling institutional environment can allow thousands of entrepreneurs to flourish. Economists have tested how much individual leaders actually change national outcomes, and the answer is instructive. One influential study used the deaths of leaders in office—transitions no one planned—to measure their effect on economic growth. It found that leaders can matter a great deal, but that their influence is strongest in countries where institutions place few limits on their power.12 A later study, estimating the contribution of each leader individually, found that very few leaders made a measurable difference at all, and that a country’s growth during a leader’s tenure is a poor guide to how much that leader actually contributed.13 Read together, these findings point to the same conclusion. Where institutions are weak, a nation’s fortunes depend heavily on the luck of who holds power. Where institutions are strong, progress survives changes of leadership. Botswana is often cited as an African example of the second pattern: a country whose institutions sustained stability and growth across successive leaders after independence.14 Its circumstances—a small population and substantial diamond revenues—differ greatly from Nigeria’s, and it is no template to copy. But it illustrates the point. Ordinary leaders presiding within strong institutions have often achieved more than gifted leaders struggling against weak ones. Neither leadership nor institutions alone explain national outcomes. They interact. Good leadership can strengthen institutions. Strong institutions can preserve the gains of good leadership. Weak institutions can undermine even sincere reformers. And institutions can fail in a subtler way. A country can possess every formal structure of a modern state—ministries, agencies, regulators, anti-corruption commissions—and still find that those structures do not perform their functions. Development researchers describe this as states that come to *look like* capable states without *acting* like them.15 The building is there. The work is not being done. The distinction is important. **Individuals create moments. Institutions create patterns.** ## A Different Way to Think The title of this book is intentionally unsettling. *Nobody Is the Problem.* It is not an attempt to deny responsibility. It is not an invitation to excuse corruption, poor leadership, misconduct, or institutional failure. It is not an argument against accountability. Individuals make choices, and those choices have consequences. Public officials remain accountable for the authority entrusted to them. Citizens remain responsible for the obligations of citizenship. The argument of this book is simply that if the same problems appear repeatedly across different administrations, generations, and personalities, then we should also examine the systems within which those individuals operate. This shift in perspective changes the conversation. Instead of asking only who occupies public office, we ask how public office is structured. Instead of asking only whether leaders are honest, we ask whether institutions reward honesty and detect misconduct. Instead of asking only whether citizens obey the law, we ask whether the law is applied consistently enough to deserve public confidence. Instead of asking only: **“Who failed?”** We should also ask: **“Why did the system allow this failure to occur—and why has it occurred before?”** Those two questions belong together. Without the first, we excuse misconduct. Without the second, we guarantee its repetition. ## But Someone Did Steal the Money A thoughtful reader may object at this point, and the objection deserves to be stated in its strongest form. *This is an excuse. Specific people stole specific money. Specific officials took* *bribes, inflated contracts, and abandoned projects. To say that “nobody is the* *problem” is to let them off the hook.* The objection is not imaginary, and Nigerians themselves give it weight. In a nationally representative survey conducted in mid-2024, eight in ten Nigerians said corruption had increased over the previous year—up from four in ten in 2017. Seven in ten said most or all police officials were involved in corruption; more than six in ten said the same of the Presidency, and more than half said so of judges and magistrates. Among those who had sought help from the police, two-thirds reported paying a bribe to get it.16 These findings should not be softened. Misconduct is real, and those who commit it are responsible for it. But look again at what the same survey reveals. The problem it describes is not confined to one office, one administration, or one group of individuals. It appears across the police, the legislature, the executive, the courts, the tax authorities, and local councils at the same time. And only one Nigerian in ten believed that ordinary people could report corruption without fear of retaliation.17 That is the signature of a system, not of a few bad actors. When misconduct is easy to commit, difficult to detect, rarely punished, and dangerous to report, it will be committed by whoever happens to hold office. Remove one official and another, facing the same incentives, will often make the same choices. This is why decades of replacing individuals—often with genuine public enthusiasm—have so rarely produced lasting change. The research on leadership points in the same direction. Leaders matter most precisely where institutions constrain them least.18 Weak institutions do not make individuals innocent. They make the nation dependent on the hope that whoever comes next will be better than whoever came before. So this book does not ask readers to stop holding people accountable. It asks them to demand accountability *and* to ask why accountability has so often failed to hold. ## The Book You Are About to Read This is not a book about politics alone. It is a book about the architecture of national life. We will begin by learning to see systems: how nations really work, why institutions matter more than individuals over time, and how lasting change actually happens. We will then examine Nigeria’s foundations: the history that shaped its institutions, the Constitution that gives them authority, and the unwritten rules and incentives that determine how they behave. We will also confront the strongest objection to this book’s title—corruption—and ask what the evidence says about how it is reduced. From there we turn to the institutions of national life. We will examine education because schools shape future citizens. We will examine healthcare because healthy populations expand national capability. We will examine the civil service because governments require professional administration. We will examine public finance because national priorities are expressed through budgets. We will examine justice because rights depend upon institutions capable of protecting them. We will examine politics and elections because the way leaders are chosen shapes the incentives they face once in office. We will examine security because freedom cannot flourish where fear dominates daily life. We will examine infrastructure because economic opportunity depends upon reliable systems. We will examine the private sector because enduring organizations reveal important lessons about institutional resilience. We will then consider how authority is shared across a federation and what citizens owe the institutions that serve them. Finally, we will look at what Nigeria already gets right, what other nations have learned, and how institutions can be reformed—before returning, in the last chapter, to the question with which this book begins. Throughout the journey, one question will remain constant: **How can institutions enable ordinary people to achieve extraordinary collective outcomes?** ## An Invitation This book does not claim to possess every answer. It asks readers to reconsider familiar questions. It invites policymakers to think institutionally rather than react episodically. It invites citizens to evaluate systems as well as personalities. It invites students to see governance not merely as politics, but as the design and performance of enduring institutions. Most importantly, it invites all of us to replace blame with diagnosis. Because accurate diagnosis is the beginning of meaningful reform. If we diagnose the wrong problem, even the best intentions will produce disappointing results. If we diagnose the right problem, lasting improvement becomes possible. ## The Architect’s Question Imagine you were asked not to govern Nigeria for four years, but to design Nigeria’s institutions for the next fifty. Which rules would you keep? Which incentives would you change? Which institutions would you strengthen? And how would you ensure that the country’s progress depended less on extraordinary individuals and more on systems capable of producing good outcomes consistently? Those are the questions that will guide the rest of this book. ## Looking Ahead Before we can redesign institutions, we must first learn to see them. Most of the systems that shape national life operate quietly, noticed only when they fail. The next chapter therefore steps back from personalities altogether and asks how nations really work—how countless rules, incentives, and organizations coordinate the daily efforts of millions of people. ## Institutional Mirror Before asking who should be held accountable for national outcomes, ask a more fundamental question: **What institutional arrangements consistently shape those outcomes—and how can they be strengthened?** The future of a nation is determined not only by the character of its people, but also by the quality of the institutions that allow that character to flourish.

> “The most powerful forces in a nation are often the ones its citizens cannot see. They are written into rules, repeated through habits, and reinforced by institutions.” ## The City That Never Stops Long before dawn, a city begins to wake. Electricians restore power after a night of repairs. Water treatment plants continue operating while most citizens sleep. Airport control towers guide arriving aircraft through the darkness. Police officers complete overnight patrols as new shifts prepare to begin. Nurses hand over patients to colleagues at the start of another day. Bakers remove fresh bread from ovens. Public transport operators prepare for the morning rush. By sunrise, millions of people begin moving. Children head to school. Businesses open their doors. Courts prepare their daily schedules. Hospitals receive new patients. Markets fill with buyers and sellers. Roads carry people toward work, opportunity, and responsibility. And in the background, money moves. A trader in Onitsha receives payment from a customer in Kano. A student’s fees reach a university account in seconds. A salary arrives at the end of the month. According to the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System, the digital payments it processed in 2024 were worth about ₦1.07 quadrillion, with some 11.2 billion transfers on its instant-payment platform alone.1 Almost none of the people involved gave a moment’s thought to the network of banks, switches, settlement rules, and standards that made each transfer possible. To most citizens, these activities appear ordinary. Yet together they represent one of humanity’s greatest achievements. Modern society functions because countless institutions perform thousands of interconnected tasks every single day. Most people notice them only when they fail. ## The Fish That Never Saw Water There is an old observation often attributed to different thinkers: *If you want to understand water, don’t ask the fish.* The fish has lived in water all its life. It swims through it every day. It depends on it completely. Yet because water is everywhere, it becomes almost invisible. Human beings experience systems in much the same way. We drive on roads designed by institutions we have never met. We obey laws written by people we will never know. We attend schools built upon educational philosophies we did not choose. We open bank accounts, apply for passports, pay taxes, seek justice, and vote in elections—all through systems that quietly shape our opportunities and constraints. Most days, we think about the people within those systems. Rarely do we think about the systems themselves. That is understandable. People have faces. Systems do not. Yet invisible does not mean unimportant. Gravity cannot be seen, but every building is designed around it. In the same way, institutions quietly shape the daily life of a nation, whether citizens notice them or not. ## The Invisible Architecture Imagine removing traffic regulations from a busy intersection. At first, experienced drivers may proceed cautiously. Within minutes, uncertainty grows. Congestion follows. Eventually, movement slows to confusion. The problem is not that drivers suddenly became incapable. The problem is that the rules coordinating their behaviour disappeared. Now imagine extending that idea beyond traffic. Remove reliable courts from commerce. Remove standards from education. Remove regulation from banking. Remove professional administration from government. Remove public health systems during a disease outbreak. Modern society would become unpredictable, not because people forgot how to work, but because the institutional framework that coordinated their efforts had weakened. Nigerians do not need to imagine what happens when a coordinating system falters. In 2024, the national electricity grid suffered nine system collapses—four total and five partial—according to the Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission.2 Each total collapse plunged much of the country into darkness. The response to that unreliability is equally revealing. The World Bank’s 2014 Enterprise Survey found that the average Nigerian firm experienced 384 power outages in a single year. Households and businesses responded by generating their own power. The World Bank estimates that more than 22 million generators are in use in Nigeria, with a combined capacity estimated at eight times the capacity connected to the national grid, and that Nigerians have spent some ₦3.7 trillion (about $12 billion) buying and running them.3 Consider what this means. When one public system does not perform reliably, millions of households and businesses are forced to become their own power companies—each buying fuel, maintaining machines, and absorbing costs that a functioning system would have shared. The failure of a single institution is multiplied across an entire economy. Institutions are the invisible architecture of national life. Like the foundations beneath a building, they are often overlooked precisely because they are expected to perform reliably. And like foundations, their weakness is felt in every room. ## Beyond Great Leaders History often celebrates extraordinary individuals. Visionary presidents. Influential judges. Innovative entrepreneurs. Respected teachers. Brilliant scientists. Their contributions deserve recognition. Yet no individual, however gifted, can educate an entire nation alone. No president can personally enforce every law. No judge can hear every dispute. No entrepreneur can create prosperity without functioning markets, reliable contracts, skilled workers, and stable financial systems. Consider a beautifully lit theatre. The audience applauds the actors. The lead performer receives flowers. Critics praise the performance. Few people leave discussing the lighting engineer, the stage manager, the costume department, the sound technician, or the rehearsals that made the evening possible. The visible performance depends on invisible systems. If the backstage organization collapses, even the most talented actors struggle to succeed. Nations operate in a similar way. Political leaders stand on the public stage. Behind them are civil servants, courts, schools, regulators, auditors, local governments, financial institutions, constitutions, traditions, and countless formal and informal rules. When these supporting structures function well, leadership is amplified. When they function poorly, leadership is constrained. **Leadership matters. Institutions determine whether leadership endures.** ## What Is a System? A system is more than a collection of parts. It is a set of relationships. A hospital is not merely a building filled with doctors. It is the interaction between medical training, funding, procurement, record-keeping, regulation, leadership, ethics, and patient trust. A university is not simply classrooms and lecturers. It is admissions, curriculum, research, governance, finance, accreditation, incentives, and culture working together. The systems thinker Donella Meadows argued that the behaviour of a system arises largely from its own structure—the way its parts are connected and the purposes they serve—rather than from the particular individuals or events that happen to pass through it.4 Change the people while leaving the structure intact, and the system will often go on producing the same results. A nation is no different. Government is only one institution among many. Families, businesses, religious communities, professional associations, schools, courts, markets, and civic organizations all interact to shape national outcomes. To understand Nigeria, we must study not only its leaders but also the relationships among its institutions. ## The Power of Coordination One musician can produce beautiful music. An orchestra requires something more. Each musician must understand the score. Each section must enter at the right moment. The conductor must coordinate rather than overpower. The audience hears a single performance, but that performance depends upon discipline, preparation, shared standards, and trust. Nations work in much the same way. Education prepares citizens. Healthcare protects them. Justice resolves disputes. Public finance allocates resources. Security preserves stability. Infrastructure connects communities. The private sector creates value. The civil service coordinates implementation. None of these institutions succeeds in isolation. Each depends upon the others. A weakness in one eventually affects them all. When the grid fails, hospitals run on diesel, factories raise prices, and small businesses close early. One institution’s problem becomes everyone’s cost. ## Incentives: The Quiet Architects of Behaviour People often imagine that behaviour is determined primarily by character. Character matters. But incentives matter too. A society that rewards honesty is likely to encourage more honesty. A workplace that promotes competence is more likely to attract competent people. A bureaucracy that rewards delay should not be surprised when delays become routine. Individuals respond to the environment around them. That observation does not excuse wrongdoing. It explains why certain behaviours become widespread while others remain rare. One of the most important tasks of institutional design is aligning incentives with the behaviours society wishes to encourage. ## Systems, Not Events Public debate often focuses on dramatic events. An election. A court judgment. A new policy. An economic crisis. A corruption scandal. These moments matter. But they are usually symptoms of deeper institutional patterns. ### Evidence Box: The Systems Behind the Headlines - **A bridge across six administrations.** A second bridge over the River Niger was reportedly first planned under the Babangida administration in the late 1980s and was flagged off as a public–private partnership under Obasanjo. Under Jonathan, a partnership arrangement involving the sovereign wealth fund was agreed in 2014 and early works began. The contract was cancelled for review in 2016. In 2018, a dedicated Presidential Infrastructure Development Fund was created; work resumed, and the bridge was commissioned on 23 May 2023.5 •**Thousands of unfinished projects.** In 2011 the Presidential Projects Assessment Committee, chaired by Ibrahim Bunu, counted 11,886 federal capital projects that had been started but not completed—many of them abandoned—and estimated that ₦7.78 trillion would be needed to finish them.6 •**The same pattern, year after year.** Since 2015, monitors from Tracka, a citizen project-tracking platform run by the civic organization BudgIT, have visited federally funded projects in communities across the country. Of the 2015 constituency projects they tracked, about one-third were completed. Of 852 projects from the 2016 budget, about 40 per cent. Of 1,404 federal projects tracked in 2023–24, about half—while 352 were either never executed or abandoned, after some ₦99.6 billion had been allocated to them. Of 2,760 projects from the 2024 budget, tracked across 30 states, again only about half showed evidence of delivery.7 - **A test of the teachers.** In 2017, the Kaduna State Government reported that about 21,780 of roughly 33,000 primary school teachers—around two- thirds—failed to reach the required score on an assessment based on primary four material.8 *Each of these was reported as news. Each is better understood as the output of a* *system.* ![Figure 2.1. Share of tracked federally funded projects found completed. The 2015 and 2016 figures cover constituency projects only. Source: BudgIT Tracka findings, as reported by TheCable (2016), Sahara Reporters (2017), The ICIR (2025) and BusinessDay (2026).](/static/book/fig-032-03.jpg)

Figure 2.1. Share of tracked federally funded projects found completed. The 2015 and 2016 figures cover constituency projects only. Source: BudgIT Tracka findings, as reported by TheCable (2016), Sahara Reporters (2017), The ICIR (2025) and BusinessDay (2026).

Look at each case again with systems in mind. The Second Niger Bridge was promised by leader after leader across more than three decades. The repeated delays cannot all be explained by the shortcomings of six different administrations. What changed at the end was the funding mechanism. The new fund, managed by the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority, was created, in the Authority’s own words, “to de-risk the projects and provide a funding mechanism to ensure timely completion.”9 The bridge was commissioned five years later. That does not prove the new mechanism alone explains completion, but it suggests where the obstacles lay: in how the project was financed and managed, not only in who was in charge. ![The Second Niger Bridge at Onitsha, January 2024. Photo: MikeJanetta / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.](/static/book/fig-033-04.jpg)

The Second Niger Bridge at Onitsha, January 2024. Photo: MikeJanetta / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Nearly twelve thousand abandoned projects cannot be explained by twelve thousand careless officials. Nor can a completion rate that has hovered between one-third and one-half across a decade of tracking, under different presidents, different legislatures, and different ministers. These figures point to how projects are planned, budgeted, procured, funded, and handed over when administrations change—to a system that makes starting a project far easier than finishing one. And the Kaduna results, which were disputed by the teachers’ union and met with protests,10 raise a question that goes beyond the individual teachers tested. What recruitment, training, certification, and promotion systems placed those teachers in front of children in the first place? Dismissing teachers may be one response. Unless the system that hired them changes, it may simply hire others like them. If we focus only on events, we risk treating symptoms while ignoring causes. Institutional thinking asks a different question: **What system consistently produces this outcome?** ## Why This Perspective Matters When we focus only on personalities, every election feels like starting over. When we understand systems, we begin asking different questions. How are decisions made? Who has authority? Who has oversight? What happens when rules are broken? Which incentives encourage integrity? Which incentives undermine it? How easily can institutions learn from mistakes? These questions move us beyond personalities toward the architecture of governance itself. Instead of searching constantly for exceptional individuals, we begin designing institutions that enable ordinary people to perform exceptionally. Instead of expecting every reform to depend upon one leader, we ask how reforms can survive changes in leadership. Instead of celebrating isolated success stories, we examine how successful systems can become ordinary practice. Nigeria already shows that this is possible. The same country whose grid struggles to stay on processes billions of electronic payments a year, most of them so reliably that nobody notices. The difference between the two is not the talent of the Nigerians who use them, or the intelligence of those who work in them. It is the design, incentives, and discipline of the systems themselves. Strong nations are not those that occasionally perform well. They are those whose institutions make good performance routine. That is the difference between isolated excellence and sustainable development. ## A Different Way to Think The most enduring changes in history have often come not from replacing every individual within a system but from redesigning the system so that ordinary people could succeed more consistently. This is why nations that build strong institutions are less dependent on extraordinary leaders. Their progress becomes repeatable. Their successes become sustainable. Their future becomes less fragile. ## The Architect’s Question Imagine that you cannot choose the next president, governor, minister, or public servant. The only power you have is to redesign the rules under which they will all operate. Which rules would you change first? And what kind of behaviour would those new rules encourage? ## Looking Ahead If institutions are the invisible architecture of society, then the next question becomes unavoidable. Who builds them? Who protects them? Who reforms them when they no longer serve the public well? The next chapter explores one of the most common misunderstandings in public life: The belief that nations are transformed primarily by extraordinary leaders. Leadership matters profoundly. But leadership alone is never enough. To understand why, we must examine the relationship between individuals and the institutions they inherit. ## Institutional Mirror Think about the institutions you interacted with today. The road you travelled. The electricity you used—or the generator you started when it failed. The bank that processed your payment. The internet that connected your devices. The school, hospital, court, office, or business that shaped your day. How many of them worked so well that you hardly noticed them? And how many became visible only when they failed? That is the nature of institutions. Their greatest success is often their quiet reliability.

> “The greatest legacy of a leader is not the number of problems solved during a tenure, but the number of problems that remain solved after the leader has gone.” ## The Search for a Saviour History is full of societies searching for extraordinary individuals. When economies falter, citizens search for a financial genius. When crime rises, they search for a fearless commander. When corruption spreads, they search for an incorruptible reformer. When institutions weaken, they search for a political messiah. Nigeria is no exception. Every election season produces familiar language. “This is the leader we have been waiting for.” “Only this person can rescue the nation.” “Everything depends on this election.” These statements are understandable. They reflect genuine hope and a desire for change. But they also reveal a deeper assumption—that the destiny of a nation rests primarily on the qualities of one individual. It is an attractive idea. It is also an incomplete one. ## The Day After Imagine a nation waking up the morning after a new president has been sworn into office. The campaign has ended. The celebrations have faded. The promises have been made. Yet across the country, life continues much as it did the day before. Flights still depart according to schedule. Hospitals continue treating patients. Judges hear cases already before them. Teachers return to their classrooms. Banks open their doors. Ports receive cargo. Power stations continue generating electricity. Tax officials process revenue. Local governments provide essential services. The president has changed. The nation has not stopped. This simple reality reveals one of the most important truths about governance. No leader governs alone. Every administration inherits institutions that were built, neglected, strengthened, or weakened long before it arrived. The quality of those institutions often determines how much any leader can accomplish. ## Why We Believe in Strong Leaders Human beings naturally gravitate toward stories with heroes. Heroes simplify complexity. A single face is easier to remember than an institutional framework. A campaign speech is easier to follow than a constitutional debate. We remember presidents more easily than constitutions, reformers more easily than the civil servants who implemented their reforms, and entrepreneurs more easily than the systems that allowed their businesses to grow. Leadership is visible. Institutions often are not. It is emotionally satisfying to believe that one exceptional person can transform an entire society. And sometimes remarkable leaders do accelerate change. History offers many examples of courageous individuals who inspired reform, expanded opportunity, or guided nations through moments of crisis. Leadership matters. Character matters. Vision matters. But none of these qualities operate in isolation. Every leader governs within an environment of laws, institutions, incentives, traditions, bureaucracies, and public expectations. A leader may announce reform. Only institutions can implement it consistently. ## Leadership Has Limits Imagine appointing the finest surgeon in the world to a hospital with no electricity, broken equipment, inconsistent medical supplies, and unpaid staff. The surgeon’s skill remains extraordinary. Yet the outcomes will almost certainly fall short of what that same surgeon could achieve in a well-managed hospital. The lesson is obvious. Performance depends not only on talent but also on the environment in which talent is exercised. The same principle applies to governance. A visionary education minister cannot transform schools without capable teachers, functioning ministries, reliable funding, and effective accountability. A determined police chief cannot guarantee public safety without professional recruitment, modern training, community trust, and an independent justice system. A finance minister cannot ensure fiscal discipline if institutions responsible for budgeting, auditing, procurement, and revenue collection remain weak. Capable leaders can improve weak systems. But weak systems also limit capable leaders. Recognizing this does not diminish leadership. It places leadership in its proper context. ## When a Leader Clearly Mattered Fairness requires us to begin with the strongest case against this chapter’s argument. At the start of the 2000s, counterfeit medicines were a national emergency in Nigeria. Under the leadership of Professor Dora Akunyili as Director-General of the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control, the agency confronted counterfeiters with unusual determination. According to a report issued by the agency in 2006, the average share of counterfeit drugs in circulation fell from about 41 per cent in 2001 to about 16.7 per cent.1 No honest account of that period can pretend that leadership was irrelevant. A determined individual, willing to accept great personal risk, changed what a public institution was prepared to do. But the case raises the question this chapter is about. What happens after such a leader leaves? If the gains rested mainly on one person’s courage, they would always be vulnerable to the arrival of a less determined successor. If they were built into inspection systems, enforcement procedures, professional standards, and public expectations, they would have a far better chance of enduring. The value of a great leader is measured twice: once by what is achieved during the tenure, and again by what survives it. **Leadership can accelerate progress. Institutions determine whether that progress lasts.** ## The Empty Chair Every institution eventually faces the same moment. The founder retires. The president leaves office. The chief executive steps down. The head teacher completes a distinguished career. The chief judge reaches retirement. An empty chair waits for someone new. At that moment, an institution reveals its true character. If everything depends on the individual who has just departed, uncertainty follows. Decisions slow. Confidence weakens. Progress stalls while everyone waits to see what the new leader will do. But if the institution has been built upon clear values, capable people, sound systems, and established procedures, the transition becomes far less dramatic. The chair changes. The mission continues. Lagos State offers an example. When a new administration took office in 1999, the state’s internally generated revenue was reported at about ₦600 million a month. Tax administration was reorganized, and in 2006 the revenue board was made an autonomous, self-accounting agency. By 2006 it averaged about ₦5 billion a month, and early in 2007 it was reported at between ₦7 billion and ₦8 billion. The growth did not stop when the administration that began the reform left office. It continued through the tenures of three further governors. In 2024, the Lagos State Internal Revenue Service alone collected more than ₦1 trillion—a first for a sub-national revenue agency in Nigeria.2 ![Figure 3.1. Lagos State internally generated revenue, average per month, 1999, 2006, and 2024 (the 2024 figure is the revenue service’s annual collection divided by twelve). Sources: BusinessDay; ThisDay, February 19, 2025, as cited in the notes.](/static/book/fig-041-05.jpg)

Figure 3.1. Lagos State internally generated revenue, average per month, 1999, 2006, and 2024 (the 2024 figure is the revenue service’s annual collection divided by twelve). Sources: BusinessDay; ThisDay, February 19, 2025, as cited in the notes.

Political continuity also played a part; all four governors came from the same political tradition. But a reform that survives four changes of leadership has clearly become something more than one leader’s personal project. It has become part of how the state works. Institutions provide continuity. They preserve knowledge. They establish procedures. They create expectations. Most importantly, they reduce the need to begin again every time leadership changes. A nation that depends entirely on extraordinary individuals must constantly hope for another extraordinary individual. A nation with strong institutions can continue progressing even through ordinary leadership. That is institutional resilience. ## Leadership Is the Beginning, Not the Destination None of this means leadership is unimportant. On the contrary, every meaningful institutional reform begins with leadership. Someone identifies a problem. Someone challenges complacency. Someone persuades others that change is possible. Someone accepts responsibility for acting. Without leadership, institutions become rigid. Without institutions, leadership becomes temporary. Nigeria’s Treasury Single Account illustrates the partnership. For years, federal revenues were scattered across many separate accounts held by ministries, departments, and agencies, making it difficult to see or control the government’s own cash. The single-account reform was mandated under the Jonathan administration, which began a pilot in 2012 covering just over a hundred agencies. Full implementation across every federal agency was then ordered by treasury circular on 7 August 2015 under its political rival. Some twenty thousand separate bank accounts were closed, and by February 2017 the Accountant-General of the Federation reported a consolidated balance of about ₦5.2 trillion, with savings of around ₦4.7 billion a month in bank charges.3 The policy was not without controversy, particularly over the fees paid to the private firm that operated its collection platform. But its history makes the point. A reform conceived under one government was completed under another. It outlived the administration that designed it because it had become a system, not a slogan. The relationship between leadership and institutions is not one of competition. It is one of partnership. Leadership provides direction. Institutions provide continuity. Leadership creates momentum. Institutions preserve it. Leadership inspires people. Institutions organize people. When these two forces work together, reform becomes sustainable. ## Leaders Who Build Beyond Themselves The most admired leaders in history are often remembered not simply because they exercised power effectively, but because they strengthened institutions that continued functioning after they left office. When courts remain independent after a president leaves office… When public finances remain transparent after a finance minister retires… When schools continue improving after an education commissioner completes a term… When businesses thrive beyond the tenure of their founders… We are witnessing the success of institutions rather than the charisma of individuals. Consider the Bank Verification Number. Launched by the Central Bank of Nigeria and the country’s banks on 14 February 2014, it gave every enrolled bank customer a unique biometric identity.4 It has since continued through changes of central bank governor and changes of federal government. By the end of 2025, about 67.8 million people had enrolled.5 Few of them could name the officials who introduced it. They do not need to. The reform no longer depends on its founders, because it has become part of the infrastructure of everyday banking. That is what institutionalization looks like. Such leaders ask different questions. Not: **“How can I solve every problem?”** But: **“How can I build institutions that continue solving problems after I am gone?”** That shift changes everything. Instead of accumulating authority, they distribute responsibility. Instead of centralizing every decision, they develop capable teams. Instead of relying on memory, they document procedures. Instead of rewarding loyalty alone, they reward competence and integrity. Instead of creating dependence on themselves, they prepare others to lead. If every reform collapses when one person leaves office, the reform was never fully institutionalized. Strong institutions do not eliminate the importance of leadership. They multiply its impact. Leadership reaches its highest expression when it makes itself less indispensable. ## The Danger of Personal Rule A nation that depends entirely on one remarkable leader is a nation living dangerously. What happens when that leader retires? What happens when the successor lacks the same ability? What happens when unforeseen crises arise? If progress depends on personality alone, progress becomes fragile. The same is true of safeguards that depend on personal restraint rather than binding rules. In 2004, Nigeria created an Excess Crude Account to save oil revenue earned above the budgeted price—a cushion for the years when prices fell. By 2008, the account held more than $20 billion. Yet no law established it; the Constitution names only the Federation Account and the Consolidated Revenue Fund as the homes of federal revenue.6 Then the pressures began. State governors went to court to demand that the savings be shared. Withdrawals continued across successive administrations, some for purposes that could be defended and others that were disputed. By March 2020, the Accountant-General told the Senate that the balance stood at $71.8 million.7 In July 2022, it was reported at $376,655.8 No single leader emptied the account. That is precisely the lesson. It survived only for as long as those in power chose to leave it alone, because nothing sufficiently binding prevented them from doing otherwise. A safeguard that depends on the self-restraint of whoever holds office is not really a safeguard at all. Crises make the point from the other direction. During natural disasters, economic shocks, public health emergencies, or security threats, citizens rightly look to leaders for reassurance, clarity, and decisive action. But even in crisis, leaders depend upon institutions that already exist. When a traveller carrying the Ebola virus arrived in Lagos in July 2014, Nigeria had never faced the disease. What it did have was an Emergency Operations Centre, established in 2012 to coordinate the campaign against polio. Within days, that structure was repurposed: polio staff and systems were redeployed to trace contacts, manage cases, and coordinate the response. In total, 894 contacts were identified and followed. The outbreak was limited to 20 cases and 8 deaths, and investigators credited the rapid, institution-based response with helping to contain it early.9 ![A resident of the Nigeria Field Epidemiology and Laboratory Training Program administers oral polio vaccine in Pakka, Adamawa State, January 2014. Photo: CDC Global / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.](/static/book/fig-045-06.jpg)

A resident of the Nigeria Field Epidemiology and Laboratory Training Program administers oral polio vaccine in Pakka, Adamawa State, January 2014. Photo: CDC Global / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

A crisis rarely creates institutional strength. It reveals whether that strength already exists. ### Evidence Box: Reforms That Lasted—and One That Did Not - **Lagos State revenue:** about ₦600 million a month in 1999; around ₦6 billion a month by 2006; more than ₦1 trillion collected by the state revenue service in 2024, across four governors.10 •**Treasury Single Account:** piloted in 2012, completed from 2015 under a rival administration; about 20,000 accounts closed and ₦5.2 trillion consolidated by February 2017.11 •**Bank Verification Number:** launched 2014; about 67.8 million enrolments by the end of 2025.12 •**Ebola response, 2014:** a polio-era emergency centre repurposed within days; outbreak limited to 20 cases.13 •**Excess Crude Account:** more than $20 billion in 2008; $376,655 in July 2022.14 *The reforms that lasted were embedded in agencies, laws, and everyday* *systems. The one that collapsed depended on the restraint of whoever held* *power.* Institutions exist to reduce fragility. They preserve standards, distribute responsibility, create continuity, and ensure that public life does not begin anew with every transition of power. Strong institutions do not eliminate the need for capable leaders. They make good leadership more effective and bad leadership less destructive. ## The Same Lesson in Every Sector The principle applies everywhere. A school succeeds when excellence becomes part of its culture rather than the gift of one exceptional principal. A hospital becomes trusted when quality care survives changes in medical leadership. A ministry becomes effective when policies continue regardless of who occupies the minister’s office. A company earns lasting respect when customers continue receiving excellent service after its founder has departed. One reason successful companies endure is that they invest in systems. Policies are documented. Responsibilities are clearly defined. Financial controls exist regardless of who occupies the chief executive’s office. Succession is planned. Performance is measured. Knowledge is transferred. No serious organization expects one individual to remember everything or make every decision indefinitely. The organization survives because its systems are stronger than any single personality. Public institutions require the same discipline. The sectors may differ. The institutional principle remains the same. ## The Nigerian Opportunity Nigeria has produced distinguished leaders in government, business, academia, medicine, engineering, law, faith communities, civil society, science, technology, and the arts. The country has never lacked talent. Nor has it lacked reforms that work. The examples in this chapter—a revenue service, a payments identity, a consolidated treasury, an emergency operations centre—show that Nigerian institutions can be built to outlast the people who create them. The greater challenge has been ensuring that individual excellence consistently becomes institutional excellence. When successful practices remain tied to individuals, progress is difficult to sustain. When they become embedded in institutions, they become part of the nation’s permanent capacity. That transformation—from personal achievement to institutional capability—is one of the central themes of this book, and the transition every developing nation must eventually make. ## A Different Way to Think Perhaps the highest compliment a society can pay a leader is not: **“We cannot survive without you.”** Perhaps it is: **“The systems you strengthened continue to serve us long after your departure.”** That is the difference between governing for applause and governing for posterity. It is leadership measured in decades rather than election cycles—leadership that plants trees under whose shade future generations will sit. ## The Architect’s Question Imagine you are advising a newly elected president. You have only one recommendation to offer. Would you advise the president to solve as many immediate problems as possible? Or would you advise building institutions that enable future leaders—and ordinary public servants—to solve problems more effectively, even decades later? The answer to that question reveals how we understand leadership itself. ## Looking Ahead If institutions matter more than personalities in the long run, another question naturally follows. How are strong institutions created? Do they emerge by chance? Are they simply inherited? Or can they be deliberately built, strengthened, and reformed? The next chapter examines how nations actually change—and why lasting transformation is rarely as sudden as it appears. ## Institutional Mirror Think of an organization you admire. Now imagine that its most respected leader resigned tomorrow. Would the organization continue to perform well? If the answer is yes, its strength lies in its institutions. If the answer is no, its greatest challenge may not be leadership—it may be the absence of systems capable of sustaining excellence. Then think about the best leader you have ever worked with, learned from, or admired, and ask: **Did that leader leave behind a stronger institution—or simply fond memories?**

sections.opening: People love stories of sudden transformation. A struggling business becomes a global company. A poor nation becomes prosperous. A failing institution becomes a model of excellence.
sections.markdown:
> “Lasting national change rarely arrives like lightning. More often, it is built like a cathedral—one stone, one generation, and one institution at a time.” ## The Overnight Success That Took Decades People love stories of sudden transformation. A struggling business becomes a global company. A poor nation becomes prosperous. A failing institution becomes a model of excellence. Looking back, these changes often appear dramatic. Living through them, however, is very different. Most lasting transformations are slow. They begin with reforms that attract little attention. A law is amended. A public institution is reorganized. A new accountability mechanism is introduced. A generation of professionals is trained. Budgets become more transparent. Courts become slightly more independent. Schools gradually improve. None of these changes dominates the headlines. Yet together they reshape a nation. History often remembers the breakthrough. It forgets the decades of preparation. ## The Telephone Revolution That Was Not Sudden Few changes in Nigerian life have felt more sudden than the arrival of the mobile phone. At the end of the 1990s, Nigeria had roughly 400,000 working telephone lines for a population of well over 100 million people. Growth had averaged about 10,000 new lines a year for four decades. More than ten million people were reported to be waiting for a connection, some of them for years.1 Then, in January 2001, the government auctioned digital mobile licences. Within a year, the new operators had signed up more than 1.5 million subscribers. By 2003 there were about 3.1 million; by 2008, about 60 million.2 By May 2026, the Nigerian Communications Commission counted nearly 190 million active mobile subscriptions.3 ![Figure 4.1. Fixed telephone lines before liberalization (1999) and active mobile subscriptions in selected years, in millions. Subscriptions count lines, not people. Sources: Nigerian Communications Commission; Techpoint Africa; Innovation Village.](/static/book/fig-051-07.jpg)

Figure 4.1. Fixed telephone lines before liberalization (1999) and active mobile subscriptions in selected years, in millions. Subscriptions count lines, not people. Sources: Nigerian Communications Commission; Techpoint Africa; Innovation Village.

It looked like a revolution that happened overnight. It was not. The regulator that made it possible, the Nigerian Communications Commission, had been created by decree in 1992.4 An earlier attempt to sell licences was cancelled in 2000 amid doubts about its integrity. A reconstituted Commission then designed a public auction, published its rules and prequalification requirements in advance, and engaged independent consultants to run it. Each licence was priced at $285 million.5 In 2003, the National Assembly passed the Nigerian Communications Act, which put the regulator and the liberalized market on a firm legal footing.6 The change Nigerians experienced in a few years rested on a decade of institution-building that few of them ever saw: a regulator, a set of rules, a credible process, and a law. Remove any one of those, and the “overnight” revolution would almost certainly have taken far longer—or not happened at all. ![Computer Village, Ikeja, Lagos, 2019, a major market for mobile phones and accessories. Photo: Lightfast Media / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.](/static/book/fig-052-08.jpg)

Computer Village, Ikeja, Lagos, 2019, a major market for mobile phones and accessories. Photo: Lightfast Media / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

## A Generation Against a Virus Public health offers an even longer example. In 1996, African heads of state committed themselves to eradicating polio, and the “Kick Polio Out of Africa” campaign began. At the time, the disease was estimated to paralyse some 75,000 children across the continent every year.7 Nigeria became one of the last places on earth where wild poliovirus still circulated. Its last case was recorded in 2016. In August 2020, after the required years without a single case, the African region was declared free of wild poliovirus.8 That achievement belongs to no single government, minister, or donor. It was the product of nearly a quarter of a century of vaccination campaigns, surveillance systems, laboratory networks, community engagement, and coordination structures—including the emergency operations centre whose later role in containing Ebola we saw in the previous chapter. It survived changes of president, changes of health minister, and periods of fierce local resistance. It was not a breakthrough. It was an accumulation. ## Why Revolutions Rarely Finish the Job History contains many revolutions. Some overthrew kings. Others ended military rule. Some replaced constitutions. Others transformed economies. Revolutions can remove governments. They cannot, by themselves, build capable institutions. A new flag does not create an effective civil service. A new anthem does not produce honest procurement systems. A new president does not automatically create an independent judiciary. Nigeria knows this lesson from its own history. Several of its military governments came to power promising to correct the failures of those before them. When the army overthrew the civilian government on 31 December 1983, for instance, it justified its intervention by pointing to corruption, economic mismanagement, and the incompetence of civilian rulers.9 The promise of sudden correction was powerful, and many citizens initially welcomed it. Yet across roughly three decades of military government, the problems each intervention promised to fix—corruption, weak administration, economic fragility—proved remarkably durable. Whatever judgement one reaches about individual regimes, the broader lesson is hard to avoid. Seizing power is fast. Building institutions is slow. And the first does not guarantee the second. Political transitions can create opportunities. Institutional development determines whether those opportunities endure. ## Historical Lens: Rebuilding After Crisis Different countries have emerged from periods of conflict, authoritarian rule, or economic hardship through very different paths. Yet comparative research reveals a recurring lesson: durable progress tends to depend less on dramatic moments and more on sustained improvements in institutions. Some strengthened their civil service before pursuing ambitious economic reforms. Others invested heavily in education and administrative capacity. Some focused on judicial independence and regulatory stability. None followed exactly the same path. What they shared was persistence. Institutional reform became a long-term commitment rather than a short-term political slogan. For Nigeria, the lesson is not that another country’s model can be copied wholesale. It is that enduring national renewal usually requires patient, cumulative work rather than expectations of instant transformation. ## The Power of Incremental Reform Incremental change is often misunderstood. It is mistaken for weakness. Yet many of the world’s strongest institutions evolved through continuous improvement rather than constant reinvention. An effective tax authority is not created in a single year. A trusted court system is not built in one administration. A professional public service develops through consistent recruitment, training, evaluation, and accountability over many years. Nigeria’s 2015 general election shows what accumulated reform can make possible. On 28 March 2015, for the first time in the country’s history, an incumbent president was defeated at the polls—and conceded.10 That moment is remembered for the decision of one man to accept the result. But it rested on years of less visible work by the electoral commission, including permanent voter cards and electronic card readers used to verify voters at polling units. Observers credited these tools with making it far harder to inflate vote totals, and credited the commission’s leadership with holding firm on them under pressure.11 The lesson is not that Nigerian elections were thereby perfected. Later elections have produced their own disputes, and electoral institutions, like all institutions, can regress as well as improve. The lesson is that a historic political moment was made possible by patient, technical, institutional reform that preceded it. Development researchers have studied how this kind of change actually happens. Their conclusion is that capability in public institutions is rarely built by importing a ready-made blueprint and imposing it all at once. It is built by identifying specific problems, trying solutions, learning from what fails, and adjusting—again and again—with the involvement of the people who must make the solutions work.12 Progress is often invisible until enough improvements accumulate to become unmistakable. ### Evidence Box: “Sudden” Changes That Took Years - **Mobile telephony:** regulator created in 1992; failed licensing attempt cancelled in 2000; transparent auction in January 2001; enabling Act in 2003; about 400,000 lines in 1999 grew to nearly 190 million mobile subscriptions by 2026.13 - **Polio:** continental commitment in 1996; Nigeria’s last wild case in 2016; African region declared free in August 2020.14 •**Elections:** permanent voter cards and card readers introduced ahead of the 2015 polls; first defeat of an incumbent president in March 2015.15 •**Banking:** minimum capital raised from ₦2 billion to ₦25 billion in 2004–05, reducing the number of banks from 89 to 25; further crises followed, and a new recapitalization, with minimums of ₦50 billion to ₦500 billion, was launched in 2024.16 *Each change looked sudden to those who lived through it. Each was the product* *of years of institutional preparation—and each still requires maintenance.* ## Reform Is Never Finished The banking story in that evidence box carries a warning. The consolidation of 2004 and 2005 was one of the most dramatic reforms in Nigeria’s economic history. In little more than a year, a crowded and fragile banking sector of 89 institutions was reduced to 25 better-capitalized banks.17 Yet within a few years several banks were in serious difficulty, and a state asset- management company was created in 2010 to absorb their bad loans. In 2024, the Central Bank launched another recapitalization, raising minimum capital requirements once again.18 This does not mean the earlier reform failed. It means that institutions, like buildings, require maintenance. Rules that fit one economy must be revised as the economy changes. Supervisors must keep pace with the banks they supervise. A reform that is treated as a single event, rather than the start of a continuing process, will eventually be overtaken by the problems it was designed to solve. Lasting change is not a destination a nation reaches. It is a discipline a nation maintains. ## Why Patience Is Not Passivity Calling for patience does not mean accepting failure. Patience without action becomes complacency. Action without patience often becomes instability. Institutional reform requires both urgency and endurance. Citizens are right to demand better performance. Leaders are right to pursue reform. But both should recognize that the deepest improvements are usually measured not only by what changes today, but by what continues improving tomorrow. The mobile telephone, the defeat of polio, and the peaceful transfer of power in 2015 all required people who were impatient with the status quo. They also required institutions that kept working long after the initial enthusiasm had faded. ## A Different Way to Think The question is not whether Nigeria can change. Nigeria’s own history shows that it can. The better question is: **What kind of change lasts?** The answer rarely lies in replacing one set of personalities with another. It lies in creating institutions that improve, adapt, and endure across generations. The future belongs to societies that prepare for challenges before they become emergencies. That is the work of institutional design. ## Looking Ahead If lasting change is built one institution at a time, then every reform begins with an inheritance. No generation starts from nothing. It receives institutions shaped by those who came before—some strong, some fragile, many still unfinished. That is where our attention now turns: to Nigeria itself, its history, its constitutional evolution, and the foundations upon which its present institutions stand. ## Institutional Mirror Think of a reform you have seen announced with great enthusiasm. Was it designed to produce a headline—or to keep improving long after the announcement was forgotten? Now think of a change in your own life that you take for granted—the phone in your pocket, perhaps. **How many years of unseen institutional work made that ordinary thing possible?** The difference between those two kinds of reform is the difference between a moment and a transformation.
