sections.markdown:
## Part II — Diagnosing Nigeria > “No nation can reform what it refuses to understand. Diagnosis is not an act of pessimism; it is the beginning of responsible hope.” Every nation carries a history that continues to influence its present. Some institutions evolve gradually over centuries. Others are created during moments of crisis, negotiation, or political transition. Nigeria’s institutions bear the imprint of indigenous traditions, colonial administration, constitutional experiments, military rule, democratic renewal, and decades of economic and social transformation. To understand the Nigeria of today, we must first understand the institutional journey that produced it. This is not a search for blame. History cannot be changed. But institutions can. The chapters in this part examine the foundations of Nigeria’s public life—not to condemn the past, but to discover the lessons that can strengthen the future. Only when we understand how institutions were built, why they evolved as they did, and where they have succeeded or struggled can we begin the work of meaningful reform. --- > “History is not a prison from which a nation cannot escape. It is the blueprint that explains why the building stands as it does.” ## We Did Not Begin Where We Are No nation appears fully formed. Every country is the product of countless decisions made over generations—some deliberate, some accidental, some visionary, and some deeply flawed. Constitutions are negotiated. Borders are drawn. Institutions are established. Economies evolve. Cultures interact. Conflicts reshape priorities. Each generation inherits a nation it did not create and leaves behind one it has, in some measure, transformed. Nigeria is no exception. To understand today’s Nigeria, we must resist the temptation to begin with today’s headlines. Modern Nigeria is the outcome of centuries of political organization, trade, migration, cultural exchange, colonial administration, constitutional development, military intervention, democratic transition, and continuous adaptation. Understanding that journey is essential—not because history excuses present failures, but because it explains the foundations upon which present institutions were built. ## Before There Was Nigeria Long before the name Nigeria appeared on maps, the land it now describes was home to diverse societies with their own political traditions, systems of justice, methods of trade, and forms of community leadership. Across different regions emerged kingdoms, emirates, city-states, and communities. Trade connected many of these societies across West Africa and beyond. Ideas, religions, technologies, and commercial relationships crossed political boundaries long before colonial rule. Their institutions took strikingly different forms. Some were centralized. The Oyo Empire, which reached the height of its power between roughly 1650 and 1750, was the most important and authoritative of the early Yoruba states.1 Yet even its ruler, the *alaafin*, did not govern without limits. Historians describe a council of hereditary kingmakers, the Oyo Mesi, led by the Basorun, who could reject a ruler judged tyrannical or unfit; by custom, a rejected alaafin was expected to take his own life.2 Power at the centre was real, but it was bounded by institutions designed to restrain it. Others were deliberately decentralized. Among the Igbo, communities lived in self-governing villages or federations of villages, and authority was dispersed among societies of elders and age-grade associations that shared the functions of government.3 In parts of the Niger Delta and the Cross River region, similar arrangements prevailed, with secret societies playing a prominent role in administration. These institutions differed widely, but they shared one important characteristic. They reflected the realities of the societies that created them. This reminds us of two principles that will recur throughout this book. The first is that institutional life in Nigeria did not begin with colonial administration or with independence. Nigeria inherited multiple traditions of governance—including traditions of accountability, consultation, and limits on rulers. The second is that **institutions are not abstract ideas. They are human responses to practical challenges.** ## The Colonial Encounter and the Birth of a Modern State The modern Nigerian state did not emerge from a single community, language, or political tradition. It was formed through a gradual process of political consolidation under British colonial administration. On 1 January 1914, the Northern and Southern Protectorates were merged into the Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria, governed from Lagos.4 ![A building described by its photographer as Frederick Lugard’s office at the time of the 1914 amalgamation, photographed in 2024. Photo: Harriwillz / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.](/static/book/fig-062-09.jpg)

A building described by its photographer as Frederick Lugard’s office at the time of the 1914 amalgamation, photographed in 2024. Photo: Harriwillz / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The colonial period marked one of the most consequential institutional turning points in Nigerian history. Colonial authorities did not merely establish political control. They introduced new administrative structures, legal frameworks, revenue systems, and relationships between the state and society. The system most associated with the period was indirect rule: local government was left in the hands of traditional rulers, operating under the supervision of British officers. It worked most smoothly in the northern emirates, where centralized administrative structures already existed. Where such structures did not exist, it rested on weaker foundations, and the British did not always understand the customs they claimed to be preserving.5 Some institutions were designed primarily to maintain order and facilitate administration. Others supported commerce, taxation, transportation, or resource extraction. These arrangements reflected the priorities of the colonial government, which did not always align with the long-term objective of building a self-governing democratic state. The new political entity was designed primarily for administrative efficiency rather than national identity. That distinction would have lasting consequences. The architecture of representative government came late. A legislative council with a handful of elected members from Lagos and Calabar was created in 1922, but its powers were limited and the northern provinces lay outside its control. Regional assemblies followed in 1946; a central House of Representatives in 1951. Only in 1954 did a constitution create a fully federal system of three regions, each with its own premier, cabinet, legislature, and civil service.6 The regional structure that would dominate the politics of the First Republic was therefore barely six years old at independence. Understanding these complexities is essential. History becomes less useful when it is reduced to heroes and villains. Its greater value lies in showing how institutional choices create enduring consequences. The challenge before later generations was not simply to govern a territory. It was to build a shared national project among peoples whose institutional experiences had often developed independently. ## Independence and a New Responsibility When Nigeria attained independence on 1 October 1960, optimism was widespread.7 The country possessed abundant natural resources, a growing educated class, vibrant regional economies, and considerable international goodwill. Its economy rested largely on agriculture. In the first half of the 1960s, agricultural products accounted for about four-fifths of the country’s exports, and agriculture produced well over half of national output.8 Political authority changed hands. Institutional responsibility did as well. The new nation inherited administrative structures, legal traditions, educational systems, public services, and constitutional arrangements that required adaptation to the realities of an independent, democratic society. Building national unity across immense linguistic, cultural, and religious diversity required institutions capable of managing differences peacefully while promoting a shared civic identity. Economic development demanded public institutions that could transform natural resources into broad-based prosperity. Democratic governance required constitutions that balanced representation, accountability, and stability. These were not uniquely Nigerian challenges. Many newly independent states confronted similar questions. What differed were the institutional choices made in response. Political sovereignty had been achieved. Institutional consolidation had only begun. ## The Arrival of Oil One development would reshape those choices more than almost any other. Commercial quantities of oil were first discovered at Oloibiri in 1956, and exports began in 1958.9 Within two decades, the economy had been transformed. By 1974, oil accounted for more than 80 per cent of federal revenues and more than 90 per cent of export earnings.10 Non-oil exports, which had dominated the economy at independence, have accounted for less than a tenth of total exports since the mid-1970s.11 Oil brought enormous resources. It also changed the relationship between the state and its citizens. A government funded mainly by taxes must persuade, bargain with, and answer to the people who pay them. A government funded mainly by oil revenue collected at the centre faces weaker pressure of that kind. Scholars of resource-rich countries have documented how such revenue can weaken accountability, concentrate power, and intensify competition for control of the centre.12 This does not mean oil determined Nigeria’s fate. Some resource-rich countries have built strong institutions. But it helps explain why the struggle for control of the federal government—and of the revenue it distributes—became such a central feature of Nigerian politics. ## Years of Transition Nigeria’s post-independence history included periods of democratic government, military administration, civil war, constitutional reform, economic restructuring, and democratic restoration. Each period left an institutional legacy. The very shape of the federation changed repeatedly. Nigeria entered independence with three regions; a fourth, the Mid-Western Region, was created in 1963. In May 1967, on the eve of a civil war that would last until 1970, the regions were abolished and replaced by twelve states. Seven more followed in 1976, two in 1987, nine in 1991, and six in 1996, producing the thirty-six states that exist today.13 ![Figure 5.1. Number of regions or states in Nigeria, 1960–2026. Sources: as cited in the notes.](/static/book/fig-066-10.jpg)

Figure 5.1. Number of regions or states in Nigeria, 1960–2026. Sources: as cited in the notes.

### Evidence Box: Turning Points in Nigeria’s Institutional Inheritance - **1914:** Northern and Southern Protectorates amalgamated (1 January).14 •**1922–1954:** From a limited legislative council to a fully federal system of three regions.15 •**1956–1958:** Oil discovered at Oloibiri; exports begin.16 •**1960:** Independence (1 October); agriculture provides about four-fifths of exports.17 •**1963–1996:** From four regions to thirty-six states—every change after 1963 decreed by a military government.18 •**1974:** Oil provides over 80 per cent of federal revenue and over 90 per cent of export earnings.19 *Each of these was a choice, or the consequence of one. Each continues to shape* *the institutions Nigerians live with today.* One feature of that history deserves emphasis. Every change to the number of states after 1963 was made by a military government. The structure of the federation—how many units it has, how they are funded, and how much they depend on the centre—was shaped less by negotiation among citizens than by decree. Some reforms strengthened public administration. Others centralized authority. Some expanded participation. Others constrained it. Some institutions demonstrated resilience despite political change. Others struggled to adapt. History therefore becomes more than a sequence of governments. It becomes a record of institutional choices and their long-term consequences. ## The Institutions That Endured Despite periods of political uncertainty, many Nigerian institutions continued to function. Schools continued educating new generations. Universities produced scholars, professionals, and innovators. Courts continued interpreting the law. Businesses created employment and investment. Religious and traditional institutions remained influential within communities. Professional associations upheld standards within their respective fields. These examples remind us that nations are rarely defined solely by their moments of crisis. They are also shaped by the institutions that continue serving society despite changing political circumstances. Institutional resilience often receives less attention than institutional failure. Yet both deserve careful study. ## Inherited—But Not Fixed One temptation in public discourse is to explain every contemporary challenge by appealing to history. Colonialism. Military rule. Constitutional design. Ethnic diversity. Oil. Each undoubtedly influenced Nigeria’s development. But history explains. It does not excuse. One of the most persistent misunderstandings in public debate is the belief that inherited institutions permanently determine a nation’s future. History suggests otherwise. Institutions influence possibilities. They do not eliminate choice. Countries revise constitutions. They reform public services. They modernize regulatory systems. They strengthen courts. They redesign fiscal arrangements. They expand educational opportunities. The institutional inheritance of one generation becomes the reform agenda of the next. The question is therefore not whether history matters. It does. The more important question is whether today’s institutions are learning from history or merely repeating it. ## The Historical Lens Every generation receives three inheritances. The first is history—the events that cannot be changed. The second is institutions—the rules and organizations that can be reformed. The third is responsibility—the choices that determine what will be passed to future generations. History explains where a nation begins. Institutions determine how it functions. Citizens and leaders together decide where it goes next. ## A Nation Still Being Built Many nations imagine themselves as finished products. Nigeria is better understood as an ongoing project. Its institutions continue evolving. Its democracy continues maturing. Its economy continues diversifying. Its citizens continue redefining what national identity means in a changing world. This perspective replaces fatalism with responsibility. If institutions are human creations, they remain capable of human improvement. ## Why This Matters Modern Nigeria cannot be understood through a single event, a single leader, or a single historical period. Its institutions reflect layers of history: indigenous governance traditions, colonial administration, constitutional negotiation, military rule, oil, democratic transition, and ongoing reform. Recognizing this complexity changes the conversation. Instead of asking, **“Who created Nigeria’s problems?”** we begin asking, **“Which institutional choices have shaped today’s realities, and how can they be improved?”** History provides the starting point. It does not dictate the destination. ## Looking Ahead History explains where institutions came from. The next question is equally important: What gives those institutions their legal authority today? The answer lies in the Constitution. Before we can evaluate how Nigerian institutions perform, we must understand the document that establishes their powers, defines their responsibilities, and limits their authority. That constitutional framework is the subject of the next chapter. ## Institutional Mirror Every institution carries a history. Some inherit strengths. Some inherit weaknesses. Some inherit both. The question for every generation is not whether history has shaped its institutions. The question is whether it will allow history to define their future—or whether it will build institutions worthy of the future it hopes to create.

sections.markdown:
> “A constitution does not govern a nation. People do. But a constitution determines how power is acquired, exercised, limited, and transferred—and in doing so, it shapes the possibilities of governance.” ## The Blueprint Before the Building Imagine that you are invited to inspect two buildings. The first is magnificent. Its exterior is impressive, its paint fresh, and its entrance grand. Yet after a closer look, you discover that the foundation is weak, the plumbing unreliable, and the electrical system dangerously inconsistent. The second building is less spectacular. It attracts little attention. But its foundation is solid, its structure carefully engineered, and its systems maintained with discipline. Decades later, it continues to serve its purpose. The difference is not appearance. It is design. No architect begins construction without a blueprint. Before the first foundation is laid, the blueprint determines where the walls will stand, how the weight will be distributed, where electricity and water will flow, and how every part of the building will relate to the others. A nation is no different. Before governments can govern, before courts can interpret laws, before elections can be conducted, there must be an agreed framework that defines authority, allocates responsibility, and establishes limits. That framework is the Constitution. ![The National Assembly complex, Abuja, 2018. Photo: Kabusa16 / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.](/static/book/fig-071-11.jpg)

The National Assembly complex, Abuja, 2018. Photo: Kabusa16 / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Most citizens rarely read their country’s constitution. Many will never own a copy. They encounter it only indirectly—through elections, court decisions, public services, taxation, and policing. Yet almost every significant interaction between the citizen and the state is shaped by it. Behind each of these lies a document that answers fundamental questions. Who may exercise public power? How is that power obtained? How is it limited? Who ensures that those limits are respected? These are constitutional questions. Without answers to them, government becomes uncertain and public authority becomes vulnerable to abuse. ## The State Is Not the Government One of the greatest sources of confusion in public discussion is the tendency to treat the terms *government* and *state* as though they mean the same thing. They do not. A government is temporary. It is elected or appointed for a defined period. It changes through elections, constitutional succession, resignation, or other lawful means. The state is permanent. It includes the enduring institutions through which public authority is exercised: the Constitution, the courts, the civil service, the armed forces, regulatory agencies, and the legal framework that survives changes in political leadership. Governments come and go. The state remains. This distinction matters because it changes how we think about national success and failure. If a change of government causes every institution to become unstable, then the challenge is larger than politics. It is institutional. Strong states are capable of maintaining continuity even as governments change. That continuity is one of the defining characteristics of mature constitutional systems. ## Why Nations Need Constitutions Every organized society eventually confronts the same question: **Who should exercise power—and under what limits?** Without agreed rules, political authority becomes uncertain. Competing claims to legitimacy multiply. Rights become difficult to protect. Disputes become harder to resolve peacefully. Constitutions exist to answer these questions before crises arise. They establish institutions. They distribute authority. They protect fundamental rights. They define relationships between different levels of government. They provide mechanisms for accountability. And they create orderly procedures for political succession and constitutional amendment. Many people think of the Constitution as a book read only by lawyers and judges. That view misses its broader significance. The Constitution is the operating framework of the state. It is not merely about law. It is about institutional design. Just as the rules of a game shape how players behave, constitutional rules shape how public institutions interact. ## Power Must Be Organized Before It Can Be Controlled Every society requires authority. Laws must be enforced. Public resources must be managed. National security must be protected. Disputes must be resolved peacefully. But power without structure easily becomes arbitrary. The genius of constitutional government is not that it eliminates power. It organizes it. Legislatures make laws. The executive implements them. The judiciary interprets them. Independent institutions perform specialized responsibilities. Each institution has defined powers. Each also has defined limits. This distribution is not intended to create competition. It is intended to create balance. When institutions understand both their authority and their limits, the state functions with greater predictability and legitimacy. In short, a constitution transforms power from personal authority into public authority governed by rules. That transformation is one of the greatest achievements of constitutional government. ## Nigeria’s Constitutional Journey Nigeria’s constitutional history reflects the country’s search for a political framework capable of governing a large, diverse, and complex federation. Successive constitutional arrangements have attempted to answer enduring questions. How should power be distributed? How should different regions be represented? How should diversity be accommodated? How should rights be protected? How should governments be held accountable? The answers have evolved over time. Colonial constitutional arrangements reflected administrative priorities rather than democratic self-government. The Independence Constitution represented the transfer of political authority to Nigerian leadership. Subsequent constitutional developments responded to changing political realities, including republican status, military intervention, democratic restoration, and constitutional amendment. The present Constitution carries the marks of that history. It opens with the words, “We the people of the Federal Republic of Nigeria … do hereby make, enact and give to ourselves the following Constitution.”1 Yet it was not adopted by a constituent assembly or a referendum. It was brought into force by a military decree—the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria (Promulgation) Decree No. 24 of 1999, signed by General Abdulsalami Abubakar on 5 May 1999—and took effect on 29 May 1999, the day civilian rule was restored.2 Critics have long argued that this origin weakens the document’s claim to speak for the people. Others reply that a constitution’s legitimacy can grow through use: through more than two decades of elections held under it, courts that interpret it, and a National Assembly and state assemblies that have repeatedly amended it. Both positions contain truth. What matters for our purposes is the lesson they share. A constitution’s authority depends not only on the words it contains but on the process that produced it and the institutions that sustain it. Understanding this evolution reminds us that constitutions are not static monuments. They are living frameworks shaped by experience, negotiation, and reform. ## Federalism: Unity and Diversity Nigeria adopted a federal system because of its size, diversity, and complexity. Federalism seeks to balance two important objectives. The first is national unity. The second is regional autonomy. The Constitution distributes governmental responsibilities among the Federal Government, the states, and local government institutions. In principle, this allows decisions to be made at the level most appropriate to the issue. National defence, foreign affairs, and monetary policy require national coordination. Other matters may benefit from greater local knowledge and responsiveness. Money is where federalism becomes concrete. Revenue collected into the Federation Account is shared among the three tiers according to a formula: 52.68 per cent to the Federal Government, 26.72 per cent to the states, and 20.60 per cent to local governments. That formula has remained largely unchanged since 1992, modified only by executive orders in 2002—in August 2026 the Revenue Mobilisation Allocation and Fiscal Commission said it had completed a review, but no new formula takes effect until the National Assembly enacts it— even as the country, its economy, and the responsibilities of each tier have changed enormously. The Revenue Mobilisation Allocation and Fiscal Commission launched a fresh review in 2025.3 ![Figure 6.1. The vertical revenue-sharing formula for the Federation Account. Sources: BusinessDay, August 19, 2025; ThisDay, April 20, 2022.](/static/book/fig-075-12.jpg)

Figure 6.1. The vertical revenue-sharing formula for the Federation Account. Sources: BusinessDay, August 19, 2025; ThisDay, April 20, 2022.

The effectiveness of federalism depends not merely on constitutional text but also on cooperation, fiscal arrangements, institutional capacity, and political culture. Federalism is therefore not simply a legal structure. It is a continuing practice of shared governance—one this book returns to in greater depth in Chapter Nineteen. ## Rights and Responsibilities One of the Constitution’s most visible purposes is the protection of rights. Citizens rightly value freedoms of expression, association, religion, movement, and participation in public life. These rights are essential to democratic society. But constitutions do more than protect freedoms. They also establish responsibilities. Government must govern within the law. Public officials must exercise authority responsibly. Citizens must respect lawful institutions while participating constructively in public life. A constitutional democracy therefore rests upon a relationship of mutual responsibility. Rights flourish where institutions are capable of protecting them. Institutions earn legitimacy when they exercise power in accordance with the Constitution. ## The Constitution on Paper and in Practice No constitution, however carefully drafted, governs by itself. Words on paper do not implement policies. Articles do not build schools. Sections do not prosecute crime. Clauses do not deliver healthcare. People do. Institutions do. A constitution may contain admirable principles. The more difficult question is whether those principles consistently shape public life. Courts may be constitutionally independent. Do they possess the resources and institutional support necessary to function effectively? Oversight institutions may exist. Are they empowered to carry out their responsibilities without undue interference? Fundamental rights may be guaranteed. Can ordinary citizens enforce those rights in practice? Some constitutional promises are not even designed to be enforced by courts. Chapter II of the Constitution sets out the “Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy.” It directs the state to ensure that “there are adequate medical and health facilities for all persons,” and to provide, when practicable, “free, compulsory and universal primary education,” free secondary education, free university education, and free adult literacy programmes.4 But section 6(6)(c) provides that the judicial powers of the courts “shall not, except as otherwise provided by this Constitution, extend to any issue or question” about whether the state has met those objectives.5 In other words, the Constitution promises some of the things citizens care about most, and then places those promises largely beyond the reach of the courts. Their fulfilment depends almost entirely on the willingness and capacity of governments—and on the pressure citizens bring to bear. These questions move us beyond constitutional design toward constitutional performance. A constitutional provision is a promise. An effective institution is the fulfilment of that promise. ### Evidence Box: A Judgment and Its Aftermath - **The ruling.** On 11 July 2024, in a suit brought by the Attorney-General of the Federation against the thirty-six states, the Supreme Court ordered that Federation Account allocations meant for local governments be paid directly to them, bypassing state government accounts, and held that the funds were meant for democratically elected councils, not caretaker committees.6 •**One year later.** Allocations were still flowing through state-controlled joint accounts. In the eleven months after the ruling, about ₦3.4 trillion meant for the 774 councils was paid into those accounts. The Central Bank had required councils to produce two years of audited financial statements before receiving direct payments, and the association of local government chairmen had gone to court to seek enforcement.7 •**Two years later.** About ₦10.48 trillion was allocated to local governments between July 2024 and June 2026. The local government employees’ union said it knew of no council receiving its allocation directly from the Federation Account.8 *The highest court in the land had spoken. The Constitution’s text had been* *authoritatively interpreted. Yet the outcome it required did not follow—because* *implementation depended on institutions, incentives, and political will that the* *judgment alone could not supply.* Those who defend the delay point to real concerns: councils’ capacity to manage funds, the payment of salaries and pensions, and the absence of elected councils in some states. Those concerns deserve answers. But the episode illustrates, more clearly than any hypothetical could, the gap between constitutional text and constitutional practice. The Constitution depends on public servants who administer laws fairly, judges who interpret those laws impartially, legislators who exercise oversight responsibly, executives who respect constitutional limits, and citizens who understand both their rights and their responsibilities. The Constitution provides the architecture. Institutions provide the life. A country may possess an admirable constitutional framework and still struggle if institutions lack the capacity, resources, professionalism, or public trust needed to carry out their responsibilities. Equally, institutions that consistently ignore constitutional principles eventually weaken the very system they are meant to serve. The strength of a constitutional democracy depends not only on the quality of its constitutional text, but on the culture of constitutional obedience. ## The Constitution as a Living Framework Some people speak of constitutions as though they were frozen in time. In reality, constitutional systems evolve. They are interpreted by courts. They are shaped by legislation. They are influenced by democratic practice. In many countries, they are amended as societies change. This does not mean constitutional principles become unimportant. It means that constitutions must remain capable of serving changing societies while preserving stability, accountability, and the rule of law. Institutional maturity lies not in constant constitutional change, nor in rigid resistance to reform, but in carefully balancing continuity with necessary adaptation. ## The Nigerian Opportunity Nigeria’s constitutional framework reflects the country’s diversity, federal structure, democratic aspirations, and commitment to the rule of law. Like every constitutional system, it continues to generate discussion about representation, institutional effectiveness, fiscal arrangements, judicial independence, local governance, and the distribution of public authority. These debates are healthy when they focus on strengthening institutions rather than merely redistributing political advantage. Public debate often asks whether Nigeria needs a new Constitution. That is an important question. But an equally important one is often overlooked: **How effectively are we implementing the constitutional framework we already possess?** The fate of the local government judgment suggests that this question is not rhetorical. Some challenges may require constitutional reform. Others may require stronger institutions, improved public administration, greater civic responsibility, or more consistent application of existing laws. Distinguishing among these possibilities is essential. Otherwise, we risk searching for constitutional solutions to institutional problems—or institutional solutions to constitutional ones. Good diagnosis must come before effective reform. The Constitution should never be viewed simply as a political document. Its ultimate purpose is not to serve governments. Its purpose is to serve the nation. ## Looking Ahead The Constitution establishes formal rules. Yet every society is also shaped by rules that are never written. Customs. Norms. Political habits. Professional cultures. Public expectations. These unwritten rules often determine whether formal institutions succeed or struggle. To understand governance fully, we must therefore examine not only the laws that appear in constitutional text, but also the behavioural patterns that develop around them. That is the subject of the next chapter. ## Institutional Mirror Imagine two nations with identical constitutions. One consistently applies its constitutional principles with professionalism, restraint, and public trust. The other regularly ignores its own constitutional framework whenever it becomes inconvenient. Which nation will enjoy stronger institutions? The difference will not lie primarily in the words of the Constitution. It will lie in the habits of the institutions and the people entrusted with bringing those words to life.

sections.markdown:
> “A nation is governed not only by the laws written in its constitution, but also by the habits written into the daily lives of its people.” ## The Queue Imagine two crowded public offices. In the first, people arrive and quietly form a queue. They wait their turn. No one expects special treatment. The official serving the public follows the same procedure for everyone. The process is not perfect. It is simply predictable. Now imagine a second office. People gather, but the line quickly dissolves. Someone knows an employee inside. Another insists that age or status should move them ahead. A third quietly offers a favour. Others, seeing this, conclude that following the rules is for those without influence. The written procedures in both offices may be identical. The difference lies elsewhere. It lies in the expectations people bring with them before the first document is even stamped. Scale those two offices up to the size of a country and the same pattern holds. Two nations may have nearly identical constitutions, regular elections, separated powers, and anti-corruption agencies. Yet one consistently delivers public services and enjoys broad public trust, while the other struggles with inconsistent enforcement and declining confidence in government. The answer may not lie in the written rules alone. It may lie in the unwritten ones. That difference is political culture. ![Voters queue at a polling unit in Pantami, Gombe State, on election day, 25 February 2023. Photo: Iyusuf615 / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.](/static/book/fig-082-13.jpg)

Voters queue at a polling unit in Pantami, Gombe State, on election day, 25 February 2023. Photo: Iyusuf615 / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

## The Rules Nobody Votes On Every society lives by two sets of rules. The first are formal. They are written in constitutions, statutes, regulations, and official policies. The second are informal. They exist in expectations, customs, traditions, relationships, and shared assumptions about how things “really work.” No parliament votes on them. No judge writes them into law. Yet they shape behaviour every day. People learn them through observation rather than legislation. A new civil servant quickly discovers how promotions are actually earned. A young entrepreneur learns how contracts are really awarded. A student observes what behaviour is rewarded in school. A police officer notices what conduct is tolerated. They discover whether honesty is respected or merely admired in speeches. They learn whether punctuality matters, whether contracts are honoured, whether public property is treated as everyone’s responsibility or no one’s responsibility. These lessons often influence behaviour as much as any written law. Over time, these habits become culture. Not culture in the artistic sense. Institutional culture. ## The Power of Expectations Human beings respond to expectations. If people believe hard work is recognized fairly, they invest more effort. If they believe rules apply equally, compliance increases. If they believe institutions are predictable, trust grows. But when expectations shift in the opposite direction, behaviour also changes. If people expect procedures to be ignored, they stop relying on them. If they expect favouritism, they seek connections instead of merit. If they expect impunity, accountability becomes harder to enforce. Survey evidence suggests how deeply such expectations run in Nigeria. When Afrobarometer asked a nationally representative sample of Nigerians in 2020 whether most people can be trusted, only 7 per cent said yes. Ninety-two per cent said one must be very careful in dealing with people.1 In a society where strangers are not trusted, it becomes rational to rely on people one knows—relatives, friends, members of the same community or congregation—to get things done. The queue gives way to the connection. Not because people are dishonest by nature, but because experience has taught them that the impersonal rule may not protect them. Culture is therefore not simply what people believe. It is what people come to expect. And expectations shape behaviour long before laws are ever invoked. ## Culture Is Not Destiny Political culture is frequently misunderstood. Some people treat it as an excuse. Others treat it as an accusation. Neither approach is helpful. Political culture is simply the collection of habits, expectations, and shared beliefs that influence how people relate to authority, institutions, and one another. Every institution has one. Schools have cultures. Hospitals have cultures. Businesses have cultures. Courts have cultures. Government ministries have cultures. Families have cultures. Some encourage professionalism. Others tolerate mediocrity. Some reward initiative. Others discourage innovation. Some welcome constructive criticism. Others punish honest disagreement. Changing leadership without changing institutional culture often produces only temporary improvement. When the leader leaves, the old habits quietly return. Lasting reform requires changing both systems and expectations. ## Patronage and Performance One of the enduring challenges in many societies is balancing personal relationships with institutional fairness. Relationships are an important part of every community. Families, friendships, and networks provide support and resilience. Problems arise when personal loyalty consistently overrides institutional responsibility. If appointments are made primarily because of personal connections rather than competence, institutions gradually lose capacity. If contracts are awarded without transparent competition, public confidence declines. If rules apply differently depending on who is involved, trust erodes. The same logic reaches the ballot box. According to a national survey by the National Bureau of Statistics, about 22 per cent of voters in the 2023 general elections were offered money or another inducement in exchange for their vote, up from 17 per cent in 2019. In the North-West, more than half of citizens reported being offered money or favours.2 Meanwhile, participation has fallen steeply. Turnout in presidential elections was about 69 per cent in 2003, 59 per cent in 2011, and around 43 per cent in 2015. In 2023, only about 25 million of 93.5 million registered voters—roughly 27 per cent—cast a ballot.3 ![Figure 7.1. Turnout in presidential elections as a share of registered voters. The 2015 and 2019 figures are calculated from reported registration and votes cast. Source: INEC figures compiled by The ICIR (2023).](/static/book/fig-085-14.jpg)

Figure 7.1. Turnout in presidential elections as a share of registered voters. The 2015 and 2019 figures are calculated from reported registration and votes cast. Source: INEC figures compiled by The ICIR (2023).

Low turnout and vote buying reinforce each other. When most citizens stay home, a relatively small number of purchased votes carries more weight. And when citizens believe that outcomes are bought, staying home seems more reasonable. These outcomes are not inevitable. They are the predictable consequences of incentives that reward one form of behaviour over another. ## The Rules We Teach Without Speaking Children learn far more than formal lessons. They watch adults. They observe how conflicts are resolved. They notice whether promises are kept. They learn whether public property deserves respect. Young employees study senior colleagues. New public servants observe experienced officials. Citizens learn from the daily conduct of institutions. In this way, political culture is constantly transmitted. Not through textbooks. Through example. Every generation teaches the next what institutions truly expect. The question is whether those lessons strengthen or weaken public life. ## Trust: The Invisible Currency Economists often discuss money. Lawyers discuss justice. Politicians discuss power. Institutional thinkers must also discuss trust. One of the greatest resources any nation possesses cannot be mined, taxed, or manufactured. Trust allows strangers to cooperate. It allows contracts to be signed with confidence. It allows citizens to believe that today’s effort will receive tomorrow’s reward. It strengthens democratic participation and encourages investment. Trust lowers the cost of cooperation. When trust declines, every transaction becomes more expensive. Businesses spend more on protecting themselves. Citizens spend more time navigating bureaucracy. Governments devote greater resources to enforcement. A society with low trust pays hidden costs every day. Trust grows slowly. It can disappear quickly. Strong institutions protect trust because they behave consistently, transparently, and fairly. Building trust therefore becomes an institutional objective, not merely a moral aspiration. Nigeria’s pattern of trust is revealing. In Afrobarometer’s 2024 survey, fewer than one in five Nigerians said they trusted the President, the National Assembly, the police, or the electoral commission “somewhat” or “a lot.” The courts fared only slightly better, at about one in four. Yet more than half trusted traditional leaders, and nearly six in ten trusted religious leaders.4 Nigerians, in other words, are not a people without trust. They extend it readily to institutions that are close to them, that they can observe, and that they believe answer to them. What is missing is trust in the formal institutions of the state. ### Evidence Box: What Nigerians Expect - **Trust in each other:** 7 per cent say most people can be trusted; 92 per cent say one must be very careful (2020).5 •**Tolerance of difference:** about 90 per cent would like, or not mind, having neighbours from a different ethnic group; 86 per cent, neighbours of a different religion (2020).6 •**Trust in institutions (“somewhat” or “a lot”), 2024:** President 19 per cent; police 17 per cent; electoral commission 16 per cent; courts 25 per cent; traditional leaders 51 per cent; religious leaders 58 per cent.7 •**Democracy:** 64 per cent prefer democracy to any other system of government, down from 70 per cent in 2022; 82 per cent are “not very” or “not at all” satisfied with how it works (2024).8 •**Elections:** 22 per cent of voters offered inducements in 2023; presidential turnout fell from about 69 per cent in 2003 to about 27 per cent in 2023.9 *The problem these figures describe is not hostility between Nigerians. It is low* *confidence that formal institutions will treat people fairly—and the behaviour that* *low confidence produces.* ## The Feedback Loop Institutions shape culture. Culture shapes institutions. This relationship creates a powerful feedback loop. When institutions reward integrity, integrity becomes more common. When institutions tolerate misconduct, misconduct becomes more common. Citizens observe these patterns. They adjust their expectations. Those expectations influence future behaviour. Breaking negative cycles therefore requires more than changing individuals. It requires changing the incentives that produce recurring behaviour. ## Changing Culture Without Despair Political culture is sometimes described as though it were permanent. It is not. Cultures change. They evolve when institutions reward different behaviours. They evolve when leaders model integrity. They evolve when citizens refuse to normalize practices that weaken public life. They evolve through education, technology, and institutional reform. Throughout history, societies have transformed political cultures not by demanding instant moral perfection, but by steadily strengthening institutions. Professional civil services, independent courts, transparent procurement systems, merit-based recruitment, and civic education have all contributed to changing expectations over time. The process was gradual. Sometimes difficult. Always deliberate. The lesson is consistent. **Culture changes most sustainably when institutions reinforce the behaviours society wishes to encourage.** ## The Nigerian Opportunity Nigeria’s political culture, like that of every nation, contains both strengths and weaknesses. Across the country, one finds remarkable resilience, entrepreneurship, generosity, community spirit, innovation, and determination. One also encounters habits—favouritism, impunity, the quiet expectation that rules bend for the connected—that weaken institutional performance when left unchallenged. The evidence also contains a strong reason for hope. Despite deep dissatisfaction, most Nigerians still prefer democracy to any alternative. And in the same survey that recorded such low trust in strangers, about nine in ten Nigerians said they would welcome, or not mind, neighbours from a different ethnic group or of a different political persuasion.10 The raw material of a cooperative civic culture is present. What it lacks is institutions that consistently reward cooperation. The question is not whether Nigeria has a political culture. Every nation does. The question is which habits deserve reinforcement and which require reform. Many public debates ask whether Nigeria’s greatest challenge is leadership, corruption, or the Constitution. These are important questions. But another deserves equal attention: **What behaviours do our institutions consistently reward?** Until that question is answered honestly, reforms may address symptoms while leaving the underlying incentives unchanged. Political culture is not separate from institutions. It is both their product and their partner. ## Looking Ahead Culture influences behaviour. But behaviour is also shaped by incentives. People respond not only to values, but to the rewards and consequences built into institutions. Why do good people sometimes produce disappointing institutional outcomes? Why do some systems encourage excellence while others unintentionally reward poor performance? That question leads us to one of the most important principles in institutional design: Incentives. ## Institutional Mirror Think about the institutions you interact with most often. What behaviours do they quietly reward? What behaviours do they discourage? If someone observed those institutions for one year without reading a single policy document, what would they conclude the real rules are? Those are the unwritten rules that shape institutional life. And those are often the rules that determine whether institutions flourish or fail.

sections.markdown:
> “People do not merely respond to laws; they respond to the incentives that laws and institutions create. Change the incentives, and you often change the outcomes.” ## The Honest Employee Imagine two equally honest young graduates. Both begin work on the same day. The first joins an organization where promotions are based on competence, performance is measured fairly, corruption is punished consistently, and excellence is rewarded. The second joins an organization where advancement depends primarily on personal connections, accountability is weak, rules are applied selectively, and integrity is often ignored. Five years later, the two individuals may behave very differently. Not because their character changed overnight. But because the institutions around them rewarded different behaviours. This is one of the most important lessons in institutional thinking. People make choices. But institutions shape the environment within which those choices are made. ## Beyond Good Intentions Most people begin their careers with aspirations to contribute meaningfully to society. Teachers hope to educate. Doctors hope to heal. Police officers hope to protect. Civil servants hope to serve. Entrepreneurs hope to create value. Judges hope to uphold justice. Yet institutions influence whether these aspirations are sustained, strengthened, or gradually eroded. When excellence is recognized, people strive for excellence. When accountability is consistent, professional standards improve. When misconduct carries few consequences while integrity receives little recognition, behaviour begins to adjust accordingly. This is not because human nature suddenly changes. It is because incentives shape decisions. ## What Is an Incentive? An incentive is any feature of a system that encourages, discourages, rewards, or penalizes particular behaviour. Some incentives are financial. Others are professional. Some are social. Others are legal or political. Some reward honesty. Others reward manipulation. Some encourage innovation. Others encourage delay. Promotion based on performance creates one incentive. Promotion based solely on seniority creates another. Transparent procurement encourages one pattern of behaviour. Opaque procurement encourages another. Independent oversight changes incentives. Weak oversight changes them differently. Institutions create these incentives whether intentionally or unintentionally. They continuously communicate what they truly value—not only through policies, but through the outcomes they reward. The scholar Robert Klitgaard summarized the incentives behind corruption in a simple formula: corruption tends to flourish where an official has a monopoly over a decision, broad discretion in making it, and little accountability for the result.1 The formula is useful precisely because it says nothing about anyone’s character. It points instead to features of the system that can be redesigned. That is why institutional design matters. ## Behaviour Is Often Rational When citizens repeatedly behave in ways that appear frustrating or counterproductive, our first instinct is often moral judgment. Sometimes that judgment is justified. But another question deserves equal attention. **What behaviour does the system reward?** If public servants receive recognition for solving problems, many will seek solutions. If they are rewarded simply for avoiding responsibility, risk-avoidance becomes rational. If entrepreneurs face unpredictable regulations, many will delay investment. If taxpayers see little connection between taxes paid and public services received, voluntary compliance becomes more difficult. Nigeria’s own survey data shows how these incentives play out. In 2023, according to the third national corruption survey by the National Bureau of Statistics, conducted with the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, about 27 per cent of Nigerians who dealt with a public official paid a bribe—slightly fewer than the 29 per cent recorded in 2019. Public officials received an estimated 87 million bribes that year, worth some ₦721 billion, or about 0.35 per cent of GDP.2 But the same survey contains a finding that matters just as much. More than 70 per cent of Nigerians who were asked for a bribe in 2023 refused on at least one occasion. And the share of people who suffered negative consequences after refusing fell, from 49 per cent in 2019 to 38 per cent in 2023.3 Most people, in other words, do not want to pay. Whether they do depends heavily on what refusing will cost them. When the cost of honesty falls, more people can afford to be honest. ![Figure 8.1. Share of Nigerians who paid a bribe when dealing with a public official, and share who suffered negative consequences after refusing, 2019 and 2023. Source: National Bureau of Statistics and United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, Corruption in Nigeria: Patterns and Trends (2024), as cited in the notes.](/static/book/fig-094-15.jpg)

Figure 8.1. Share of Nigerians who paid a bribe when dealing with a public official, and share who suffered negative consequences after refusing, 2019 and 2023. Source: National Bureau of Statistics and United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, Corruption in Nigeria: Patterns and Trends (2024), as cited in the notes.

People respond not only to ideals. They also respond to incentives. Recognizing this does not excuse harmful behaviour. It explains why certain patterns become widespread. ## Why Institutions Produce Predictable Outcomes Consider two examination halls. ![Students writing an examination at Augustine University, Ilara-Epe, Lagos State, 2025. Photo: Addjimedu / Wikimedia Commons, CC0.](/static/book/fig-095-16.jpg)

Students writing an examination at Augustine University, Ilara-Epe, Lagos State, 2025. Photo: Addjimedu / Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

In the first, students believe that success depends on preparation, discipline, and genuine understanding. The examination is supervised fairly, cheating is consistently detected, and results reflect merit. In the second, some students believe that connections, leaked questions, or bribery can influence outcomes. Even those who wish to act honestly begin to wonder whether integrity places them at a disadvantage. The written examination rules in both halls may be identical. The difference lies in the incentives created by the institution. The second hall is not hypothetical. In 2024, the West African Examinations Council withheld the results of 215,267 candidates in its school certificate examination over alleged malpractice—nearly 12 per cent of the 1.8 million who sat it.4 Behind each of those results is a decision by a student, and often by a teacher, parent, or school, that cheating was worth the risk. When similar behaviours are rewarded repeatedly, similar outcomes should not surprise us. If innovation is consistently encouraged, innovation becomes more common. If competence is recognized, more people invest in competence. If corruption is tolerated, corrupt practices become increasingly rational for those seeking advantage. Institutions often produce exactly the outcomes they are designed—or allowed—to produce. This observation is neither cynical nor deterministic. It is diagnostic. ## When Good People Enter Weak Systems Many reform efforts begin with hope. Capable people enter public office determined to make a difference. Some succeed. Others become frustrated. Still others gradually adapt to the existing institutional culture. Why? Because systems exert pressure. A well-designed institution supports integrity. A poorly designed institution may make integrity costly. New leaders enter old systems. Over time, the systems shape the leaders as much as the leaders shape the systems. Researchers who study corruption have described why this happens. Where corruption is systemic, it behaves less like a crime committed by a few and more like a collective-action problem. If an official expects that everyone around them is taking bribes, refusing brings personal cost and little public benefit, because the system will carry on regardless. Anti-corruption strategies that assume honest supervisors will discipline dishonest subordinates tend to fail in such settings, because the supervisors face the same incentives.5 This does not eliminate personal responsibility. It simply reminds us that courage alone cannot permanently compensate for institutional weakness. Lasting reform requires changing both people and systems. ## Incentives Across Society Institutional incentives are not limited to government. A business that rewards customer service is likely to improve customer satisfaction. A university that rewards research and teaching quality is more likely to strengthen academic performance. A hospital that values patient safety develops different habits from one that measures only administrative convenience. Families also create incentives. Children notice which behaviours earn praise, correction, trust, or responsibility. Religious organizations cultivate particular habits. Professional associations establish standards of conduct. Communities reinforce expectations about cooperation, honesty, and civic responsibility. Every institution teaches behaviour. Sometimes intentionally. Sometimes unintentionally. The question is always the same: **What behaviour is this institution encouraging?** ## The Institutional Feedback Loop Once incentives shape behaviour, behaviour begins to shape expectations. Citizens expect delays. Officials expect informal payments. Businesses expect uncertainty. Students expect mediocrity. Or, in healthier systems: Citizens expect professionalism. Officials expect accountability. Businesses expect predictable regulation. Students expect excellence. Expectations become culture. Culture then reinforces institutions. This is how both progress and decline become self-sustaining. ## Reform Begins with Redesign Many reforms focus on replacing individuals. Sometimes that is necessary. But replacing people without changing incentives often produces disappointing results. Lasting reform asks deeper questions. Are the incentives aligned with the institution’s purpose? Do promotion systems reward merit? Are accountability mechanisms consistent? Are responsibilities matched with authority? Can citizens observe and evaluate institutional performance? Across the world, successful institutional reforms have often focused less on changing slogans and more on changing incentives. Civil service reforms introduced merit-based recruitment. Judicial reforms strengthened independence and security of tenure. Procurement reforms increased transparency and competition. Tax reforms simplified compliance while improving enforcement. Although implemented in different ways across countries, these reforms shared a common principle: **Change the incentives, and behaviour gradually follows.** Nigeria has seen what such redesign can achieve. For years, federal payrolls were padded with “ghost workers”—names that drew salaries without corresponding employees. Exhortations against the practice achieved little. What changed matters was a change in the system: moving staff onto the Integrated Payroll and Personnel Information System and linking payments to Bank Verification Numbers, so that each salary had to be matched to a real, biometrically verified person. By May 2016, the federal government’s continuous audit team reported that more than 43,000 ghost workers had been removed from the payroll, saving about ₦50 billion.6 No one had to become more virtuous for this to work. The system simply made a particular form of dishonesty much harder to commit and much easier to detect. ### Evidence Box: Incentives in Numbers - **Bribery:** about 27 per cent of Nigerians who dealt with a public official paid a bribe in 2023 (29 per cent in 2019); about 87 million bribes worth roughly ₦721 billion.7 •**Refusal:** more than 70 per cent of those asked for a bribe refused at least once; negative consequences of refusing fell from 49 per cent (2019) to 38 per cent (2023).8 •**Examinations:** 215,267 of 1,805,216 candidates’ results withheld over alleged malpractice in the 2024 school certificate examination.9 •**Payroll reform:** more than 43,000 ghost workers removed and about ₦50 billion saved after biometric payroll verification (2016).10 *Where refusing a bribe is safer, more people refuse. Where verification is* *automatic, fraud declines. Incentives are not abstractions; they are measurable.* ## The Nigerian Opportunity Across Nigeria, there are examples of institutions that have improved because incentives became clearer. Professional organizations that enforce standards often see higher levels of public confidence. Businesses that reward innovation frequently outperform competitors. Public institutions that strengthen transparency and accountability often improve service delivery over time. These examples remind us that institutional performance is not fixed. Nigeria’s future will not be determined solely by discovering better leaders. Nor will it be determined solely by writing better laws. Its future will depend on whether institutions consistently reward the behaviours that produce public value. Integrity. Competence. Innovation. Service. Accountability. When those behaviours become the easiest path to success, institutional transformation becomes possible. This is encouraging because incentives are designed by people. And what people design, people can redesign. ## Looking Ahead Incentives explain why good people can produce disappointing outcomes. They also raise the most uncomfortable question in this book. If systems shape behaviour, what about the people who steal, take bribes, and abuse public office? Are they, too, merely products of the system? The next chapter takes that question directly. It examines corruption—the strongest objection to the argument that nobody is the problem—and asks what the evidence says about how corruption is reduced. ## Institutional Mirror Think about an institution you know well. If someone had no knowledge of its mission statement and could judge it only by the behaviour it consistently rewards, what would they conclude that institution truly values? And if those incentives remain unchanged, why should tomorrow’s outcomes be different? **Institutions become what their incentives repeatedly encourage.**

sections.markdown:
> “Justice asks who is responsible. Wisdom also asks why responsibility keeps falling in the same place.” ## The Flat in Ikoyi In April 2017, officers of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission entered an empty apartment in Ikoyi, one of the most expensive neighbourhoods in Lagos. There was no furniture worth noting. There were no occupants. There was money. Dollars, pounds sterling, and naira—about $43 million in all—had been stored in the flat. The commission had been led there by a tip received under the federal government’s new whistleblowing policy, and a Federal High Court soon ordered the cash to be temporarily forfeited to the government.1 For many Nigerians, the images confirmed what they already believed. Somebody had stolen that money. Somebody had hidden it. Somebody should go to prison. All of that may be true. And it is precisely why this chapter is necessary. ![Members of the National Youth Service Corps holding anti-corruption placards during a community outreach, 2026. Photo: Poet1803 / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.](/static/book/fig-102-17.jpg)

Members of the National Youth Service Corps holding anti-corruption placards during a community outreach, 2026. Photo: Poet1803 / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

## The Strongest Objection A book called *Nobody Is the Problem* invites an obvious reply. *Somebody is the problem. Specific people stole specific money. The cash in the* *flat did not walk there by itself.* Chapter One acknowledged this objection and promised to return to it at greater length. This chapter keeps that promise. The objection deserves respect, because it is largely correct about the facts. Corruption in Nigeria is not a rumour invented by foreign observers or political rivals. It has been documented in court judgments, audit reports, international settlements, and the testimony of millions of ordinary Nigerians. Chapter Eight described a national survey which found that about 27 per cent of Nigerians who dealt with a public official in 2023 paid a bribe—some 87 million bribes in a single year.2 Chapter One described a survey in which eight in ten Nigerians believed corruption had increased. The people who stole, and the people who demanded bribes, are responsible for what they did. Nothing in this book suggests otherwise. But the objection contains a hidden assumption: that if corruption is committed by individuals, it must be solved by dealing with individuals. That assumption is where the argument goes wrong. ## What the Evidence Shows Begin with the most widely cited international measure. Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index scores countries from 0, highly corrupt, to 100, very clean, based on assessments by experts and business people. In its 2025 index, published in February 2026, Nigeria scored 26 out of 100 and ranked 142nd of 182 countries. The global average was 42. Botswana and Rwanda ranked 41st; Ghana 76th; South Africa 81st.3 Since the index adopted its current scale in 2012, Nigeria’s score has remained in the twenties. Its highest score, 28, came in 2016.4 ![Figure 9.1. Nigeria’s score on the Corruption Perceptions Index, selected years. Sources: Transparency International, as reported in Dataphyte, TheCable, and Nairametrics.](/static/book/fig-104-18.jpg)

Figure 9.1. Nigeria’s score on the Corruption Perceptions Index, selected years. Sources: Transparency International, as reported in Dataphyte, TheCable, and Nairametrics.

Now set that flat line beside something else. Between October 2023 and mid-2026, the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission reported securing 10,872 convictions from 14,476 cases filed in court. Over roughly the same period it reported recovering about ₦1.23 trillion and $684 million, and securing the forfeiture of more than 1,100 real estate assets.5 A large share of the commission’s caseload involves cybercrime and advance-fee fraud rather than public officials. Even so, the figures represent a scale of enforcement that few countries can match. And yet the perception of corruption has barely moved. This is not a criticism of the commission’s officers, many of whom work under real danger. It is a measure of the limits of what enforcement alone can do. When convictions run into the thousands while the overall picture stays the same, the system is producing new offenders at least as fast as the courts can punish old ones. That is the signature of a system, not of a few individuals. ## Where Corruption Lives Why would a system keep producing corruption, whoever holds office? The political scientist Robert Klitgaard summarized a large body of research in a simple formula: corruption tends to flourish where officials have **monopoly** power over a decision, wide **discretion** in how to exercise it, and little **accountability** for the result.6 Corruption = Monopoly + Discretion − Accountability. The formula is not a law of nature. But it explains a great deal of Nigerian experience. Consider the official who alone decides whether a business receives a permit, according to criteria nobody else can see, with no time limit and no record of the decision. That arrangement does not require a dishonest official to produce bribery. It requires only an ordinary person under financial pressure, facing an applicant who would rather pay than wait. Replace that official with another, and the same arrangement will tend to produce the same result. Consider, too, the other side of the formula. The Auditor-General reports irregularities year after year (Chapter Thirteen). The commission secures thousands of convictions. Yet the institutions that should turn findings into consequences—legislative committees, prosecutors, courts, and agencies that must recover the money—often act slowly or not at all. When the probability of consequences is low, even serious penalties deter little. Seen this way, corruption is not only a moral failing. It is also an institutional outcome: what happens when monopoly and discretion are high and accountability is weak. ## The Cost of a Single Bribe The scale of what is at stake is easy to underestimate. In January 2010, the Nigerian government signed a twenty-year gas supply and processing agreement with a company called Process & Industrial Developments (P&ID). The project was never built. P&ID took Nigeria to arbitration in London, and by 2017 a tribunal had awarded it US$6.6 billion in damages. With interest, the sum grew to about US$11 billion.7 In October 2023, the High Court in London set the award aside. The judge found that P&ID had presented false evidence, that a Nigerian government lawyer had been bribed during the arbitration, and that the company had improperly obtained and kept Nigeria’s confidential legal documents.8 The story has two lessons. The first is how much damage corruption can do. A bribe to one official, inside one legal process, came close to costing the nation billions of dollars. The second is easier to miss. Nigeria escaped that loss not because a hero appeared, but because institutions eventually worked: lawyers who kept investigating, evidence that was gathered and tested, and a court that examined it carefully. The same pattern—damage done through weak institutions, and damage limited through stronger ones—runs through this entire chapter. ## When Systems Changed If corruption were purely a matter of individual character, changing systems would make little difference. Nigeria’s own experience shows otherwise. When the federal government required public salaries to be paid only to employees whose identities were verified biometrically, more than 43,000 ghost workers disappeared from the payroll (Chapter Eight). When it consolidated government cash in a single Treasury account, about 20,000 separate bank accounts were closed, removing countless opportunities for funds to be diverted unseen (Chapter Three). When the regulator replaced a discredited licensing process with a published, competitive auction, investors gained rules they could trust after an earlier attempt had been cancelled amid doubts about its integrity, and the telecommunications sector grew into one of Africa’s largest (Chapter Four). None of these reforms relied on converting officials to honesty. Each reduced monopoly or discretion, or increased accountability. The return of stolen assets shows the same logic at international scale. Sani Abacha, who ruled Nigeria from 1993 until his death in 1998, is estimated to have plundered several billion dollars. Recovering that money took more than two decades of litigation and negotiation across several countries. Switzerland returned $322 million under a 2018 agreement; in 2020, the United States and Jersey returned a further $311 million, under an agreement that required the money to be managed by the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority and spent on specified infrastructure.9 The conditions were not an insult. They were an institution—an arrangement designed to ensure that recovered money would not simply be stolen again. ## Learning from Others Other societies have faced corruption at least as severe as Nigeria’s and reduced it. Hong Kong in the early 1970s was widely regarded as deeply corrupt, particularly in its police force. In 1974, it established an Independent Commission Against Corruption with three functions: investigating offences, preventing corruption by reviewing the procedures of government departments, and educating the public.10 The second function is the one most often forgotten. The commission did not only pursue offenders. It studied the systems that made offences easy and pressed for them to be redesigned. Georgia, discussed in Chapter Twenty-Three, reduced petty corruption sharply after 2004 by abolishing its traffic police, recruiting a new force, and using technology to reduce face-to-face discretion—though with methods that raised serious concerns about oversight. Neither case offers a template. Both offer a principle: lasting reductions in corruption come from changing the conditions under which officials work, not only from punishing the officials who fail. ## Punishment and Prevention None of this means that punishment does not matter. Prosecution expresses a society’s values. It removes offenders from positions where they can do further harm. It returns stolen assets. And where the probability of being caught and punished is genuinely high, it deters. But punishment works best as one part of a system that also prevents. A society that relies only on punishment is like a hospital that relies only on surgery: necessary, sometimes heroic, and always too late. The question for Nigeria is therefore not whether to punish corruption or to reform institutions. It is how to do both, consistently, so that each reinforces the other: - **Reduce monopoly:** allow citizens to obtain the same service from more than one office, or online, so that no single official holds the key. - **Reduce discretion:** publish criteria, time limits, and fees for public services, so that delay is not for sale. •**Increase accountability:** follow up audit findings, protect whistleblowers, publish asset declarations, and ensure that cases are concluded rather than adjourned indefinitely. •**Increase transparency:** publish contracts, budgets, and payments, so that citizens, journalists, and monitors such as Tracka can check them. •**Recover and protect assets:** return stolen funds through arrangements that make them hard to steal a second time. ### Evidence Box: Corruption in Numbers - **Perception:** Nigeria scored 26 out of 100 on the 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, ranking 142nd of 182 countries; the global average was 42.11 •**Experience:** about 27 per cent of those who dealt with a public official paid a bribe in 2023 (Chapter Eight). •**Enforcement:** 10,872 convictions secured by the EFCC between late 2023 and mid-2026, and about ₦1.23 trillion and $684 million recovered.12 •**Cost of a single bribe:** an arbitration award of about $11 billion against Nigeria, set aside in 2023 after a court found bribery and false evidence.13 •**Asset recovery:** $322 million returned from Switzerland (2018) and $311 million from the United States and Jersey (2020) of funds attributed to Sani Abacha.14 *Enforcement catches offenders. Institutions decide how many new ones there will* *be.* ## The Nigerian Opportunity Nigeria does not lack laws against corruption, agencies to investigate it, or courts to try it. Nor does it lack citizens who refuse to pay bribes: Chapter Eight showed that most Nigerians asked for a bribe have refused at least once. What it needs is to tilt the system decisively towards those citizens and officials—to make honest conduct easier, safer, and more rewarding than dishonest conduct, in every office and every transaction. Every reform that removes an unnecessary approval, publishes a hidden fee, digitizes a payment, protects a whistleblower, or concludes a prosecution contributes to that shift. None is dramatic. Together, they change the odds. ## Looking Ahead Corruption flourishes where institutions are weak. But institutions are ultimately staffed, led, and reformed by people—people formed, in large part, by the schools they attended. The next chapter therefore turns to education: the institution that shapes the future custodians of every other institution. ## Institutional Mirror When the next corruption scandal breaks, ask the questions that the objection asks: Who did it? Will they be punished? Then ask two more. **What made it possible?** **And what will stop the next person from doing the same?** A nation that asks only the first two questions will spend its future catching thieves. A nation that also asks the last two can begin to run out of them.
