> “Every nation eventually becomes the classroom it builds. The lessons taught today become the institutions inherited tomorrow.” ## The Child Who Will Lead Tomorrow Every morning across Nigeria, millions of children put on school uniforms, gather their books, and begin another day of learning. Some walk long distances to reach their classrooms. Some travel through crowded cities. Others attend schools in communities where teachers work with limited resources but remarkable dedication. Somewhere today, a child is learning to read. In another classroom, a teenager is preparing for examinations. In a university laboratory, a young researcher is searching for answers. In a technical college, an apprentice is mastering a trade. None of them knows what role they will eventually play. One may become a judge. Another an engineer. Another a governor. Another a teacher. Another an entrepreneur. Another a civil servant. Parents make sacrifices to pay school fees, purchase textbooks, and provide opportunities they hope will lead to a better future. Teachers prepare lessons believing that today’s classroom may shape tomorrow’s doctor, scientist, artist, or public servant. Within every classroom sits possibility. But possibility alone does not build a nation. It must be developed through institutions capable of transforming potential into competence, character, and citizenship. The future of every nation begins long before its elections. It begins in its classrooms. ![Pupils taking a computer-based test, 2017. Photo: Advancedsolver / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.](/static/book/fig-112-19.jpg)

Pupils taking a computer-based test, 2017. Photo: Advancedsolver / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

### Evidence Box: Nigeria’s Education System at a Glance - **Scale (2024/2025 annual school census):** about 230,800 schools, 39.8 million learners, and 1.19 million teachers; a learner-to-teacher ratio of 33.6 to 1; 49.6 per cent of learners and 55.7 per cent of teachers are female. Only about 54 per cent of schools had submitted their census returns.1 •**Children not in school:** UNESCO estimates about 20 million out-of-school children and youth; UNICEF puts the number of primary-age children out of school at about 10.2 million.2 •**Children in school but not learning:** World Bank estimates suggest that more than three-quarters of Nigerian children cannot read and understand a simple text by age ten—about 37 million of 50.7 million children aged seven to fourteen.3 - **Funding:** education has received roughly 6 to 8 per cent of the federal budget each year from 2022 to 2026, against the international benchmark of 15 to 20 per cent of public expenditure.4 •**Money left unused:** in August 2026, the Universal Basic Education Commission reported more than ₦65 billion in federal matching grants that states had not accessed, and about ₦267 billion in previously released intervention funds lying idle.5 *These figures describe not one problem but several: children outside the system,* *children inside it who are not learning, money that is too little, and money that is* *not used.* ## Every Institution Begins in a Classroom Every profession begins somewhere. The judge once sat at a classroom desk. The surgeon first learned biology from a teacher. The engineer solved early mathematics problems in school. The entrepreneur developed curiosity long before establishing a business. The civil servant who drafts national policy once learned to read, write, and reason under the guidance of educators. Every institution we admire—or criticize—is ultimately staffed by people whose habits of thought were shaped somewhere. Education is therefore often described as a social service. It is more accurately understood as a long-term institutional investment. When that system performs well, every other institution benefits. When it performs poorly, every other institution eventually bears the cost. Nigeria’s education system now serves nearly 40 million learners in some 230,000 schools, staffed by about 1.19 million teachers. These figures reveal not only the scale of the system but also the extraordinary administrative demands placed upon governments at the federal, state, and local levels. Managing a system of this magnitude requires more than funding; it requires capable institutions, reliable data, effective planning, and sustained accountability. Even the data reveals the challenge. When the 2024/2025 national school census was published, fewer than six in ten schools had submitted their returns.6 A system that cannot yet fully count its own schools will struggle to plan for them. Education is not merely another public service. It is the institution that prepares people to build every other institution. ## Beyond Certificates Education is often measured by enrolment figures, examination results, graduation rates, or the number of degrees awarded. These measures matter. But they are incomplete. For many years, education policy around the world focused primarily on expanding access. That objective remains important. However, international evidence increasingly emphasizes that attendance alone does not guarantee learning. UNESCO now encourages countries to assess education through broader indicators that include learning outcomes, teacher quality, equity, inclusion, foundational literacy and numeracy, and the overall capacity of education systems to prepare young people for modern economies. This distinction is critical for Nigeria. A nation may successfully increase school enrolment while still facing significant challenges in educational quality. Nigeria faces both challenges at once. Millions of children are not in school at all. And among those who are, World Bank estimates suggest that a large majority cannot read and understand a simple text by the age of ten.7 The second problem is less visible than the first, but it may be just as serious. A child who sits in a classroom for six years without learning to read has been enrolled, but not educated. ![Figure 10.1. Estimated number of Nigerian children aged seven to fourteen who cannot read and understand a simple text by age ten. Source: World Bank estimates, as reported in BusinessDay, March 13, 2025.](/static/book/fig-115-20.jpg)

Figure 10.1. Estimated number of Nigerian children aged seven to fourteen who cannot read and understand a simple text by age ten. Source: World Bank estimates, as reported in BusinessDay, March 13, 2025.

The deeper question is: **What kind of citizen does the education system produce?** Does it cultivate curiosity? Does it reward integrity? Does it encourage critical thinking? Does it develop competence? Does it prepare young people to solve problems rather than merely repeat information? A society may produce millions of certificates while still struggling to produce enough skilled professionals, ethical leaders, innovative entrepreneurs, and effective public servants. Credentials have value. Capability has greater value. ## Knowledge, Skills, and Character Education does more than teach people to read, write, and calculate. It teaches them how to think. How to question. How to cooperate. How to solve problems. How to evaluate evidence. How to respect differences. How to exercise responsibility. How to serve society. Strong education systems cultivate three forms of development. First, they develop **knowledge**. Students acquire understanding of language, mathematics, science, history, technology, and the arts. Second, they develop **skills**. Critical thinking. Communication. Creativity. Collaboration. Adaptability. Problem-solving. Third, they develop **character**. Integrity. Discipline. Respect. Curiosity. Perseverance. Responsibility. These three dimensions reinforce one another. Knowledge without character can be misused. Character without knowledge may limit opportunity. Skills without either are difficult to sustain. In this sense, education is not simply preparation for employment. It is preparation for citizenship. A nation’s schools are not only producing workers. They are producing the future custodians of its institutions. ## Schools as Institutional Laboratories Every school is an institution. Whether intentionally or not, it teaches incentives. If students learn that honesty is rewarded, they carry that expectation into adulthood. If cheating is tolerated, they learn another lesson. If teachers are supported, professionalism grows. If excellence is consistently recognized, ambition is directed toward achievement rather than shortcuts. If schools reward rote memorization without understanding, or credentials without competence, the consequences eventually extend far beyond the classroom. Earlier chapters have already shown two warning signs. In 2017, about two-thirds of the primary school teachers tested in Kaduna State failed to reach the required score on an assessment based on primary four material (Chapter Two). In 2024, the results of more than 215,000 candidates in the school certificate examination were withheld over alleged malpractice (Chapter Eight). Each is a signal of what the system has been rewarding. Education therefore shapes more than knowledge. It shapes institutional expectations. ## The Teacher as an Institution Builder Education policy often focuses on buildings, curricula, examinations, and technology. These are important. Yet every successful education system ultimately depends upon people. Teachers do more than deliver lessons. They shape expectations. They model professionalism. They encourage curiosity. They reward effort. They cultivate confidence. Every interaction between teacher and student communicates something about learning, discipline, fairness, and aspiration. In this way, teachers help build not only educated individuals but institutional culture itself. ## The Cost of Weak Human Capital When educational systems fail to develop human capability, the consequences extend far beyond the classroom. Businesses struggle to recruit skilled workers. Hospitals face shortages of trained professionals. Courts depend on fewer experienced advocates. Public administration loses technical capacity. Innovation slows. Productivity suffers. Weak education eventually becomes weak governance, weaker economic growth, and reduced national competitiveness. Human capital is not one sector among many. It is the foundation upon which every sector depends. ## Education in a Federal System Nigeria’s constitutional structure also shapes how education is governed. Education is primarily a concurrent responsibility, meaning that both the Federal Government and the states have legislative and administrative roles, while local governments also play important implementation functions, particularly in basic education. This arrangement reflects the country’s federal design and requires coordination among all three tiers of government. This has important implications. When educational outcomes vary across states, the explanation is rarely found in constitutional text alone. Differences may also arise from institutional capacity, financing, policy implementation, teacher recruitment, governance, and local administrative effectiveness. Understanding these distinctions helps avoid simplistic conclusions about responsibility. The Universal Basic Education system shows how federal design shapes incentives. The federal government sets aside funds for basic education through the Universal Basic Education Commission, but states can draw on matching grants only if they provide an equal amount of counterpart funding themselves. The design is meant to encourage shared commitment. In practice, it can leave money stranded. In August 2026, the Commission reported that more than ₦65 billion in matching grants had not been accessed because states had not provided their counterpart funds, and that about ₦267 billion in previously released intervention funds was lying idle.8 Here is a vivid example of the book’s central argument. The problem is not simply that there is too little money for schools. Money exists. The system that connects it to classrooms—counterpart funding, state budgeting, procurement, and implementation capacity—is where it stalls. No single official can be blamed for billions of naira sitting unused across many states. The pattern is institutional. ## The Private Sector’s Lesson Nigeria’s private sector provides an important institutional insight. Across industries such as manufacturing, banking, telecommunications, and technology, several organizations have demonstrated the ability to build systems that endure beyond individual leaders. They recruit talent. They train employees. They establish performance standards. They measure results. They adapt to changing markets. Their continued existence under the same national conditions faced by public institutions suggests an important conclusion. Institutional quality matters. The success of companies such as Dangote Industries, major commercial banks, and leading technology firms does not imply that they operate without challenges. Rather, it shows that disciplined governance, clear incentives, professional management, and continuous investment in people can produce resilient organizations even in demanding environments. The lesson is not that government should operate exactly like a corporation. The lesson is that sustainable institutions require intentional design, capable people, and consistent accountability. ## Education Beyond Government Education is not the responsibility of government alone. Families teach values. Communities transmit culture. Businesses develop professional skills. Universities generate knowledge. Civil society encourages civic participation. Professional associations uphold standards. A nation’s learning ecosystem extends far beyond formal classrooms. When these institutions reinforce one another, human capital grows more rapidly. When they work at cross-purposes, progress becomes more difficult. ## Education and National Development Countries that transformed their economies over the past century followed different political paths, but many shared one commitment: sustained investment in education, teacher quality, technical skills, research, and institutional capacity. They recognized that roads, factories, hospitals, and digital infrastructure require educated people to design, build, maintain, and improve them. Natural resources may generate wealth. Education generates capability. Capability allows societies to adapt to changing technologies, compete globally, strengthen democratic participation, and solve increasingly complex problems. Their experiences remind us that educational reform is not measured only by spending. It is measured by outcomes, consistency, and the ability to prepare citizens for the demands of a changing society. For this reason, education should not be viewed merely as social spending. It is one of a nation’s most important long-term investments. By that standard, Nigeria’s federal investment remains modest. Education’s share of the federal budget has hovered between about 6 and 8 per cent in recent years.9 The international benchmark adopted by UNESCO member states is 15 to 20 per cent of total public expenditure.10 States and local governments also fund education, so the federal share does not capture all spending. But the gap between benchmark and practice is wide—and, as the unused matching grants show, raising allocations will achieve little unless the institutions that spend them work. ## The Nigerian Opportunity Nigeria possesses one of the youngest populations in the world. This demographic reality presents both a challenge and an extraordinary opportunity. If educational institutions consistently equip young people with knowledge, practical skills, ethical foundations, and the capacity for innovation, the country strengthens every sector simultaneously. Every conversation about Nigeria’s future eventually returns to one question: **Who will build the institutions of tomorrow?** The answer is sitting in today’s classrooms, workshops, laboratories, and training centres. The question is therefore not simply whether more children attend school. It is whether the education they receive prepares them to strengthen the institutions they will one day inherit. If we wish to strengthen institutions, we must first strengthen the people who will lead, manage, and sustain them. The classroom is the first institution of national renewal. ## Looking Ahead Education develops human capability. Healthcare protects it. A nation that educates its people but fails to preserve their health limits the return on one of its greatest investments. The next chapter therefore turns to another indispensable institution of national development: healthcare. Together, education and health form two of the most important foundations of human capital. ## Institutional Mirror Imagine the Nigeria you hope to see in twenty years. Now ask yourself: **What kind of classrooms would have to exist today to make that future possible?** The answer may reveal that the future of every institution begins long before people enter public office, courtrooms, hospitals, laboratories, or boardrooms. It begins where children first learn to think, to question, to cooperate, and to dream.

sections.markdown:
> “A nation’s greatest resource is not beneath its soil but within its people. Healthcare protects the human capacity upon which every other institution depends.” ## The Night the Ambulance Never Came It is two o’clock in the morning. A father wakes to find his young daughter struggling to breathe. Panic spreads through the household. They rush to the nearest health facility, only to discover there is no doctor on duty. The family is directed to another hospital several kilometres away. Precious time is lost in traffic, paperwork, and the search for available care. Across town, another family faces a different emergency. An expectant mother requires urgent medical attention, but the nearest facility lacks essential equipment. Healthcare workers do everything they can with the resources available, yet everyone in the room understands that the outcome depends as much on the health system as on medical skill. These stories are not unique to Nigeria. Every country has moments when individuals depend entirely on the strength of its healthcare institutions. But in Nigeria they are far too common. According to the latest United Nations estimates, Nigeria’s maternal mortality ratio in 2023 was 993 deaths per 100,000 live births, and the country accounted for about 29 per cent of all maternal deaths in the world—more than any other nation.1 Most of those deaths are preventable. They occur not because the medical knowledge to prevent them does not exist, but because the institutions that should deliver it—at the right place, at the right time—do not. The question is not whether illness will occur. The question is whether the institutions designed to protect life are prepared when it does. ## The Waiting Room A waiting room is one of the few places where every distinction begins to fade. The successful entrepreneur sits beside the market trader. The civil servant waits alongside the student. The teacher, the judge, the mechanic, the farmer, and the engineer all become patients before they become professionals. Illness is one of humanity’s great equalizers. It reminds us that beneath every title, occupation, and achievement is a human life that depends upon health. When healthcare institutions function well, most people notice them only briefly. When they fail, families remember the experience for years. Behind every consultation, diagnosis, surgery, vaccination, and emergency response stands an institution whose purpose is not merely to treat disease, but to preserve the nation’s most valuable asset—its people. ## Healthcare Is More Than Hospitals When people think about healthcare, they often picture doctors, nurses, hospitals, and medicines. These are important. But they are only the visible part of a much larger system. Healthcare also depends on institutions that: - train medical professionals; •regulate medicines and medical devices; •finance health services; •collect public health data; •monitor disease outbreaks; •maintain laboratories; •manage vaccination programmes; •inspect health facilities; •coordinate emergency responses. Primary healthcare centres, community health workers, maternal and child health services, health education, environmental sanitation, and medical research all belong to the same system. A modern healthcare system is an ecosystem of institutions working together toward a common purpose: protecting human life. Healthcare succeeds when these components work together rather than in isolation. ![Kagarawal Primary Health Centre, Gombe State, January 2022. Photo: Atibrarian / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.](/static/book/fig-124-21.jpg)

Kagarawal Primary Health Centre, Gombe State, January 2022. Photo: Atibrarian / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Primary healthcare centres are meant to be the front door of that system—the place where most Nigerians first meet it. In 2025, monitors from BudgIT’s Tracka platform visited 5,099 public primary healthcare centres across all thirty-six states and the Federal Capital Territory. They found that only about one in seven had a doctor, and roughly half had no nurse or midwife. Only half were connected to grid electricity; fewer than two-thirds had access to water. Barely half met the standard of operating around the clock. And only about one in seven had an ambulance.2 The father in the story that opened this chapter was not unlucky. He was meeting the system as it is. ![Figure 11.1. Share of 5,099 public primary health care centres, visited in all 36 states and the FCT in 2025, that met each condition. Source: BudgIT, Primary Health Care (PHC) Accountability Report (2026).](/static/book/fig-125-22.jpg)

Figure 11.1. Share of 5,099 public primary health care centres, visited in all 36 states and the FCT in 2025, that met each condition. Source: BudgIT, Primary Health Care (PHC) Accountability Report (2026).

## The Purpose of a Health System Every effective health system seeks to achieve four broad objectives. First, it promotes health by preventing disease before treatment becomes necessary. Second, it provides accessible and quality care when illness occurs. Third, it protects citizens from catastrophic financial hardship caused by medical expenses. Fourth, it responds rapidly to public health emergencies. These objectives require more than medical expertise. They require planning, financing, coordination, logistics, accountability, and public trust. In other words, they require institutions. ## Health as National Capacity Healthcare is often discussed as a social service or a humanitarian issue. It is that. But it is also an economic institution, a security institution, and a development institution. Healthy children learn more effectively. Healthy workers are more productive. Healthy entrepreneurs build stronger businesses. Healthy public servants make better decisions. Healthy communities are more resilient during crises. Conversely, weak health systems impose hidden costs across society. Families may fall into poverty because of medical bills. In Nigeria, according to the federal health ministry, households themselves paid about 72 per cent of total health expenditure in 2022, largely out of pocket at the point of care.3 When illness strikes, it is usually the family—not an insurer or the state—that pays. Employers lose skilled workers. Students miss school. Communities become more vulnerable to disease outbreaks. Hospitals do not merely restore individuals. They preserve a nation’s capacity to work, innovate, create, and govern. The health of citizens and the health of the economy are deeply connected. ## Prevention Before Cure One of the greatest achievements of modern public health is the recognition that preventing disease is often more effective than treating it. Safe drinking water. Routine immunization. Proper sanitation. Nutrition. Health education. Early diagnosis. Environmental protection. These measures rarely receive dramatic headlines. Yet they save countless lives. Strong healthcare systems therefore do more than respond to illness. They reduce the likelihood that illness occurs in the first place. Immunization shows both the promise and the gap. Nigeria has achieved what few thought possible: the elimination of wild poliovirus, described in Chapter Four. Yet in 2024, according to WHO and UNICEF estimates, about 2.1 million Nigerian children had not received a single routine vaccine dose—more “zero-dose” children than in any other country.4 The same country that defeated a virus through decades of institutional effort has not yet built a routine system that reaches every child. The healthiest societies are not necessarily those with the largest hospitals. They are often those whose institutions prevent avoidable disease. ## Institutions Before Emergencies One of the greatest tests of a health system is how it performs during a crisis. Pandemics, disease outbreaks, natural disasters, and humanitarian emergencies reveal strengths and weaknesses that may remain hidden during ordinary times. Countries with reliable surveillance systems, trained personnel, emergency logistics, and public confidence often respond more effectively than those attempting to build institutions in the middle of a crisis. Preparation cannot begin after the emergency arrives. It must already exist. This is why resilient institutions matter. ## Public and Private Healthcare Nigeria’s healthcare landscape includes both public and private providers. Public institutions play a central role in ensuring equitable access, disease surveillance, regulation, and national health programmes. Private hospitals, clinics, diagnostic centres, pharmacies, and faith-based providers also contribute significantly to service delivery, innovation, and investment. The relationship between these sectors should not be viewed as a competition. It is a partnership. The question is not whether one sector should replace the other. The question is whether both operate within a regulatory and institutional framework that promotes quality, accountability, and access for all citizens. ## The Healthcare Workforce Every healthcare system ultimately depends on people. Doctors. Nurses. Pharmacists. Laboratory scientists. Community health workers. Midwives. Therapists. Public health professionals. Researchers. Hospital administrators. Support staff. Buildings do not heal patients. People do. Their education, motivation, working conditions, professional development, and retention determine the system’s capacity. Retention has become one of Nigeria’s most pressing health challenges. In April 2024, the Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria reported that of some 130,000 doctors registered since 1963, only about 58,000—fewer than 45 per cent—had renewed their practising licences.5 Not every missing licence represents emigration; some doctors have retired, died, or left medicine. But the figure points to a workforce draining away faster than it is being replaced. The individual decisions behind it are understandable. The pattern is institutional: pay, working conditions, equipment, and career prospects that persuade trained professionals to leave. When skilled professionals are adequately supported, institutions become stronger. When they are consistently overstretched or unsupported, institutional performance suffers regardless of infrastructure. Healthcare workers thrive where institutions enable them to perform at their best. ## Trust as Medicine Patients often seek treatment at moments of vulnerability. They trust that diagnoses are accurate. That medicines are safe. That confidential information will remain protected. That decisions are guided by professional judgment rather than personal interest. Trust cannot be manufactured overnight. It is earned through consistent institutional behaviour: transparent regulation, professional accountability, reliable standards, and compassionate care. When healthcare institutions earn public trust, people seek care earlier, comply with treatment more consistently, and participate more willingly in public health programmes. Trust itself becomes a public health asset. ## The Nigerian Opportunity Nigeria has produced healthcare professionals whose expertise is recognized around the world. The country’s medical schools, teaching hospitals, research institutions, and healthcare workers have demonstrated remarkable dedication, often under demanding conditions. The challenge is not a shortage of talent. It is strengthening the institutions that enable that talent to serve the nation effectively and sustainably. Investment in primary healthcare, workforce development, technology, research, financing, and institutional accountability has the potential to improve not only health outcomes but also productivity, educational attainment, and long-term economic development. The success of a healthcare system is not measured only by the number of hospitals it contains. It is measured by whether citizens can receive timely, affordable, safe, and effective care when they need it most. Protecting life is one of the oldest responsibilities of organized government. Fulfilling that responsibility requires more than compassion. It requires institutions capable of planning, coordinating, financing, regulating, and continually improving healthcare for generations. Financing remains the foundation. In April 2001, African heads of state met in Abuja and pledged to allocate at least 15 per cent of their annual budgets to health. A quarter of a century later, the federal government’s proposed 2026 budget allocated about ₦2.48 trillion to health—roughly 4.3 per cent of the total.6 Yet the picture is not uniform. An analysis of 2026 state budget proposals found that nine states, including Kano, Kaduna, Ogun, Oyo, and Kwara, had met the Abuja target.7 Some of the most promising commitments are coming not from the centre but from the states. ### Evidence Box: Vital Signs of the Health System - **Maternal deaths:** 993 per 100,000 live births in 2023; about 29 per cent of the world’s maternal deaths.8 •**Primary healthcare (5,099 facilities visited, 2025):** 13.8 per cent with a doctor; 50.4 per cent with at least one nurse or midwife; 51.4 per cent with grid electricity; 62 per cent with water; 53.5 per cent meeting 24-hour operating standards; 13.9 per cent with an ambulance.9 •**Immunization:** about 2.1 million zero-dose children in 2024, the highest number of any country.10 •**Who pays:** households funded about 72 per cent of health spending in 2022.11 •**Workforce:** about 58,000 of 130,000 registered doctors had renewed their licences (2024).12 •**Funding:** federal health allocation about 4.3 per cent of the 2026 budget, against the 15 per cent Abuja pledge; nine states met the pledge in their 2026 proposals.13 *Each figure reflects decisions about funding, staffing, maintenance, and* *accountability made over many years and by many hands. Together they* *describe a system, not a single failure.* Healthcare should therefore be viewed not simply as expenditure. It is an investment in national capability. ## Looking Ahead Education prepares people for public service. Healthcare preserves their capacity to serve. But no institution can function effectively without an organization responsible for implementing public policy. That responsibility belongs to the civil service. The next chapter examines one of the least understood yet most important institutions in national governance: the professional public service that connects government decisions to everyday reality. ## Institutional Mirror Imagine a nation with world-class hospitals but weak public health institutions. Now imagine another with modest hospitals but strong preventive care, trusted primary healthcare, and effective disease surveillance. Which nation is likely to produce healthier outcomes over time? The answer reminds us that healthcare is not simply about treating illness. It is about designing institutions that protect health before illness becomes inevitable.

sections.markdown:
> “Governments make promises. Civil services turn promises into policies, policies into programmes, and programmes into public outcomes.” ## The Minister’s First Day A newly appointed minister arrives at the ministry with energy, ideas, and ambition. There are speeches to deliver, policies to announce, and expectations to meet. Yet before any reform can begin, one reality becomes clear. The minister does not run the ministry alone. Behind every political office stands an institution that existed long before the minister’s appointment and will remain after the minister leaves. Files are maintained by career officers. Budgets are prepared by professional administrators. Projects are monitored by technical departments. Payrolls are managed by established systems. Procurement follows administrative procedures. Records stretch back decades. This is the civil service. Its work is often invisible to the public. Yet without it, modern government would struggle to function. ![The Federal Secretariat complex, Abuja, home to many federal ministries, 2021. Photo: OtuNwachinemere / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.](/static/book/fig-133-23.jpg)

The Federal Secretariat complex, Abuja, home to many federal ministries, 2021. Photo: OtuNwachinemere / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

## Monday Morning Consider the first working day after a national election. The election may have transformed the political landscape. New leaders may be preparing to assume office. Policies may soon change. Cabinets may be reshuffled. Yet across ministries, departments, and agencies, thousands of public servants report to work as they did the previous week. Files continue to move. Budgets continue to be processed. Hospitals continue providing care. Schools continue teaching. Public records continue to be maintained. Government does not begin again after every election. It continues because institutions continue. At the centre of that continuity stands the civil service. ## The Bridge Between Policy and Reality Democratic politics naturally attracts public attention. Elections, campaigns, debates, and cabinet appointments dominate the headlines. The daily work of governance, however, depends on a different institution. The civil service is the permanent administrative arm of the state. Its purpose is not to compete in elections. Its purpose is to ensure continuity, professionalism, and effective implementation regardless of which political party forms the government. Political leaders establish priorities. They present manifestos. They announce reforms. They propose budgets. They introduce legislation. But between every political decision and every practical outcome stands an institution responsible for turning ideas into action. Political leaders determine direction. Civil servants provide institutional capacity. One decides what should be done. The other determines how it can be done. A policy that exists only in a speech changes nothing. A policy that is professionally implemented changes lives. ## The Purpose of a Civil Service An effective civil service performs several indispensable functions. It translates political decisions into implementable programmes. It advises elected officials using technical expertise and institutional memory. It prepares budgets, administers public resources, drafts regulations, supervises implementation, evaluates performance, and preserves the continuity of government. In short, it transforms political vision into administrative reality. Without this capacity, even the best ideas remain speeches rather than achievements. ## Continuity and Institutional Memory Democratic societies expect political leadership to change. That change is healthy. It allows citizens to evaluate performance and choose new directions. Yet if every election required rebuilding the machinery of government from the beginning, no nation could function effectively. Every organization accumulates knowledge. Experienced officials understand procedures. They preserve records. They advise incoming leaders. They understand why previous reforms succeeded or failed. They remember legal precedents, administrative challenges, and operational realities that may not appear in official documents. This institutional memory is invaluable. It prevents governments from repeating avoidable mistakes and helps new administrations build upon earlier achievements rather than starting from the beginning every four years. A professional civil service provides stability without preventing democratic change. It enables governments to change while ensuring that the state continues to function. Countries with strong administrative continuity are often better able to sustain long-term development strategies. ## Professionalism Before Politics A professional civil service is built on principles rather than personalities. Public servants are entrusted with responsibilities that affect millions of lives. They manage public resources. Administer programmes. Enforce regulations. Provide technical advice. Maintain public records. Their legitimacy depends on competence, impartiality, integrity, and continuity. Citizens should expect public officials to administer the law fairly regardless of political affiliation, ethnicity, religion, or personal relationships. Professional public administration does not mean the absence of personal beliefs. It means the discipline to serve the public interest regardless of political transitions. Professionalism does not eliminate disagreement. It ensures that disagreement occurs within institutions governed by clear rules. The more predictable and impartial the administration, the greater the public’s confidence in government itself. ## Merit and Motivation No institution consistently outperforms the quality of the people within it. Recruitment, promotion, training, evaluation, and leadership development are therefore institutional—not merely personnel—questions. When appointments reward competence, institutions accumulate expertise over time. When advancement depends primarily on factors unrelated to performance, organizational capacity gradually weakens. Recruitment is where this matters first. In July 2023, three commissioners of the Federal Character Commission—the body charged with ensuring fair representation in public employment—told a House of Representatives committee that recruitment slots were being sold and that relatives of officials had been placed in well-paid agencies. The commission’s chairman denied the allegations and said they were a response to her own refusal to sell jobs.1 Whatever the truth of the specific claims, the hearing was part of a wider parliamentary investigation into employment racketeering across ministries, agencies, and tertiary institutions. Where public jobs can be bought, the people who fill them have been selected for something other than competence—and the institution pays for it for decades. The issue is not simply fairness. It is effectiveness. ## Capacity Is a National Asset The quality of a civil service cannot be measured solely by its size. Its true strength lies in its capacity. Can it design effective policies? Can it analyse evidence? Can it manage complex projects? Can it monitor performance? Can it adapt to technological change? Can it deliver services efficiently? Can it learn from experience? These capabilities determine whether ambitious national plans become practical achievements. Administrative competence is therefore not a bureaucratic luxury. It is a strategic national resource. It is also a substantial national investment. More than 600,000 federal civil servants, working across some 508 ministries, departments, and agencies, are now managed through the government’s integrated payroll and personnel system.2 Their salaries, together with the cost of servicing public debt, absorb a very large share of federal revenue; one analysis of official budget figures found that in the first seven months of 2025, personnel costs and debt service together exceeded the federal government’s entire revenue.3 When so much of the budget is committed before a single road is built or a single clinic is equipped, the productivity of every public servant becomes a question of national importance. ## Reforming the Engine While It Is Running Unlike a private company, governments cannot suspend operations while they reorganize. Schools must remain open. Hospitals must continue treating patients. Security agencies must perform their duties. Revenue must still be collected. This makes civil service reform particularly demanding. Reformers must improve systems without interrupting the delivery of essential public services. Calls for reform often focus on organizational charts. New departments. Merged agencies. Revised reporting lines. Structural changes can sometimes improve efficiency. But lasting reform reaches deeper. It examines recruitment. Training. Performance evaluation. Promotion. Digital transformation. Ethical standards. Leadership development. Institutional culture. Accountability. A stronger organizational chart cannot compensate for weak institutional incentives. Even restructuring, however, can prove extraordinarily difficult. In 2011, the government set up a committee, chaired by the former Head of the Civil Service Stephen Oronsaye, to review the federal government’s 541 parastatals, commissions, and agencies. Its 2012 report recommended reducing statutory agencies from 263 to 161—scrapping 38, merging 52, and returning 14 to their parent ministries.4 The government’s white paper rejected most of the recommendations. Successive administrations set up committees to review the report again. In February 2024, twelve years after it was submitted, the federal government approved its full implementation, with a twelve-week deadline.5 Implementation since then has been selective. Some mergers were announced; major revenue-generating and regulatory bodies were left untouched. Within months, a new federal ministry had been created, and the National Assembly has continued to pass bills establishing new agencies, some of which overlap with bodies that already exist.6 The pattern is instructive. Every agency has a mandate, staff, a budget, and supporters in government and the legislature. Creating an agency distributes benefits to identifiable people; merging or closing one imposes costs on them, while the savings are spread thinly across everyone. Without an institution that changes those incentives—a rule, for instance, that every proposal for a new agency must show it does not duplicate an existing one—the system will tend to grow, whatever any single administration intends. ![Figure 12.1. Key events in the history of the Oronsaye report on rationalizing federal agencies. Sources: Sahara Reporters (2024); Arise News (2024); The ICIR (2026).](/static/book/fig-139-24.jpg)

Figure 12.1. Key events in the history of the Oronsaye report on rationalizing federal agencies. Sources: Sahara Reporters (2024); Arise News (2024); The ICIR (2026).

Successful reform therefore depends on careful planning, broad institutional support, staff development, and sustained political commitment—aligning people, processes, technology, and purpose. ## Learning from Success Nigeria’s own experience demonstrates that institutional improvement is possible. In June 2026, the Office of the Head of the Civil Service concluded a review of its five-year Federal Civil Service Strategy and Implementation Plan, reporting gains in the digitization of government processes, workforce management, and capacity building, and setting out a next phase of reform.7 Across different periods, reforms in areas such as public financial management, treasury systems, digital government services, procurement, tax administration, and regulatory modernization have shown that administrative institutions can evolve. The private sector offers similar lessons. Large Nigerian enterprises that have endured for decades did not survive through vision alone. They invested in systems, professional management, succession planning, internal controls, and continuous staff development. The lesson is clear. Organizations become sustainable when they depend less on extraordinary individuals and more on strong institutional processes. ## The Nigerian Opportunity ### Evidence Box: The Civil Service in Numbers - **Workforce:** more than 600,000 federal civil servants across about 508 ministries, departments, and agencies on the integrated payroll and personnel system (2026).8 •**Cost:** personnel costs and debt service together exceeded total federal revenue in January–July 2025, according to an analysis of official budget figures.9 •**Restructuring:** the 2012 Oronsaye report proposed cutting statutory agencies from 263 to 161; its full implementation was approved only in February 2024.10 •**Recruitment:** allegations of sold recruitment slots at the Federal Character Commission were aired before a House of Representatives committee in July 2023 and denied by the commission’s chairman.11 •**Payroll integrity:** more than 43,000 ghost workers removed through biometric payroll verification by 2016 (Chapter Eight). *A civil service is not judged by its size or its cost alone, but by what it delivers for* *both. These figures suggest why the question of how public servants are* *recruited, organized, and motivated is central to Nigeria’s future.* Nigeria’s civil service has played an essential role in maintaining governmental continuity through periods of political transition, constitutional change, economic reform, and democratic consolidation. Across the federation, countless public servants perform their duties with professionalism and dedication, often under demanding circumstances. The opportunity before Nigeria is to strengthen the systems that enable excellence to become the norm rather than the exception. Investment in professional development, merit-based advancement, digital governance, transparent performance management, and institutional accountability can significantly improve public service delivery. Every citizen experiences the civil service, whether directly or indirectly. A passport application. A driver’s licence. A tax assessment. A school inspection. A hospital budget. A court registry. A business permit. When the civil service performs effectively, government becomes more reliable, predictable, and trustworthy. When it performs poorly, citizens lose confidence not only in individual agencies but in the state itself. For this reason, civil service reform is not an administrative luxury. It is a national development strategy. A nation’s ambitions can never exceed the capacity of the institutions responsible for implementing them. ## Looking Ahead The civil service manages public programmes. Those programmes require public resources. How governments raise, allocate, manage, and account for those resources determines whether national priorities become reality. The next chapter therefore examines another foundational institution: public finance. For institutions can only deliver sustainably when financial stewardship is transparent, responsible, and accountable. ## Institutional Mirror Before asking whether government policies are succeeding, ask another question: **Do our institutions have the administrative capacity to implement those policies consistently, fairly, and effectively?** A policy without implementation is an intention. A capable civil service transforms intention into public value.

sections.epigraph: Every budget is a moral document. It reveals not only what a nation can afford, but what it chooses to value.
questions: Does our system consistently ensure that public resources produce measurable public value?
sections.opening: In a government office, officials gather around a conference table. Representatives from education argue for more classrooms. Health officials request additional funding for primary healthcare. Engineers seek resources for roads and bridges.
sections.markdown:
> “Every budget is a moral document. It reveals not only what a nation can afford, but what it chooses to value.” ## The Budget Meeting In a government office, officials gather around a conference table. Representatives from education argue for more classrooms. Health officials request additional funding for primary healthcare. Engineers seek resources for roads and bridges. Security agencies present their operational needs. Agriculture officials advocate for irrigation and rural development. Every proposal has merit. Every request addresses a genuine public need. Yet the available resources are limited. The question is no longer simply, “What should government do?” The question becomes: **“How should government decide?”** Every family understands this dilemma. At the beginning of a new month, income is limited. The children need school fees. The rent is due. Food must be purchased. Savings should be set aside. Unexpected emergencies must be anticipated. Choosing one expense often means postponing another. The family’s future depends not simply on how much money it earns, but on how wisely it manages what it has. The same principle applies to nations. Public finance begins where ambition meets reality. ![The headquarters of the Central Bank of Nigeria, Abuja, 2017. Photo: GodwinPaya / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.](/static/book/fig-143-25.jpg)

The headquarters of the Central Bank of Nigeria, Abuja, 2017. Photo: GodwinPaya / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

## Beyond Revenue Many citizens judge government finances by a single measure: How much money does the government earn? That is only part of the story. Public finance asks a broader set of questions. How is revenue generated? How predictable is that revenue? How is it allocated? How efficiently is it spent? Who monitors its use? What systems exist to prevent waste? How are future obligations financed? Every public institution depends upon the answers. Schools require teachers, classrooms, and learning materials. Hospitals require medicines, equipment, and trained professionals. Roads require construction and maintenance. Courts require personnel and infrastructure. Security agencies require training, technology, and logistics. Public finance is the bloodstream of government. When resources are managed responsibly, institutions function more effectively. When they are mismanaged, institutional performance weakens regardless of policy intentions. Public finance is therefore not simply about money. It is about stewardship—and about the institutions that manage public resources responsibly. ## Revenue and the Social Contract Before governments can spend, they must raise revenue. Taxes. Royalties. Customs duties. Fees. Returns from public investments. Natural resource revenues. Borrowing. Each source carries responsibilities as well as opportunities. Taxes occupy a unique place in the relationship between citizens and the state. When citizens contribute part of their income to government, they do so with an expectation. They expect security. They expect justice. They expect infrastructure. They expect education. They expect healthcare. Taxes are therefore more than financial transactions. They are expressions of trust. Governments ask citizens to contribute today in exchange for public goods that benefit society as a whole. The strength of that relationship depends heavily on transparency, accountability, and performance. Where citizens believe public resources are managed responsibly, voluntary compliance tends to improve. Where confidence declines, tax compliance often becomes more difficult. Trust strengthens compliance. Compliance strengthens revenue. Revenue strengthens public institutions. The relationship is circular. Nigeria has recently tried to reset that relationship by law. In June 2025, the President signed four tax reform acts—the Nigeria Tax Act, the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, the Nigeria Revenue Service (Establishment) Act, and the Joint Revenue Board (Establishment) Act—which took effect on 1 January 2026.1 Their aim is to simplify a tax system long criticized as fragmented and to broaden a revenue base that has relied heavily on oil. The base is narrow. By the internationally comparable measure used by the OECD, Nigeria collected tax equal to about 8 percent of its GDP in 2023, roughly half the average of 16 percent across the thirty-eight African countries covered by the same study. The Nigeria Revenue Service, using a broader measure, reports higher figures and a rising trend, with tax collections growing from about ₦21 trillion in 2024 to ₦28.3 trillion in 2025.2 Whether they succeed will depend less on the text of the laws than on the institutions that administer them, and on whether citizens come to believe that what they pay returns to them as public value. ## Budgets as National Priorities Every budget answers a simple but profound question: **What matters most?** No nation can fund every desirable programme immediately. Choices must be made. Resources directed toward one priority are unavailable for another. Budgets therefore communicate values as much as numbers. Financial decisions reveal priorities more clearly than speeches. A government that consistently invests in education, healthcare, infrastructure, justice, research, and institutional capacity signals its long-term priorities through action rather than rhetoric. A government that repeatedly postpones maintenance, underfunds essential services, or accumulates unsustainable obligations sends different signals. Budgeting is not merely accounting. It is governance in numerical form. It is also, too often, a promise rather than a plan. The civic-technology group BudgIT, through its Tracka platform, sends monitors to check whether federally funded capital projects actually exist on the ground. In its review of 2,760 projects from the 2024 budget across thirty states, it found evidence of completion for only about half (see Chapter Two). Of ₦15.07 billion released for projects that its monitors judged to have been delivered fraudulently—through diversion, repeat payment, or substandard work—₦8.61 billion was affected.3 The federal government reported that the 2024 budget as a whole had reached about 80 percent implementation, but that figure covers salaries and running costs as well as capital projects.4 The gap between the two numbers is the gap between money released and value delivered. ## Institutions That Protect Public Money Public resources belong to the people. Governments administer them in trust. Collecting revenue is only the beginning. Effective public finance depends on institutions that ensure funds are used lawfully, efficiently, and transparently. Legislatures authorize expenditure. Treasury institutions manage public funds. Auditors examine compliance. Procurement systems regulate public purchasing. Anti-corruption agencies investigate misconduct. Courts enforce legal accountability. Each institution performs a distinct role. When one fails, pressure increases on the others. When they function together, public confidence grows. Transparent procurement, independent auditing, legislative oversight, public financial reporting, internal controls, digital payment systems, and citizen access to information are not administrative formalities. They are institutional safeguards. Strong accountability protects honest public servants, deters misuse of resources, and strengthens public confidence. Transparency does not eliminate every problem. But it makes problems easier to detect and correct. Accountability is therefore an institutional ecosystem rather than the responsibility of any single agency. Nigeria has many of these institutions in law. The Fiscal Responsibility Act and the Public Procurement Act, both passed in 2007, set rules for budgeting, borrowing, and public purchasing. The Office of the Auditor-General for the Federation audits federal spending every year. Its findings show both the value of the institution and the limits of its power. In July 2026, the Auditor-General sent the National Assembly a report on federal ministries, departments, and agencies for the 2024 financial year that identified more than ₦1.34 trillion in irregularities and internal- control failures: payments without supporting documents, contracts awarded irregularly, revenue that was collected but not remitted, and cash advances never accounted for.5 Such reports are referred to the legislature’s public accounts committees. A bill to strengthen the independence of the federal audit service has been passed by the National Assembly but, at the time of writing, had not been signed into law.6 The auditor can find the problem. Whether anything happens next depends on other institutions doing their part. ## Borrowing and Future Generations Governments occasionally borrow to finance development, respond to emergencies, or invest in long-term infrastructure. Borrowing is not inherently irresponsible. When wisely invested in infrastructure, education, healthcare, energy, or technology, borrowed resources may strengthen future prosperity. But borrowing also creates obligations. Today’s decisions become tomorrow’s repayments. Future generations inherit not only roads, schools, hospitals, and power systems. They also inherit financial obligations. Good public finance therefore asks not only whether borrowing is affordable today, but whether the investments it finances will generate lasting value for future generations. Intergenerational fairness is one of the least discussed but most important principles of fiscal governance. Nigeria’s public debt has risen sharply. At the end of 2015, the total debt of the federal government, the states, and the Federal Capital Territory stood at about ₦12.6 trillion.7 By June 2026, it was ₦166.79 trillion.8 Part of this increase is an accounting change rather than new borrowing: in 2023, ₦22.7 trillion of overdrafts that the federal government had taken from the Central Bank—known as Ways and Means advances—were converted into formal debt, and the devaluation of the naira raised the naira value of foreign loans.9 But the cost of servicing that debt is real. The World Bank estimated that debt service absorbed about 96 percent of federal government revenue in 2022.10 Since then, revenue has grown and the ratio has fallen. Even so, the Budget Office’s implementation report for 2024 shows the federal government paying ₦11.89 trillion in debt service out of revenue of ₦19.35 trillion—about 61 kobo of every naira it earned.11 The debt itself is smaller as a share of the economy than in many countries, especially after the 2025 revision of Nigeria’s GDP figures; the difficulty lies in how little revenue the government raises to pay for it. ![Figure 13.1. Nigeria’s total public debt, 2015–2026. The 2023 increase includes ₦22.7 trillion of Central Bank overdrafts converted into formal debt. Source: Debt Management Office, as reported in the notes.](/static/book/fig-149-26.jpg)

Figure 13.1. Nigeria’s total public debt, 2015–2026. The 2023 increase includes ₦22.7 trillion of Central Bank overdrafts converted into formal debt. Source: Debt Management Office, as reported in the notes.

Borrowing is a decision made today and paid for by people who may not yet be able to vote. ## Lessons from the Private Sector Successful businesses understand that growth depends on disciplined financial management. Revenue must be tracked. Expenditure must be justified. Investments must produce value. Internal controls must reduce waste. Audits strengthen confidence. Long-term planning guides decision-making. Governments differ from businesses in important ways. Their objectives include public welfare rather than profit. Yet the institutional principles of financial discipline, transparency, planning, and accountability remain remarkably similar. The lesson is not to manage government as a corporation. The lesson is that every enduring institution must manage resources with integrity. ### Evidence Box: Following the Money - **Public debt:** ₦12.6 trillion at the end of 2015; ₦166.79 trillion in June 2026, of which ₦91.59 trillion was domestic.12 •**Debt service:** about 96 percent of federal government revenue in 2022, according to the World Bank; about 61 percent in 2024, from Budget Office figures.13 •**Capital projects:** about half of 2,760 tracked 2024 federal capital projects found completed on the ground.14 •**Audit:** more than ₦1.34 trillion in irregularities and control failures identified in federal MDAs for 2024.15 •**Tax base:** tax revenue of about 8 percent of GDP in 2023 (OECD measure), against an African average of 16 percent.16 •**Tax reform:** four new tax laws in force from 1 January 2026.17 *Public money is not lost in one place. It leaks at many points—in how it is raised,* *allocated, spent, and accounted for. Each leak has an institutional remedy.* ## The Nigerian Opportunity Nigeria possesses significant economic potential. Its population, entrepreneurial energy, natural resources, expanding digital economy, and growing private sector provide opportunities for sustainable national development. Realizing that potential depends partly upon strengthening public financial management. Predictable budgeting. Efficient revenue administration. Transparent procurement. Prudent debt management. Independent oversight. Timely auditing. Performance- based expenditure. Digital financial systems. These institutional improvements do more than protect public funds. They strengthen public trust and improve the quality of public services across every sector. Money alone does not create development. But without disciplined institutions to manage public money, development becomes difficult to sustain. A nation’s prosperity depends not only on the wealth it possesses. It depends on the wisdom with which that wealth is governed. ## Looking Ahead Public finance provides resources. Justice ensures that those resources—and the authority to manage them—are exercised according to law. Without trusted legal institutions, financial accountability becomes difficult to sustain. The next chapter therefore examines one of the oldest responsibilities of government: the administration of justice. ## Institutional Mirror Before asking whether government spends enough, ask another question: **Does our system consistently ensure that public resources produce measurable public value?** Public finance is not judged by the size of the budget alone. It is judged by the lives that budget improves.

sections.epigraph: The rule of law is not proven by the existence of laws. It is proven by the confidence that those laws will be applied fairly, consistently, and without fear or favour.
questions: Can ordinary citizens reasonably expect those laws to protect them equally?
sections.opening: Two entrepreneurs decide to invest their life savings in separate businesses. Both sign contracts. Both hire employees. Both borrow money.
sections.markdown:
> “The rule of law is not proven by the existence of laws. It is proven by the confidence that those laws will be applied fairly, consistently, and without fear or favour.” ## Two Business Owners Two entrepreneurs decide to invest their life savings in separate businesses. Both sign contracts. Both hire employees. Both borrow money. Both expect the law to protect their investments. Months later, disputes arise. The first entrepreneur turns to the courts. The case is heard fairly. Evidence is examined. The judgment is delivered within a reasonable time. The decision is enforced. Business continues. The second entrepreneur also seeks justice. Years pass. Hearings are repeatedly adjourned. Records are misplaced. Costs continue to rise. The uncertainty discourages further investment. The dispute eventually becomes more expensive than the original business itself. Neither entrepreneur merely needed a judge. They needed an institution capable of delivering justice. When people believe an independent institution can resolve disagreements fairly, they seek lawful solutions. When they believe justice depends upon wealth, influence, or personal connections, they begin searching for alternatives. Some abandon the investment. Others avoid future partnerships altogether. Still others attempt to settle disputes outside lawful institutions. The contract is not broken simply because disagreement occurs. It is broken when confidence in impartial justice disappears. That difference shapes entire economies. ![The High Court of Lagos State, Lagos Judicial Division, 2019. Photo: Comradeayobami / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.](/static/book/fig-154-27.jpg)

The High Court of Lagos State, Lagos Judicial Division, 2019. Photo: Comradeayobami / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

## What Is the Rule of Law? The rule of law is often misunderstood as simply having laws. Every nation has laws. Some have thousands. The true question is different. **Do those laws govern everyone equally?** The rule of law rests upon several principles. No individual is above the law. Government itself is subject to legal limits. Rights are protected. Disputes are resolved by independent institutions. Judicial decisions are respected and enforced. Legal processes are predictable rather than arbitrary. Every modern society depends upon this predictability. Citizens need confidence that contracts will be enforced. Families expect protection for their rights and property. Communities rely on peaceful mechanisms for resolving conflict. Governments themselves depend upon lawful authority rather than arbitrary power. The rule of law does not eliminate disagreement. It provides a peaceful way to manage it. By the measure of the World Justice Project, which surveys households and legal experts in more than 140 countries, Nigeria has a long way to go. Its 2025 Rule of Law Index placed Nigeria 120th of 143 countries, with a score of 0.41 out of 1, and 26th of the thirty-eight African countries assessed. Rwanda, the highest-ranked African country, scored 0.63.1 Such indices have limitations—they rely partly on perceptions and compress complex systems into single numbers—but they measure something that matters: whether the people who live under a legal system believe it works. ## Justice Beyond the Courtroom Courts are the visible face of justice. But justice begins long before a judge delivers a decision. Police investigate offences. Prosecutors evaluate evidence. Lawyers represent parties. Judges interpret the law. Court registries maintain records. Legal aid makes representation accessible. Correctional institutions implement lawful sentences. Alternative dispute resolution mechanisms resolve many conflicts outside the courtroom. Each institution performs a distinct function. Justice is therefore not one institution. It is an ecosystem. Weakness in one part affects confidence in the whole. Nowhere is this clearer than in Nigeria’s custodial centres. In February 2026, the Controller-General of the Nigerian Correctional Service told a House of Representatives committee that the centres held 80,812 people. Of these, 51,955—about 64 percent—had not been convicted of any offence. They were awaiting trial.2 Some have waited for years. The World Justice Project has reported cases of people held without trial for more than a decade.3 ![Figure 14.1. Status of people held in Nigeria’s custodial centres, February 2026. Source: Nigerian Correctional Service, as reported in BusinessDay, February 12, 2026.](/static/book/fig-156-28.jpg)

Figure 14.1. Status of people held in Nigeria’s custodial centres, February 2026. Source: Nigerian Correctional Service, as reported in BusinessDay, February 12, 2026.

This is not a failure of the prisons alone. A person may be detained because the police have not completed an investigation, because a prosecutor has not filed charges, because a case file has been lost, because a court has adjourned repeatedly, because the accused cannot afford a lawyer or bail, or because no one is tracking how long he has been held. Each institution can point to another. The result is the same: tens of thousands of people, presumed innocent by the Constitution, living in conditions designed for the convicted, at public expense. Nigeria has written the remedy into law. The Administration of Criminal Justice Act of 2015 sets time limits on remand, requires arrests to be recorded and reported, and provides for the inspection of places of detention. Because Nigeria is a federation, each state must adopt its own version; all thirty-six had done so by 2023, but implementation depends on funding, coordination, and record-keeping that remain uneven.4 The law is a good one. What it needs is institutions that apply it every day. ## Why Investors Watch the Courts The rule of law is not only a constitutional principle. It is an economic institution. Before investing, businesses ask practical questions. Will contracts be enforced? Can property rights be protected? Will commercial disputes be resolved fairly? Can regulatory decisions be challenged through lawful procedures? Where answers to these questions inspire confidence, investment becomes less risky. Where uncertainty dominates, businesses demand higher returns to compensate for greater risk—or invest elsewhere. Banks depend upon reliable property rights. Innovation flourishes where intellectual property receives legal protection. Labour markets function better where employment rights are respected. Trust in legal institutions lowers the cost of cooperation throughout society. Justice therefore influences economic growth as much as legal philosophy. ## Equality Before the Law Perhaps the greatest promise of constitutional democracy is that the law applies equally to all. The wealthy and the poor. The powerful and the powerless. Public officials and private citizens. Majorities and minorities. Equality before the law does not require identical circumstances. It requires impartial principles. Citizens are more likely to obey laws voluntarily when they believe those laws are applied consistently. If similar cases receive dramatically different treatment because of wealth, influence, ethnicity, religion, or political affiliation, public trust gradually erodes. The legitimacy of a justice system depends not only on its decisions but also on public confidence in its impartiality. Justice must therefore not only be done. It must be seen to be done. ## Delayed Justice One of the oldest observations in legal thought is that justice delayed can become justice denied. Lengthy delays increase costs. Witnesses become unavailable. Evidence deteriorates. Businesses postpone investment. Families remain in uncertainty. Victims lose confidence. Accused persons wait for resolution. Timely justice is therefore not simply an administrative objective. It is part of substantive justice itself. Efficiency strengthens fairness. Nigeria has also shown that delay is not inevitable. In 2002, Lagos State opened the Lagos Multi-Door Courthouse, described as Africa’s first court-connected centre for alternative dispute resolution. Instead of waiting years for a trial, parties to a commercial, family, or neighbourhood dispute could be referred to mediation or arbitration. In 2014 and 2015, about two-thirds of the matters it concluded were settled, and other states, including Enugu, have since established multi-door courthouses of their own.5 The institution did not make judges unnecessary. It made courts more effective by ensuring that the cases reaching them were the ones that truly needed a judge. ## Institutions Before Individuals History remembers distinguished judges. Yet no justice system can depend upon exceptional individuals alone. Justice depends upon institutions capable of applying the law with independence, professionalism, competence, and integrity. Strong judicial institutions ensure that fairness survives changes in personnel. Transparent appointment processes. Professional judicial and legal education. Reliable court administration. Digital case management. Adequate funding. Ethical oversight. Respect for judicial independence. Some of these features are improving. In 2024, the federal government enacted a law increasing the salaries and allowances of judicial officers by about 300 percent.6 Better pay does not guarantee integrity, but poorly paid judges are more exposed to pressure, and a profession that cannot attract its best lawyers to the bench weakens over time. Together, these institutional features help transform justice from personal virtue into organizational capacity. No justice system is perfect. Every system faces pressure. Institutional strength lies in the capacity to uphold legal principles even when doing so is difficult. ## Learning from Comparative Experience Across the world, countries with stronger rule-of-law traditions differ in language, religion, culture, and political history. What they often share is not identical legal systems. They share institutional consistency. Court decisions are generally respected. Contracts are enforceable. Administrative decisions can be reviewed. Citizens possess meaningful legal remedies. The lesson is not that one legal tradition is universally superior. The lesson is that institutions become trusted when they apply the law consistently over time. ### Evidence Box: Justice in Numbers - **Rule of law:** 120th of 143 countries in the World Justice Project Rule of Law Index 2025 (score 0.41 of 1).7 •**Pre-trial detention:** 51,955 of 80,812 people in custodial centres—about 64 percent—were awaiting trial in February 2026.8 •**Reform law:** the Administration of Criminal Justice Act 2015 sets time limits on remand; states must adopt their own versions.9 •**Dispute resolution:** the Lagos Multi-Door Courthouse, opened in 2002, settled about two-thirds of the matters it concluded in 2014–15.10 •**Judicial pay:** salaries and allowances of judicial officers raised by about 300 percent in 2024.11 *The rule of law is measured not by the number of laws on the books, but by how* *long an ordinary person waits for justice—and whether he can trust the result.* ## The Nigerian Opportunity Nigeria possesses a long-established judicial tradition supported by constitutional institutions, legal practitioners, universities, customary courts, and a legal profession that has contributed significantly to the country’s democratic development. Like every justice system, it continues to face opportunities for improvement in areas such as efficiency, accessibility, case management, technological modernization, legal aid, and public confidence. Every citizen eventually depends upon the justice system. A family resolving inheritance. A business enforcing a contract. A journalist defending freedom of expression. A worker seeking employment rights. A victim seeking accountability. A government defending lawful authority. Without confidence in the law, constitutions weaken. Contracts become uncertain. Public finance suffers. Investment declines. Citizens increasingly rely on informal arrangements rather than formal institutions. A trusted justice system, by contrast, encourages investment, protects rights, resolves conflict peacefully, and reinforces the legitimacy of every other public institution. The rule of law is therefore not simply one institution among many. It is the framework that allows all other institutions to function with legitimacy. ## Looking Ahead Courts settle disputes about how power is used. Elections settle who holds it. Both depend on rules that losers as well as winners are willing to accept. When those rules are trusted, power changes hands peacefully. When they are not, every contest becomes a crisis. The next chapter therefore examines the institution through which Nigerians choose their leaders: politics and elections. ## Institutional Mirror Before asking whether we have enough laws, ask another question: **Can ordinary citizens reasonably expect those laws to protect them equally?** A nation is governed not by the number of its laws, but by the confidence that justice will prevail regardless of status, wealth, or influence.

notes.2: Godsgift Onyedinefu, “Prisons under Strain as 2 of Every 3 Inmates Awaiting Trial,” *BusinessDay*, February 12, 2026, reporting figures presented by Sylvester Nwakuche, Controller-General of the Nigerian Correctional Service, as of February 9, 2026.
