sections.markdown:
> “An election does not only choose a leader. It teaches every future candidate what it takes to win.” ## The Price of a Form In April 2022, Nigeria’s ruling party announced what it would cost to seek its nomination for president. The price of the nomination and expression-of-interest forms was ₦100 million. Not for a campaign. Not for posters, rallies, or advertisements. For the forms alone—the right to ask the party’s delegates for their votes. The main opposition party set its own price at ₦40 million. For governor, the ruling party charged ₦50 million; for the Senate, ₦20 million; for the House of Representatives, ₦10 million.1 Seven years earlier, the same party’s presidential form had cost ₦27 million. The figures provoked outrage, and the outrage was understandable. But this book has asked readers to look past outrage to incentives. So consider the question an economist would ask. If a person must spend tens or hundreds of millions of naira simply to enter a contest—before the far larger costs of campaigning—what will that person need to do once in office? Some will be wealthy enough not to care. Some will be sponsored by others who expect a return. Some will borrow against the future. Very few will be ordinary citizens with good ideas and little money. The price of a form is not only a fee. It is a filter. And it shapes who governs long before a single voter reaches a polling unit. ## Why Elections Are Institutions Elections are often discussed as events: a campaign, a vote, a result. They are better understood as institutions. An election is a set of rules that determines who may stand, how parties choose their candidates, how campaigns are financed, how votes are cast and counted, how results are announced, and how disputes are resolved. Each of those rules creates incentives. Together, they determine what kind of person is likely to win—and what that person will believe they owe, and to whom. This is why the question “Who should we elect?” is never sufficient. It must be accompanied by another: **What does our electoral system reward?** Chapter Seven showed that participation has been falling. Turnout in presidential elections declined from about 69 per cent in 2003 to about 27 per cent in 2023, and about one voter in five reported being offered an inducement in 2023. Chapter Twenty described how a citizens’ campaign lowered the constitutional age limits for office. This chapter looks at the machinery between those two points: the parties, the rules, and the institutions that turn votes into power. ## The Gate Before the Ballot For most offices, the decisive contest in Nigeria does not take place on election day. It takes place earlier, inside the parties. A party primary decides who will appear on the ballot. In many states, one party is so dominant that its nomination is effectively the election. And in most primaries, the people who choose are not ordinary party members but delegates—a few thousand people, sometimes fewer, whose votes can decide who governs millions. ![Figure 15.1. Cost of presidential nomination and expression-of-interest forms in Nigeria’s two largest parties. Source: Ayantola Alayande, “Parading Millions,” Dataphyte, April 23, 2022.](/static/book/fig-164-29.jpg)

Figure 15.1. Cost of presidential nomination and expression-of-interest forms in Nigeria’s two largest parties. Source: Ayantola Alayande, “Parading Millions,” Dataphyte, April 23, 2022.

When entry fees are high and the electorate is small, the incentives are predictable. Aspirants compete for the support of delegates and the patrons who influence them. Money becomes a qualification. Loyalty to a sponsor can matter more than loyalty to voters. And candidates who reach office after spending heavily face constant pressure to recover what they spent and to reward those who backed them. None of this requires any individual politician to be unusually greedy. It requires only that the rules make money decisive. Change the rules—cap fees, make primaries more open, enforce limits on campaign spending, publish party finances—and the incentives change with them. The same filter affects who is absent from politics. The European Union’s observers of the 2023 elections listed discrimination against women in political life among their six priority concerns.2 When the cost of entry is measured in tens of millions of naira, and the networks that supply that money are overwhelmingly male, the result is not an accident. It is an outcome of the system. ## Counting the Vote: Technology and Trust If primaries decide who is on the ballot, the counting decides whether the result is believed. The Electoral Act of 2022 introduced two technologies intended to strengthen that trust: the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System, which verifies voters by fingerprint or facial recognition at the polling unit, and the Result Viewing Portal, known as IReV, through which polling-unit results were to be uploaded for the public to see. In the presidential election of February 2023, the upload of polling-unit results to the portal was seriously delayed. The failure became a central issue in the challenges that followed. In October 2023, the Supreme Court upheld the declared result. It held that the portal was not part of the formal process of collating results, and that its failure did not affect the outcome—while acknowledging that such failures could erode voters’ trust.3 The European Union’s observation mission concluded that “enduring systemic weaknesses” in electoral law and administration had eroded confidence in the electoral commission. Among its priority recommendations were a publicly accountable process for appointing members of the commission and the real-time publication of results.4 In February 2026, a new Electoral Act replaced the 2022 law. During its passage, the question of whether electronic transmission of results should be mandatory became so contentious that it provoked public protests; the final law made electronic transmission optional, with manual transmission where the internet fails.5 The electoral commission then moved the 2027 presidential and National Assembly elections to 16 January 2027, and the governorship and state assembly elections to 6 February 2027, to comply with the new law’s timelines.6 Technology cannot by itself make an election credible. But the debate shows something important. Nigerians understand that trust in an election depends not only on who wins, but on whether the process can be seen. ## When Losers Go to Court In a healthy democracy, losing candidates accept defeat and prepare for the next contest. Where trust is low, they go to court. Nigeria’s courts now play a central role in its elections. After the 2023 polls, one estimate counted more than three hundred petitions before election tribunals.7 The electoral commission budgeted more than ₦5 billion for litigation and prosecution in its 2023 election plan.8 The presidential election was settled only by the Supreme Court eight months after the vote. This has two sides. On one side, it is a sign of institutional strength. Disputes that might once have been settled by force are now settled by judges, according to rules, with reasons published for all to read. That is no small achievement in a country with Nigeria’s history. On the other side, it is a sign of institutional weakness. When so many results are contested, the ballot box has not done its job. And when the final decision on who governs rests with a small number of judges, public confidence in the judiciary becomes bound up with every political contest—a burden that Chapter Fourteen suggests the courts can ill afford. ## Parties Without Programmes Political parties are meant to be more than vehicles for candidates. In stable democracies, parties represent recognizable ideas, train future leaders, develop policies, and give voters a meaningful choice between alternatives. In Nigeria, parties have often functioned differently. Politicians move between them with remarkable ease, frequently after losing a primary or when the balance of power shifts. Since the 2023 elections, a large number of governors and legislators have left opposition parties for the ruling party. In 2019, the ruling party held 19 of the 36 governorships. By March 2026, it held 31.9 Those who defect give their own reasons—to bring development to their states, to align with the federal government, or to escape crises inside their former parties—and some of those reasons may be sincere. Ruling parties in many countries attract defectors. But the pattern carries an institutional cost. When parties stand for little beyond access to power, voters cannot choose between programmes. When opposition parties are hollowed out, the legislature and the electorate lose the competition that keeps governments accountable. And when politicians change parties without consequence, the vote a citizen cast for one party can end up serving another. The question for Nigeria is not whether any particular politician should change parties. It is what rules—on party membership, internal democracy, financing, and the status of elected officials who defect—would make parties stand for something durable. ## What Has Worked None of this means Nigerian elections cannot improve. They have improved before. In 2015, an incumbent president was defeated for the first time, and conceded. Chapter Four showed how voter cards and card readers, introduced in the preceding years, helped make that result credible. In 2018, a citizens’ campaign changed the Constitution to open public office to younger candidates (Chapter Twenty). In 2023, polling-unit results were published on a public portal for anyone to check—a level of transparency unimaginable a generation earlier, even if it fell short when it mattered most. Each of these advances came from rules and institutions, not from the virtue of any single election cycle. Each can be built upon. ![Attahiru Jega, chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission from 2010 to 2015, speaking at Chatham House, London, 2016. Photo: Chatham House / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.](/static/book/fig-168-30.jpg)

Attahiru Jega, chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission from 2010 to 2015, speaking at Chatham House, London, 2016. Photo: Chatham House / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

### Evidence Box: Elections in Numbers - **Cost of entry:** ₦100 million for the ruling party’s presidential forms in 2022, up from ₦27 million for the 2015 election; ₦40 million for the main opposition party.10 •**Participation:** presidential turnout fell from about 69 per cent in 2003 to about 27 per cent in 2023 (Chapter Seven). •**Disputes:** more than three hundred election petitions estimated after the 2023 elections; presidential result settled by the Supreme Court in October 2023.11 •**Party competition:** the ruling party held 19 of 36 governorships in 2019 and 31 by March 2026.12 •**New rules:** Electoral Act 2026 signed in February 2026; presidential election set for 16 January 2027.13 *An electoral system is judged not only by who wins, but by what it teaches the* *next generation of candidates about how to win.* ## The Nigerian Opportunity Nigeria has built many of the components of a credible electoral system: an independent electoral commission in law, biometric voter verification, public result portals, courts that resolve disputes, and an electorate that has shown it will remove an incumbent. The opportunity lies in completing the system: - **Lower the gate:** cap nomination fees and make primaries more open, so that ideas and public support count for more than money and patronage. •**Make the count visible:** publish polling-unit results promptly and in full, so that every citizen can check the arithmetic. •**Insulate the referee:** appoint members of the electoral commission through a transparent, publicly accountable process. •**Enforce the rules:** prosecute electoral offences, including vote buying, so that violations carry real consequences. •**Strengthen parties:** require internal democracy and transparent finances, so that parties become institutions rather than vehicles. None of these reforms depends on electing a perfect leader. Each would make it more likely that good leaders can be elected—and that bad ones can be removed. ## Looking Ahead Elections decide who governs. But governing requires an environment in which people can live, work, and vote without fear. The next chapter therefore turns to the institution charged with protecting that environment: security. ## Institutional Mirror Before the next election, ask not only which candidate deserves your vote. Ask also: **What did it cost each candidate to reach the ballot—and who paid?** **Will every vote be counted where everyone can see it?** **And if the result is disputed, will both winner and loser accept the judgment of a trusted referee?** A democracy is not secured on election day. It is secured by the rules that decide what happens before, during, and after it.

notes.1: Ayantola Alayande, “Parading Millions: Expensive Party Nomination Forms and Nigeria’s 2023 Elections,” *Dataphyte*, April 23, 2022. The ruling party announced its prices on April 20, 2022. Figures are in nominal naira.
notes.2: European Union Election Observation Mission, *Nigeria 2023 General Elections: Final Report* (June 2023), including its findings on the electronic transmission of results; summarised in the mission’s press release of June 27, 2023.
notes.3: Supreme Court of Nigeria, judgment of October 26, 2023 (Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi v. Independent National Electoral Commission and others), as reported in “Tinubu vs Atiku, Obi: Failure to Upload Results to Viewing Portal Doesn’t Invalidate Election,” Arise News, October 26, 2023.
notes.4: European Union Election Observation Mission, “Final Report: 23 Recommendations.”
notes.5: “INEC Reschedules 2027 General Election, Releases New Election Timetable,” *Premium Times*, February 26, 2026, republished by allAfrica. The Electoral Act, 2026 was signed on February 18, 2026. The dates were confirmed in INEC’s revised timetable and have not changed.
notes.6: *Premium Times*, February 26, 2026.

notes.9: “86% of Nigeria’s 36 State Governors Are Now in the APC as of March 15, 2026,” *Intelpoint*, March 2026. The count was unchanged at the time of writing.

sections.markdown:
> “Security is not merely the presence of armed institutions. It is the confidence that people can live, work, travel, and dream without fear.” ## The Journey Home A young woman finishes work late in the evening. She boards a bus and begins the journey home. A farmer prepares to transport harvested crops to the nearest market. A trader opens a shop before sunrise. Children walk to school. A manufacturer sends goods across several states. A doctor responds to an emergency call in the middle of the night. None of these ordinary activities can flourish without one invisible condition. People must believe they can carry out their daily lives with reasonable safety. Security is therefore not simply about responding to danger. It creates the environment within which normal life becomes possible. When people feel secure, they invest. They innovate. They travel. They study. They build businesses. They plan for the future. Peace becomes the foundation upon which development is constructed. For millions of Nigerians, that foundation has been shaken. In its first national survey of crime experience, the National Bureau of Statistics estimated that Nigerian households experienced about 51.9 million crime incidents between May 2023 and April 2024. It estimated 2.2 million kidnapping incidents in the same twelve months, most of them in rural areas and more than 1.4 million in the North- West alone. About two-thirds of households that experienced a kidnapping paid a ransom, averaging ₦2.7 million each; the total was estimated at ₦2.23 trillion.1 That sum is not only a measure of crime. It is a measure of how much ordinary families paid, out of their own savings, for a security that public institutions had been unable to provide. ![A police armoured vehicle and officers on the roadside, Lagos, 2009. Photo: satanoid / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.](/static/book/fig-172-31.jpg)

A police armoured vehicle and officers on the roadside, Lagos, 2009. Photo: satanoid / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

## Security as a Public Institution Many people associate security with soldiers or police officers. They are indispensable. But a modern security system is much broader. It includes intelligence services. Emergency response agencies. Border management. Correctional institutions. Cybersecurity. Disaster management. Community safety. Maritime security. Civil defence. Public health preparedness. Critical infrastructure protection. These institutions perform different functions, yet they share a common purpose: To protect life, preserve public order, defend constitutional authority, and enable society to function peacefully. Security is therefore an ecosystem rather than a single organization. In Nigeria, much of that ecosystem rests on one institution: the Nigeria Police Force, which is controlled by the federal government. In December 2024, the Minister of Police Affairs put its strength at just over 370,000 officers—roughly one for every 600 Nigerians—and announced that 30,000 new officers would be recruited each year.2 Numbers alone do not make a police force effective; training, equipment, intelligence, investigation, and integrity matter as much. But a single, centrally commanded force for a federation of more than 200 million people across 36 states has long been at the heart of Nigeria’s security debate. In 2026, that debate reached a turning point. The National Assembly passed a constitutional amendment that would permit states to establish their own police forces and, in September, transmitted it to the 36 state houses of assembly. At least 24 must approve it before it can take effect.3 Supporters argue that police closer to communities will understand local threats better and respond faster. Critics warn that state police could be used by governors against political opponents, and that many states cannot afford to fund them properly. Both concerns are institutional. The answer to them lies not in whether policing is federal or state, but in the rules, oversight, funding, and accountability that govern it. ## Prevention Before Response The most successful security institutions are often those that prevent crises before they occur. Effective intelligence. Community engagement. Early warning systems. Conflict prevention. Professional investigations. Risk assessment. Infrastructure resilience. Cyber defence. Disaster preparedness. Preventive institutions rarely attract public attention because their greatest successes are the events that never happen. Yet prevention is often the highest expression of institutional effectiveness. ## Trust and Cooperation No security institution operates alone. Communities possess information. Citizens report concerns. Businesses strengthen resilience. Traditional and religious leaders often contribute to conflict resolution. Civil society organizations support peacebuilding. The media informs the public. Security therefore depends upon cooperation. People are more likely to cooperate with institutions they trust. Trust grows through professionalism. Respect for human rights. Transparency. Accountability. Fair treatment. Consistent communication. Institutional legitimacy becomes a strategic asset. The national crime survey shows how much trust is missing. Only about a quarter of households that experienced a crime reported it to the police. Victims of home robbery reported in about a third of cases, and victims of sexual offences in fewer than one in four. The most common reason given for not reporting was a lack of confidence that the police would take meaningful action.4 The one exception was phone theft, which about nine in ten victims reported—largely, it appears, because a police report is often needed to replace a SIM card or make an insurance claim. Where reporting brings a practical benefit, people report. ![Figure 16.1. Share of crime victims who reported the crime to the police, Nigeria, May 2023–April 2024. Source: National Bureau of Statistics, Crime Experience and Security Perception Survey (2024), as reported in the notes.](/static/book/fig-176-32.jpg)

Figure 16.1. Share of crime victims who reported the crime to the police, Nigeria, May 2023–April 2024. Source: National Bureau of Statistics, Crime Experience and Security Perception Survey (2024), as reported in the notes.

Every unreported crime is information the security system never receives. A police force that is not trusted is not only less legitimate. It is also less informed, and therefore less effective. ## Security and Development Security and development reinforce one another. Communities experiencing stability are more likely to attract investment. Schools remain open. Healthcare services continue. Markets expand. Infrastructure projects progress. Tourism develops. Entrepreneurship flourishes. Likewise, sustainable development can reduce some of the conditions that contribute to insecurity by expanding opportunity, strengthening institutions, and improving public confidence. Neither security nor development should be viewed in isolation. Each strengthens the other. ## Professionalism Under the Rule of Law Security institutions exercise significant public authority. That authority carries corresponding responsibilities. Professional training. Clear legal mandates. Civilian oversight. Ethical leadership. Operational accountability. Respect for constitutional rights. Independent review mechanisms. These safeguards do not weaken security institutions. They strengthen their legitimacy. A professional security institution protects both public safety and the constitutional order it serves. Nigeria’s recent history shows what happens when that balance is lost—and how institutions can respond. In October 2020, nationwide protests under the banner #EndSARS demanded the abolition of the police Special Anti-Robbery Squad, which many young Nigerians accused of extortion, unlawful detention, and brutality. The federal government disbanded the unit, and several states set up judicial panels of inquiry to examine complaints.5 A month earlier, a new Police Act had replaced the colonial-era statute of 1943, setting out the rights of arrested persons and the duties of officers.6 Laws and panels do not by themselves change behaviour. But they create standards against which conduct can be judged, and they show that legitimacy, once lost, must be rebuilt by institutions rather than by statements. ### Evidence Box: Security in Numbers - **Crime:** about 51.9 million household crime incidents in the twelve months to April 2024.7 •**Kidnapping:** about 2.2 million incidents; ₦2.23 trillion paid in ransoms.8 •**Reporting:** about one in four households that experienced crime reported it to the police.9 •**Police strength:** just over 370,000 officers, about one for every 600 people (2024); 30,000 recruits planned each year.10 •**Reform:** a constitutional amendment permitting state police sent to state assemblies for ratification in September 2026.11 *Security is ultimately a relationship between citizens and the institutions that* *protect them. The figures suggest that both the capacity and the trust in that* *relationship need rebuilding.* ## The Nigerian Opportunity Nigeria’s security institutions have faced complex and evolving challenges, including terrorism, banditry, kidnapping, communal conflicts, piracy, cybercrime, and other threats to public safety. Across these challenges, countless members of the armed forces, police, intelligence services, civil defence, emergency responders, and community- based organizations have demonstrated courage and dedication under demanding circumstances. The opportunity ahead lies in strengthening institutional coordination, intelligence capabilities, professional training, technology, accountability, community partnerships, and preventive capacity. A secure Nigeria benefits every other institution. Education advances more effectively. Healthcare reaches more communities. Businesses invest with greater confidence. Justice is administered more consistently. National development accelerates when security creates the conditions for stability. ## Looking Ahead Security protects the environment in which society functions. Infrastructure provides the physical systems through which society operates. Roads. Railways. Electricity. Water. Ports. Airports. Digital networks. The next chapter therefore turns to another institution whose influence touches every citizen, every business, and every community: Infrastructure. ## Institutional Mirror Imagine a country where families feel safe travelling at night, businesses confidently transport goods across the country, children attend school without fear, emergency services respond quickly, and communities cooperate closely with trusted public institutions. What kinds of opportunities become possible under those conditions? Security is not merely the absence of danger. It is the presence of institutions that give people the confidence to build their lives with hope rather than fear.

sections.title: Infrastructure: Building the Foundations of National Prosperity
sections.part: Part III — The Institutions of National Life
sections.epigraph: Infrastructure is more than what a nation builds. It is the system that enables people, businesses, and institutions to connect, create, and prosper.
questions: Which country is more likely to attract investment, encourage innovation, and expand opportunity?
sections.opening: Imagine two communities separated by a river. The people on both sides are hardworking. Farmers produce food. Children attend school.
sections.markdown:
> “Infrastructure is more than what a nation builds. It is the system that enables people, businesses, and institutions to connect, create, and prosper.” ## The Bridge Imagine two communities separated by a river. The people on both sides are hardworking. Farmers produce food. Children attend school. Small businesses operate. Families care for one another. Yet moving between the two communities is difficult. During the rainy season, travel becomes dangerous. Markets remain isolated. Medical emergencies take longer to reach hospitals. Children spend more time travelling than learning. Economic opportunity becomes limited—not because people lack ability, but because they lack connection. Now imagine that a well-designed bridge is built. The people have not changed. Their talents have not changed. Their ambitions have not changed. What has changed is the institution that enables them to connect. Infrastructure does not create human potential. It unlocks it. ## Beyond Concrete and Steel Infrastructure is often associated with roads, bridges, airports, and railways. These are essential. But modern infrastructure extends much further. Electricity powers homes, hospitals, schools, and industries. Water systems protect public health. Ports connect producers to international markets. Airports connect regions and economies. Telecommunications connect people instantly across vast distances. Broadband networks enable education, innovation, digital commerce, and public services. Energy grids support industrial production. Waste management protects environmental sustainability. Infrastructure is therefore an interconnected system. Weakness in one component often affects many others. The Lekki Deep Sea Port shows both the promise and the challenge. Inaugurated in January 2023 at a reported cost of $1.5 billion, it was built and is largely owned by private investors—China Harbour Engineering Company and Singapore’s Tolaram Group—with the Lagos State Government and the Nigerian Ports Authority holding the remaining stake. It can receive ships several times larger than those that call at the older ports of Apapa and Tin Can Island.1 Yet a port is only as useful as the roads, rail links, customs procedures, and power supply that connect it to the rest of the economy. A world-class quay at the end of a congested road is one part of a system, not a system. ![The Lekki Deep Sea Port and its approach road, Lagos, August 2026. Photo: FrankvEck / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.](/static/book/fig-182-33.jpg)

The Lekki Deep Sea Port and its approach road, Lagos, August 2026. Photo: FrankvEck / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

## Infrastructure as an Economic Multiplier Few public investments have effects as widespread as infrastructure. Reliable transport reduces the cost of doing business. Stable electricity increases industrial productivity. Digital connectivity expands entrepreneurship. Efficient logistics improve agricultural markets. Clean water reduces disease. Modern ports strengthen international trade. Each improvement extends beyond its immediate purpose. Infrastructure multiplies opportunity. It allows citizens, businesses, and public institutions to achieve more with the same effort. For this reason, infrastructure is not merely expenditure. It is productive national capital. Nigeria’s own planners have tried to measure the scale of the need. The National Integrated Infrastructure Master Plan, adopted in 2014, estimated that the country would need to invest about $2.9 trillion over thirty years to raise its stock of infrastructure from roughly 35–40 percent of GDP to about 70 percent by 2043.2 No government budget can meet such a figure alone. The question is therefore not only how much to spend, but which institutions can plan, finance, build, and maintain infrastructure reliably over decades—including private investors, who will commit capital only where contracts are honoured and regulation is predictable. ## Maintenance Matters Many societies celebrate new infrastructure projects. Far fewer celebrate maintenance. Yet roads deteriorate. Bridges require inspection. Power systems need modernization. Water facilities require continuous operation. Digital networks demand constant upgrades. Maintenance is not evidence of failure. It is evidence of stewardship. Strong institutions recognize that preserving existing assets is often as important as constructing new ones. Sustainable development depends upon both building wisely and maintaining faithfully. In Nigeria, responsibility for maintaining more than 36,000 kilometres of federal roads rests with the Federal Roads Maintenance Agency. In February 2026, its managing director told the House of Representatives that years of underfunding had left a “maintenance debt” on the network, and asked that the agency be given a share of a proposed fuel surcharge to fund repairs.3 The pattern is familiar across many sectors: new projects attract ribbon-cutting ceremonies, while the budget lines that keep existing assets working are among the first to be cut. A road that is not maintained does not stay the same. It deteriorates, and its eventual repair costs far more than its upkeep would have. ## Infrastructure and Equality of Opportunity Infrastructure shapes opportunity. Reliable roads allow farmers to reach markets. Electricity extends study hours for students. Broadband enables remote learning and digital entrepreneurship. Safe water improves health outcomes. Public transport expands access to employment. Infrastructure therefore does more than improve convenience. It broadens opportunity. Well-designed infrastructure reduces the disadvantages created by geography and strengthens national integration by connecting communities, regions, and markets. Digital infrastructure is a clear example. Under its first National Broadband Plan, Nigeria set a target of 30 percent broadband penetration by the end of 2018, and met it.4 Its second plan raised the target to 70 percent by the end of 2025. By April 2026, penetration had reached about 56 percent: substantial progress, but short of the goal.5 The difference between the two plans is instructive. The first target could be met largely by expanding mobile networks where demand was already concentrated. The second requires extending fibre and towers to rural communities where returns are lower, rights-of-way are costly, and infrastructure is vulnerable to vandalism—problems that only coordinated institutions can solve. ![Figure 17.1. Broadband penetration in Nigeria: targets and results of the two National Broadband Plans. Sources: Nigerian Communications Commission data, as reported in ThisDay (2019; 2026).](/static/book/fig-185-34.jpg)

Figure 17.1. Broadband penetration in Nigeria: targets and results of the two National Broadband Plans. Sources: Nigerian Communications Commission data, as reported in ThisDay (2019; 2026).

## Planning for Generations Infrastructure projects often outlive the governments that initiate them. A railway may serve citizens for decades. A dam may support agriculture for generations. A digital backbone may shape an entire economy. This long lifespan demands long-term thinking. Projects should be selected because they address genuine public needs, deliver lasting value, and fit within broader national development strategies. Infrastructure planning is therefore an exercise in stewardship across generations. Lagos learned this the hard way. In the early 1980s, the Lagos State Government under Governor Lateef Jakande contracted foreign firms to build a metropolitan rail line. After the military coup of December 1983, the federal government cancelled the project, and a tribunal was set up to investigate how it had been awarded.6 Lagos continued to grow into one of the world’s largest cities without urban rail. The first phase of the Lagos Rail Mass Transit Blue Line—thirteen kilometres from Marina to Mile 2—was inaugurated in January 2023 and began carrying passengers in September 2023, about four decades after the original plan.7 Reasonable people still debate whether the original project was affordable. What is not in doubt is the cost of the forty years in between: the hours lost in traffic, the fuel burned, and the opportunities that never materialized. ### Evidence Box: Infrastructure in Numbers - **Investment need:** about $2.9 trillion over thirty years, according to the National Integrated Infrastructure Master Plan (2014).8 •**Ports:** Lekki Deep Sea Port, inaugurated in January 2023 at a reported cost of $1.5 billion, mostly privately financed.9 •**Roads:** more than 36,000 kilometres of federal roads, with a maintenance backlog reported by the responsible agency (2026).10 •**Broadband:** about 56 percent penetration in April 2026, against a 70 percent target for 2025.11 •**Urban rail:** Lagos Blue Line phase one began passenger service in 2023, about forty years after the city’s first metro plan.12 *Infrastructure is built in years but used for generations. Its value depends on the* *institutions that plan, finance, maintain, and connect it.* ## The Nigerian Opportunity Nigeria possesses enormous opportunities to strengthen its infrastructure. Its strategic location, growing population, entrepreneurial energy, expanding digital economy, and abundant natural resources provide a strong foundation for long-term investment. Continued improvements in transportation networks, electricity generation and distribution, broadband connectivity, water systems, urban planning, logistics, and maintenance capacity can significantly increase productivity across every sector. Infrastructure does not operate in isolation. Every improvement strengthens education, healthcare, agriculture, manufacturing, trade, tourism, public administration, and national security. Investment in infrastructure is therefore an investment in institutional effectiveness itself. ## Looking Ahead Infrastructure connects markets. Markets create businesses. Businesses generate innovation, employment, investment, and economic growth. The next chapter therefore examines another institution essential to national prosperity: The private sector. For while governments establish the environment in which economies operate, private enterprise transforms opportunity into productivity and wealth creation. ## Institutional Mirror Imagine two countries with equally talented populations. In one, electricity is reliable, transport networks function efficiently, digital connectivity is widespread, and infrastructure is maintained consistently. In the other, these systems are fragmented and unpredictable. Which country is more likely to attract investment, encourage innovation, and expand opportunity? The answer reminds us that infrastructure is not simply about construction. It is about creating the physical and digital systems that allow an entire nation to flourish.

sections.part: Part III — The Institutions of National Life
sections.epigraph: Governments create the conditions for growth. Entrepreneurs transform those conditions into prosperity.
questions: Which country is more likely to generate investment, innovation, employment, and long-term prosperity?
sections.opening: On a busy street, a woman unlocks the door to her small shop before sunrise. She arranges her goods carefully. She greets her first customers with a smile. Across town, an engineer arrives at a technology startup.
sections.markdown:
> “Governments create the conditions for growth. Entrepreneurs transform those conditions into prosperity.” ## The Small Shop On a busy street, a woman unlocks the door to her small shop before sunrise. She arranges her goods carefully. She greets her first customers with a smile. Across town, an engineer arrives at a technology startup. A farmer prepares to transport produce to market. A tailor begins the day’s first order. A manufacturer opens the factory floor. A software developer writes the first lines of code for a new application. None of these people waits for prosperity to appear. They create value. Every sale, every invention, every service, every product contributes to the economy. The private sector is not simply a collection of businesses. It is the everyday expression of human creativity, initiative, and enterprise. ![A generator repair workshop with a sign advertising point-of-sale banking services, Nigeria, 2026. Photo: Bigkotech / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.](/static/book/fig-189-35.jpg)

A generator repair workshop with a sign advertising point-of-sale banking services, Nigeria, 2026. Photo: Bigkotech / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

## Wealth Is Created Before It Is Shared Every society must first create wealth before it can distribute it. Businesses produce goods. Farmers cultivate food. Manufacturers transform raw materials. Financial institutions mobilize capital. Technology companies develop new solutions. Service providers meet countless daily needs. Together, these activities generate employment, income, innovation, investment, and tax revenue. A strong private sector expands the resources available to households and governments alike. Economic growth therefore depends not only on public policy but also on the ability of individuals and businesses to create value. ## Institutions That Enable Enterprise Entrepreneurs thrive when institutions reduce unnecessary uncertainty. Clear property rights. Reliable electricity. Efficient transport. Access to finance. Predictable taxation. Fair regulation. Contract enforcement. Digital connectivity. Skilled workers. Macroeconomic stability. These are not advantages reserved for businesses alone. They strengthen the entire economy. When institutions function well, entrepreneurs devote more energy to innovation and less to overcoming avoidable obstacles. Good institutions allow businesses to compete through productivity rather than proximity to power. Electricity shows what happens when one of these institutions fails. Members of the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria reported spending about ₦1.11 trillion on alternative sources of energy in 2024—up from ₦781.7 billion in 2023 and ₦77.2 billion in 2021. Part of that rise reflects inflation and the higher cost of diesel and gas after the reforms of 2023, but it also reflects how heavily factories depend on their own generators. In the same year, the association reported ₦2.14 trillion worth of finished goods left unsold and average capacity utilization of 57 percent.1 A manufacturer who must build a private power station before producing anything is competing with one hand tied—against foreign rivals whose governments supply electricity as a matter of course. ![Figure 18.1. Spending by members of the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria on alternative energy, 2021–2024. Source: Manufacturers Association of Nigeria, Economic Review, as reported in The Guardian (Lagos), April 22, 2025.](/static/book/fig-191-36.jpg)

Figure 18.1. Spending by members of the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria on alternative energy, 2021–2024. Source: Manufacturers Association of Nigeria, Economic Review, as reported in The Guardian (Lagos), April 22, 2025.

The same institutional logic can work in the other direction. In 2011, the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System launched an instant payment service that allowed money to move between any two bank accounts in seconds. In 2014, the Central Bank introduced the Bank Verification Number, a biometric identity for bank customers; more than 66 million have since been issued. Neither was glamorous. Both were institutions—shared rules and systems that every bank and business could rely on. On top of them, entrepreneurs built payment companies, agent banking networks, and digital lenders. In 2024 the instant payment platform carried more than 11 billion transfers worth about ₦1.07 quadrillion.2 In 2020, the American payments company Stripe acquired the Lagos-based start-up Paystack for a reported $200 million or more—at the time, one of the largest acquisitions of an African technology company.3 Paystack’s founders deserve the credit for what they built. But they built it on rails that public and industry institutions had laid. ## Innovation and Competition Competition encourages improvement. Businesses develop better products. Lower costs. Higher quality. New technologies. Better customer service. Innovation rarely emerges from comfort alone. It grows where ideas are tested, rewarded, and improved. Healthy competition therefore benefits consumers, businesses, and the broader economy. It encourages continuous learning and adaptation. Institutions that protect fair competition help ensure that success depends upon value creation rather than unfair advantage. Nigeria created such an institution relatively recently. The Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act of 2018 established the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission. In July 2024, after an investigation lasting more than three years with the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, it fined Meta and WhatsApp $220 million for practices it found to be discriminatory and exploitative towards Nigerian consumers. In April 2025, the Competition and Consumer Protection Tribunal upheld the penalty.4 Whatever view one takes of the case, it showed that a Nigerian regulator could hold one of the world’s largest companies to Nigerian rules—and that its decisions could be tested before an independent tribunal. ## Small Businesses, Great Nations Large corporations often receive public attention. Yet small and medium-sized enterprises form the backbone of many economies. They create employment. Support families. Train workers. Strengthen local communities. Encourage entrepreneurship. Expand regional development. A vibrant economy therefore depends not only on attracting large investments but also on enabling small businesses to start, survive, grow, and innovate. National prosperity is built one enterprise at a time. This is especially true in Nigeria. According to the national survey of micro, small, and medium enterprises conducted by the Small and Medium Enterprises Development Agency of Nigeria (SMEDAN) and the National Bureau of Statistics, there are about 39 million such enterprises in the country. They account for an estimated 87.9 percent of employment and 46.3 percent of GDP.5 The same survey recorded a decline of about two million enterprises between 2017 and 2020. Most of these firms are very small, informal, and fragile. Their survival depends less on grand policy than on ordinary institutions: whether the power stays on, whether a loan can be obtained, whether a contract can be enforced, and whether a market official or tax collector applies the rules predictably. ## Partnership, Not Rivalry Public institutions and private enterprise perform different responsibilities. Governments establish laws, provide public goods, regulate markets, protect competition, and invest in infrastructure. Businesses innovate, invest, employ, manufacture, distribute, and create wealth. Neither succeeds fully without the other. Weak institutions discourage investment. Weak private sectors limit economic opportunity. Prosperous societies strengthen both. Development is therefore best understood as a partnership between capable public institutions and productive private enterprise. ### Evidence Box: The Private Sector in Numbers - **Small firms:** about 39 million micro, small, and medium enterprises, accounting for an estimated 87.9 percent of employment and 46.3 percent of GDP.6 •**Self-generated power:** manufacturers spent about ₦1.11 trillion on alternative energy in 2024.7 •**Unsold goods:** ₦2.14 trillion of manufactured goods unsold in 2024; capacity utilization 57 percent.8 •**Payments infrastructure:** more than 11 billion instant transfers a year; more than 66 million Bank Verification Numbers issued.9 •**Competition:** a $220 million penalty against Meta and WhatsApp, upheld by the Competition and Consumer Protection Tribunal in 2025.10 *Entrepreneurs supply the energy. Institutions decide how much of it becomes* *prosperity.* ## The Nigerian Opportunity Nigeria possesses one of Africa’s most entrepreneurial populations. Across the country, businesses of every size demonstrate resilience, creativity, and adaptability in agriculture, manufacturing, finance, technology, entertainment, retail, logistics, professional services, and countless other sectors. The opportunity ahead lies in strengthening the institutional environment that allows enterprise to flourish. Reliable infrastructure. Transparent regulation. Access to finance. Efficient public administration. Competitive markets. Investment in skills. Research and innovation. Digital transformation. These improvements do more than help businesses. They expand employment, increase productivity, strengthen public revenue, and improve national prosperity. A thriving private sector benefits the entire society. ## Looking Ahead Markets create prosperity. Governments create national frameworks. Federal systems determine how authority, responsibility, and resources are shared across different levels of government. The next chapter therefore examines one of the defining features of Nigeria’s constitutional structure: Federalism. Understanding how powers are distributed is essential to understanding how institutions function throughout the federation. ## Institutional Mirror Imagine two countries with equally talented entrepreneurs. In one, starting a business is straightforward, contracts are enforced, infrastructure is reliable, and regulation is predictable. In the other, uncertainty dominates every stage of enterprise. Which country is more likely to generate investment, innovation, employment, and long-term prosperity? The answer reminds us that entrepreneurship begins with individual initiative, but it flourishes through institutions that reward creativity, protect fair competition, and reduce unnecessary barriers to productive enterprise.

notes.2: Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System data for 2024 (₦1.07 quadrillion, up from ₦600.3 trillion in 2023), as reported in “E-Payment Transactions in Nigeria Hit All-Time High of N1.07 Quadrillion in 2024,” *Nairametrics*, January 29, 2025; volume from Central Bank of Nigeria data, as reported by *Daily Trust*.
notes.3: “Stripe Acquires Nigeria’s Paystack for $200M+ to Expand into the African Continent,” *TechCrunch*, October 15, 2020. The price was not officially disclosed.
notes.4: “Tribunal Upholds FCCPC’s $220m Fine against Meta,” *Channels Television*, April 25, 2025.

sections.title: Federalism: Balancing Unity and Diversity
sections.epigraph: The strength of a federation lies not in concentrating power, but in distributing responsibility wisely while preserving national unity.
questions: How would such a system influence education, healthcare, infrastructure, economic development, and public trust?
sections.opening: Imagine a large family living under one roof. The family shares a common identity. They celebrate together. They protect one another.
sections.markdown:
> “The strength of a federation lies not in concentrating power, but in distributing responsibility wisely while preserving national unity.” ## The Family Home Imagine a large family living under one roof. The family shares a common identity. They celebrate together. They protect one another. They pursue a common future. Yet daily life is not managed by one person alone. Parents make some decisions. Older siblings take responsibility for others. Individual family members manage their own personal affairs. Some responsibilities are shared. Others are delegated. Still others remain personal. The family remains united not because every decision is centralized, but because responsibilities are allocated according to purpose. The same principle applies to federal systems. Unity does not require uniformity. It requires cooperation within a framework of shared responsibility. ## Why Federalism Exists Nations differ in geography, population, history, language, culture, and economic conditions. Large and diverse societies often require institutions capable of balancing national cohesion with local responsiveness. Federalism is one approach to achieving that balance. Certain responsibilities—such as national defence, foreign affairs, monetary policy, and immigration—are commonly exercised at the national level because they affect the country as a whole. Other responsibilities—such as local infrastructure, primary education, sanitation, community planning, and local economic development—may be better managed closer to the communities they directly affect. Federalism therefore recognizes that effective governance sometimes depends upon bringing decision-making nearer to citizens while preserving the unity of the state. Nigeria’s own federation has been redrawn many times. At independence it had three regions; a fourth, the Mid-West, was created in 1963. In 1967, on the eve of the civil war, the regions were replaced by twelve states. Successive military governments created more: nineteen in 1976, twenty-one in 1987, thirty in 1991, and thirty-six in 1996, together with the Federal Capital Territory.1 Each new state was intended to bring government closer to particular communities and to reduce fears of domination. Each also created a new government, legislature, civil service, and set of claims on the Federation Account. Whether those governments could sustain themselves was a separate question—and, as the evidence below suggests, often a difficult one. ![The Rivers State Government Secretariat complex, Port Harcourt, 2025. Photo: ABORISADEADETONA / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.](/static/book/fig-199-37.jpg)

The Rivers State Government Secretariat complex, Port Harcourt, 2025. Photo: ABORISADEADETONA / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

## Authority and Responsibility One of the greatest challenges in any federation is ensuring that authority and responsibility remain aligned. Institutions function best when those entrusted with responsibilities also possess the authority and resources necessary to fulfil them. If responsibilities are assigned without adequate capacity, institutions struggle. If authority is concentrated without sufficient accountability, responsiveness declines. Federal systems therefore require continual cooperation among national, state, and local institutions. The objective is not competition. It is coordination. Well-designed federal institutions encourage each level of government to perform the functions for which it is best suited. ## Diversity as a National Asset Federalism is often associated with managing diversity. Diversity should not be viewed solely as a challenge. It can also be a source of resilience. Different regions possess different strengths. Agriculture. Manufacturing. Technology. Tourism. Natural resources. Creative industries. Education. Innovation. Federal systems allow these strengths to develop while contributing to the national economy. When institutions encourage cooperation rather than rivalry, diversity becomes an advantage rather than a source of division. ## Fiscal Federalism The distribution of public responsibilities inevitably raises another question: How should financial resources be shared? Governments require adequate revenue to discharge their constitutional responsibilities. Fiscal federalism therefore examines how revenue is generated, allocated, and managed across different levels of government. The objective is not merely financial balance. It is institutional effectiveness. Resources should enable each level of government to perform its assigned responsibilities efficiently, transparently, and accountably. Financial arrangements should strengthen cooperation rather than dependency. In Nigeria, dependency is the norm. Chapter Six described the formula by which money in the Federation Account is shared among the three tiers of government. What that formula conceals is how little most states raise for themselves. The civic-technology group BudgIT compares each state’s internally generated revenue with what it spends simply to keep its government running. In its 2025 report, covering the 2024 financial year, only two states—Enugu and Lagos—raised enough of their own revenue to cover their operating costs. Five more covered at least half. In fourteen states, operating costs were more than five times internally generated revenue.2 The remainder of their spending was funded largely by allocations from the Federation Account. ![Figure 19.1. The 36 states grouped by the share of their operating expenses covered by internally generated revenue, 2024. Source: BudgIT, State of States (2025), as reported in BusinessDay, October 28, 2025. The middle group is derived from the reported totals.](/static/book/fig-201-38.jpg)

Figure 19.1. The 36 states grouped by the share of their operating expenses covered by internally generated revenue, 2024. Source: BudgIT, State of States (2025), as reported in BusinessDay, October 28, 2025. The middle group is derived from the reported totals.

This matters for more than accounting. A government that raises most of its money from its own citizens has strong reasons to listen to them and to use their money well; its citizens, in turn, have strong reasons to ask what their taxes have bought. A government that depends mainly on a monthly transfer from Abuja faces weaker pressure of this kind. Its attention is drawn upward, to the size of the next allocation, rather than outward, to the people it serves. The rankings also show that this is not fixed by geography. Enugu, which more than covered its operating costs in 2024, had not been among the states covering even half of them in the previous year’s report; Cross River, meanwhile, fell from fifth place to thirtieth in BudgIT’s overall ranking. Revenue performance can change within a few years when institutions change.3 ## Accountability Close to the Citizen One advantage often associated with decentralized governance is proximity. Citizens can more easily observe the performance of institutions operating within their own communities. Local leaders often possess greater familiarity with local priorities. Communities participate more directly in public affairs. Feedback becomes more immediate. Problems may be identified more quickly. Closer government does not automatically produce better governance. But it creates opportunities for stronger accountability when institutions function effectively. Nigeria has recently begun to test this in one of its most important sectors. In March 2023, a constitutional amendment allowed states to legislate on electricity generation, transmission, and distribution within their territories, and the Electricity Act of 2023 provided for state regulators to take over oversight of their electricity markets from the national regulator.4 Enugu, Ekiti, Ondo, Imo, and Oyo were among the first; by August 2025, eleven states had completed the transfer, and more, including Gombe, followed in early 2026.5 It is too early to judge the results. But the reform embodies the principle of this chapter: responsibility placed nearer to citizens, matched with the authority to act—and with the accountability that comes from being close enough to be seen. The same logic underlies the 2026 proposal to permit state police forces, discussed in Chapter Sixteen. In both cases, decentralization will help only if the new state institutions are capable, adequately funded, and answerable to their citizens. Moving power closer to the people is not the same as making it accountable to them. ### Evidence Box: The Federation in Numbers - **States:** 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, created in stages from three regions at independence.6 •**Self-reliance:** only 2 of 36 states covered their operating costs from their own revenue in 2024; in 14, operating costs exceeded five times their own revenue.7 •**Revenue sharing:** the vertical formula for the Federation Account has remained largely unchanged since the early 1990s (Chapter Six). •**Electricity:** at least eleven states had taken over regulation of their electricity markets by August 2025.8 •**Local government:** the 2024 Supreme Court ruling on direct payments to councils remained largely unimplemented two years later (Chapter Six). *A federation works when each level of government has clear responsibilities, the* *resources to meet them, and citizens close enough to hold it to account.* ## The Nigerian Opportunity Nigeria’s federal structure reflects both its size and its remarkable diversity. Its states and local governments differ in geography, economic activity, population, culture, and developmental priorities. This diversity presents opportunities for innovation, cooperation, and locally responsive governance. Strengthening intergovernmental coordination, clarifying institutional responsibilities, improving fiscal transparency, and expanding administrative capacity at every level can enhance the effectiveness of the federation. Federalism succeeds not merely through constitutional design but through continuous cooperation among institutions committed to serving the public interest. ## Looking Ahead Constitutions establish institutions. Institutions shape incentives. Yet institutions ultimately depend upon citizens. No legal framework, however carefully designed, can succeed without people who participate responsibly in public life. The next chapter therefore turns from government to society itself: Citizenship. For nations are sustained not only by institutions that govern them, but also by citizens who strengthen those institutions through everyday participation. ## Institutional Mirror Imagine a federation in which every level of government clearly understands its responsibilities, possesses the resources to fulfil them, cooperates with other levels of government, and remains accountable to the people it serves. How would such a system influence education, healthcare, infrastructure, economic development, and public trust? Federalism is not simply about dividing power. It is about organizing responsibility so that governance becomes more responsive, more effective, and more closely connected to the lives of citizens.

sections.markdown:
> “A nation is not sustained only by the institutions that govern its people, but also by the people who sustain their institutions.” ## The Queue A long queue forms outside a public office. Some people wait patiently for their turn. Others search for shortcuts. One person quietly joins the back of the line. Another attempts to move to the front by claiming influence. Most people notice. Some object. Others remain silent. The incident lasts only a few moments. Yet it illustrates something much larger. Citizenship is not expressed only during elections. It is expressed in countless ordinary decisions. How people obey rules. How they treat strangers. How they protect public property. How they respond when no one is watching. These everyday choices gradually shape the culture within which institutions operate. ![A volunteer with a non-governmental organization clearing refuse during an environmental sanitation exercise, 2023. Photo: SusuGeo / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.](/static/book/fig-206-39.jpg)

A volunteer with a non-governmental organization clearing refuse during an environmental sanitation exercise, 2023. Photo: SusuGeo / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

## Citizenship Beyond Nationality Citizenship is often understood as legal membership in a country. That definition is necessary. But it is incomplete. Citizenship is also a relationship. A relationship between individuals and the institutions that serve them. Rights matter. Responsibilities matter as well. Citizens expect security. Justice. Education. Healthcare. Infrastructure. Opportunity. In return, democratic societies depend upon citizens who obey lawful authority, participate peacefully, respect the rights of others, contribute to the common good, and hold public institutions accountable through lawful means. Citizenship is therefore both a privilege and a responsibility. It also begins, in a practical sense, with being known to the state. A citizen whom institutions cannot identify is difficult to protect, to serve, or to count. By July 2026, the National Identity Management Commission reported that about 136 million people had been enrolled in the national identity database and issued a National Identification Number—a large achievement, though still short of the full population.1 An identity number does not make anyone a better citizen. But it allows the relationship between citizen and state to rest on records rather than on recognition by the right official. ## Trust Begins With Everyday Conduct Nations do not develop trust only through grand reforms. Trust grows through ordinary behaviour repeated consistently. Keeping promises. Paying taxes honestly. Respecting contracts. Following traffic rules. Protecting public spaces. Reporting wrongdoing. Voting responsibly. Serving communities. Helping neighbours. Each action may appear insignificant. Together they shape civic culture. Institutional trust is built one interaction at a time. In Nigeria, that trust is low. In a national survey conducted in early 2025, the Africa Polling Institute found that 83 percent of respondents had little or no trust in the federal government, 82 percent had little or no trust in the National Assembly, and 79 percent had little or no trust in the judiciary—the lowest levels recorded across the institute’s surveys since 2019.2 In Afrobarometer’s survey ahead of the 2023 elections, only 23 percent of Nigerians said they trusted the electoral commission “somewhat” or “a lot.”3 Low trust is often treated as the fault of institutions alone. Much of it is earned. But it also has consequences that citizens share. People who do not trust institutions are less likely to pay taxes, report crimes, obey rules when no one is watching, or use lawful channels to resolve disputes—and each of those choices weakens the institutions further. Breaking that cycle requires effort from both sides: institutions that behave in ways that deserve trust, and citizens willing to extend enough of it to give reform a chance. ## Accountability Is Shared Much of this book has examined how institutions should serve citizens. An equally important question follows. How should citizens strengthen institutions? Accountability is not a one-way relationship. Public officials remain accountable to citizens. Citizens remain accountable to the law. Communities hold one another to shared standards. Civil society monitors public institutions. Journalists investigate matters of public interest. Professional associations uphold ethical standards. Universities cultivate informed debate. Democratic accountability therefore operates through many institutions working together. Citizenship becomes active rather than passive. Nigeria offers a clear example of what active, lawful citizenship can achieve. In 2016, a coalition of young Nigerians and civil society groups launched a campaign called Not Too Young To Run, arguing that the Constitution’s minimum ages for public office excluded the country’s young majority from leadership. They lobbied legislators, organized across states, and pressed for a constitutional amendment. In 2018, after the National Assembly and the required number of state houses of assembly approved it, the President signed the amendment into law. The minimum age to run for president fell from 40 to 35, and for the House of Representatives and state houses of assembly from 30 to 25. Proposals to lower the age limits for governors and senators were not adopted.4 In the 2019 elections, about twenty people aged between 25 and 30 won seats in state houses of assembly—offices that were closed to them only a year before.5 ![Figure 20.1. Minimum ages to contest for elective office in Nigeria, before and after the Not Too Young To Run amendment of 2018. Source: TheCable, May 31, 2018.](/static/book/fig-210-40.jpg)

Figure 20.1. Minimum ages to contest for elective office in Nigeria, before and after the Not Too Young To Run amendment of 2018. Source: TheCable, May 31, 2018.

The campaign did not achieve everything it sought. But it changed the Constitution through petitions, coalitions, and votes rather than through protest alone or despair. That is citizenship working as an institution. ## Civic Virtue Every successful society depends upon habits that cannot be legislated completely. Honesty. Respect. Tolerance. Responsibility. Patience. Cooperation. Service. Integrity. Empathy. These qualities are often learned first within families, schools, religious communities, neighbourhoods, and workplaces. Formal institutions reinforce them. But they cannot manufacture them alone. Laws guide behaviour. Culture gives those laws life. ## Participation Beyond Elections Voting remains one of the most important expressions of citizenship. Yet democratic participation extends much further. Attending community meetings. Serving on school boards. Supporting local initiatives. Volunteering. Joining professional associations. Creating businesses. Mentoring young people. Respecting public debate. Using evidence rather than misinformation. Participating peacefully in civic life. A healthy democracy depends not upon occasional participation but upon continuous civic engagement. Citizenship is practiced every day. ### Evidence Box: Citizenship in Numbers - **Identity:** about 136 million people enrolled in the national identity database by July 2026.6 •**Trust:** 83 percent of Nigerians surveyed in 2025 had little or no trust in the federal government; 79 percent had little or no trust in the judiciary.7 - **Electoral trust:** 23 percent trusted the electoral commission “somewhat” or “a lot” before the 2023 elections.8 •**Civic action:** the Not Too Young To Run campaign, launched in 2016, secured a constitutional amendment lowering three age limits for public office in 2018.9 •**Participation and reporting:** for voter turnout and the reporting of crime, see Chapters Seven and Sixteen. *Institutions shape citizens, and citizens shape institutions. Trust is the currency in* *which both are paid.* ## The Nigerian Opportunity Nigeria possesses one of the most vibrant and energetic populations in the world. Its people have demonstrated remarkable resilience, creativity, generosity, and entrepreneurial spirit across generations. These qualities represent tremendous national assets. The opportunity before Nigeria is to channel this energy into stronger civic institutions, deeper public trust, constructive dialogue, community participation, respect for the rule of law, and sustained engagement in public life. Institutional reform and civic responsibility are not competing ideas. They reinforce one another. As institutions become stronger, citizens gain greater confidence to participate. As citizens participate responsibly, institutions become stronger. ## Looking Ahead Citizens strengthen institutions. Institutions shape national outcomes. But improvement rarely occurs automatically. Meaningful progress requires deliberate reform. Before asking how institutions can be reformed, it is worth asking where reform has already succeeded. Nigerians who have spent years hearing what does not work may be surprised by how much does. The next chapter therefore examines what Nigeria gets right. ## Institutional Mirror Imagine a society where most citizens obey the law even when enforcement is unlikely. Where public property is treated with the same care as private property. Where disagreement remains peaceful. Where public debate values evidence over insult. Where participation extends beyond election day. How would such habits influence every institution we have examined throughout this book? Citizenship may be invisible. Yet it is one of the most powerful institutions any nation possesses, because it shapes the culture within which every other institution must operate.

The campaign was launched in 2016 by Yiaga Africa with partner youth organisations.
