sections.markdown:
> “If failure teaches caution, success teaches possibility.” ## A Different Kind of Evidence Most of this book has examined what does not work. That was deliberate. A diagnosis must be honest, and honesty about Nigeria’s institutions often means describing failure: projects abandoned, prisoners waiting years for trial, health centres without doctors, budgets consumed by debt. But a diagnosis that records only symptoms is incomplete. A doctor also asks what is still healthy, what has healed before, and what the body can do when given the right conditions. Nigeria’s record contains a great deal of health. Earlier chapters have already described some of it. The Nigerian Communications Commission built a market of nearly 190 million mobile subscriptions on a transparent licence auction (Chapter Four). Nigeria eliminated wild poliovirus (Chapter Four). Lagos State multiplied its own revenue across four successive governors (Chapter Three). A single Treasury account closed about 20,000 separate government bank accounts (Chapter Three). Biometric payroll checks removed more than 43,000 ghost workers (Chapter Eight). Nigeria’s instant payment system and Bank Verification Number became the foundation of a financial technology industry (Chapter Eighteen). Lagos opened Africa’s first court-connected dispute-resolution centre (Chapter Fourteen). This chapter adds four more cases, chosen from different parts of national life: a regulator, a public-sector reform, a state government, and a citizens’ organization. Each is examined with the same questions this book applies to failure. What problem existed? What changed? Which institution led? Which incentives shifted? What resulted? What remains unfinished? And what can others learn? The purpose is not celebration. It is explanation. ## The Regulator That Fought Back: NAFDAC **The problem.** At the beginning of the 2000s, counterfeit and substandard medicines were common in Nigerian markets. Patients could not be sure that the drug they bought contained what its label promised. The cost was measured in failed treatments and lost lives. **The intervention.** The National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control, under the leadership of Dora Akunyili from 2001, launched a sustained campaign of inspection, seizure, prosecution, and public education. By 2007, it had carried out more than one hundred destruction exercises for fake drugs valued at about $150 million and secured dozens of convictions.1 **The outcome.** In 2006, the agency reported a study showing that the share of counterfeit drugs in circulation had fallen from an average of about 41 per cent in 2001 to about 16.7 per cent in 2006, based on a survey of hundreds of samples.2 **What changed.** The agency did not rely on exhortation. It changed the odds facing those who imported and sold fake medicines: a higher probability of detection, the loss of seized stock, and exclusion from the Nigerian market. It also made the public an ally, so that buyers became inspectors. **What remains.** The NAFDAC story is often told as the story of one remarkable leader, and Akunyili’s courage was real: she survived an assassination attempt, and agency offices were attacked.3 But that framing contains a warning. Reforms closely identified with one person are vulnerable when that person leaves. The lasting test is whether the systems the agency built—inspection, registration, testing, public verification—continue to work regardless of who leads it. Substandard medicines remain a problem in Nigeria, and estimates of their prevalence vary widely with the methods used to measure them. **The lesson.** Regulation works when it changes the expected costs of breaking the rules—and when citizens are given a role in enforcing them. ## The Reform That Built a Fund: Pensions **The problem.** Before 2004, most public servants were covered by a pension scheme that was promised but not funded. Pensions were paid from each year’s budget. When releases were late or inadequate, arrears accumulated, and retirees who had served for decades were left waiting. Where private schemes were funded, the official history of the reform notes “malpractices between the fund managers and the trustees.” The National Pension Commission later concluded that the old scheme “could not be sustained.”4 **The intervention.** The Pension Reform Act of 2004, later revised in 2014, replaced the old arrangements with a contributory scheme. Employers and employees pay into individual retirement savings accounts. Licensed pension fund administrators invest the money, separate custodians hold the assets, and a regulator—the National Pension Commission—supervises the system. **The outcome.** By July 2026, assets under the scheme stood at about ₦31.5 trillion, up from about ₦20.8 trillion two years earlier, and more than 11 million contributors held accounts.5 In under a generation, Nigeria built a large pool of long-term domestic savings that had not previously existed in this form. ![Figure 21.1. Assets under the Contributory Pension Scheme, selected dates. Sources: Wikipedia summary of PenCom data (2017–2019); TheCable, February 5, 2021; Nairametrics, October 7, 2026.](/static/book/fig-217-41.jpg)

Figure 21.1. Assets under the Contributory Pension Scheme, selected dates. Sources: Wikipedia summary of PenCom data (2017–2019); TheCable, February 5, 2021; Nairametrics, October 7, 2026.

**What changed.** The reform changed who held the money and who could see it. Under the old system, pensions were a future promise competing with every other claim on the annual budget. Under the new one, contributions are set aside in accounts that belong to individual workers, managed by firms that can be supervised, and held by custodians who are separate from those who invest them. The design reduced the opportunity for funds to disappear and gave workers a personal stake in monitoring their own accounts. **What remains.** Most Nigerian workers are in the informal sector and are not yet covered. Thirty states and the Federal Capital Territory have enacted pension reform laws, but by 2026 only seven states and the FCT were fully implementing them.6 Inflation erodes the real value of savings, and the figures in this chapter are not adjusted for it. And the legacy of the old system lingers: in 2026, the government reported a ₦758 billion intervention to settle pension arrears, some dating back to 2007, for about 957,000 pensioners.7 A well-designed system is not yet a universal one. **The lesson.** Separating the money from the people who might be tempted to divert it—and giving the owners of that money the right to see it—can turn a chronic failure into a durable institution. ## The State That Built a Lane: Lagos BRT **The problem.** Lagos is one of the most congested cities in the world. For millions of workers, the daily journey between the mainland and the island could take hours, in privately operated minibuses with unpredictable fares. **The intervention.** In 2002, the Lagos State Government established the Lagos Metropolitan Area Transport Authority8 to plan and regulate public transport. In March 2008, with technical advice and financing from the World Bank, it opened a 22-kilometre bus rapid transit corridor—described at the time as the first dedicated bus route in sub-Saharan Africa. **The outcome.** By the World Bank’s account, the corridor carried more than 200,000 passengers a day and more than 120 million in its first two years. Average fares fell from ₦230 to ₦100, waiting times from 45 minutes to 10, and journey times by about 25 minutes. The buses carried about a quarter of the trips on the corridor while making up only 4 per cent of its vehicles.9 By 2025, with more corridors added, the authority reported that the bus rapid transit system carried more than 350,000 passengers a day. ![A bus rapid transit vehicle at the Mile 12 bus stop, Lagos, 2019. Photo: Olatunbosun Success / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.](/static/book/fig-219-42.jpg)

A bus rapid transit vehicle at the Mile 12 bus stop, Lagos, 2019. Photo: Olatunbosun Success / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

**What changed.** A dedicated authority gave the city a single institution responsible for planning transport across a fragmented system. A dedicated lane gave buses a reason to be faster than cars, and passengers a reason to use them. **What remains.** Rapid transit systems are only as good as their maintenance, enforcement, and continued investment in vehicles—exactly the areas in which, as Chapter Seventeen showed, Nigerian infrastructure most often falters. A lane that is not protected, or a fleet that is not replaced, will lose its advantage over time. **The lesson.** Giving one institution clear responsibility for a problem, and the authority to act across boundaries, can achieve what decades of uncoordinated effort could not. ## The Citizens Who Counted: Election Observation **The problem.** In a country where electoral results are frequently disputed, citizens need a way to know whether the announced result reflects the votes actually cast—independently of the parties and the electoral commission. **The intervention.** Nigerian civil society organizations have developed systematic, statistically based election observation. In 2019, Yiaga Africa’s Watching The Vote project deployed 3,030 observer teams to a representative random sample of 1,515 polling units and collected results from more than 98 per cent of them. Using a method known as a parallel vote tabulation, it estimated each party’s share of the presidential vote within a narrow margin of error.10 **The outcome.** Yiaga Africa reported that the official results for the two leading parties fell within its estimated ranges. It also estimated turnout at about 37.5 per cent, slightly higher than the official 35.7 per cent.11 **What changed.** For the first time on such a scale, ordinary citizens—trained, organized, and using a transparent method—could independently check a national result. That changes the incentives facing anyone who might wish to falsify one. A result that does not match an independent estimate invites scrutiny. A result that does match it carries greater legitimacy, whichever party wins. **What remains.** Statistical verification can confirm or question a national total. It cannot by itself resolve every dispute at the level of individual polling units, protect voters from intimidation, or prevent vote buying. And observers must remain demonstrably non-partisan to retain public trust. **The lesson.** Citizens can build institutions too. Accountability does not have to wait for the state to provide it. ## What the Successes Have in Common Set these four cases beside the successes described in earlier chapters, and a pattern emerges. **Clear responsibility.** Each success had an institution that clearly owned the problem: a regulator, a commission, a transport authority, a citizens’ network. **Changed incentives.** Each altered the costs and rewards facing the people involved—importers of fake drugs, managers of pension money, commuters choosing between cars and buses, anyone tempted to falsify a result. **Visibility.** Each made something visible that had been hidden: what is in a medicine, how much is in a pension account, how long a journey takes, what the true count of votes is likely to be. **Continuity.** The most durable successes survived changes of leadership and, in several cases, changes of ruling party. Those most closely tied to one individual were the most fragile. **Honest limits.** None is complete. Every case in this chapter has unfinished business. That is not a reason to dismiss the success. It is a reminder that institutions must be maintained, not merely created. These are the same principles this book has found missing in its studies of failure. That is the most important finding of this chapter. Nigeria does not need to import a foreign formula for institutional success. It needs to apply, consistently and across institutions, the formula it has already demonstrated at home. ### Evidence Box: What Nigeria Gets Right - **Medicines:** counterfeit drugs in circulation fell from about 41 per cent (2001) to about 16.7 per cent (2006), according to a study reported by NAFDAC.12 •**Pensions:** contributory pension assets reached about ₦31.5 trillion by July 2026, with more than 11 million contributors.13 •**Transport:** Lagos BRT carried more than 200,000 passengers a day, and halved fares on its corridor, after opening in 2008.14 •**Elections:** 3,030 citizen observer teams verified the 2019 presidential result through a statistical sample of 1,515 polling units.15 •**Earlier chapters:** mobile telephony and polio (Chapter Four), state revenue and the Treasury Single Account (Chapter Three), payroll verification (Chapter Eight), payment infrastructure (Chapter Eighteen), court- connected mediation (Chapter Fourteen). *Success in Nigeria is not an exception to the argument of this book. It is the* *evidence for it.* ## The Nigerian Opportunity The greatest obstacle to reform is not the absence of solutions. It is the belief that nothing works. That belief is understandable after decades of disappointment. But it is not supported by the evidence. Nigerian institutions have repeatedly solved hard problems when they were given clear responsibility, changed the relevant incentives, made their work visible, and lasted long enough to matter. The opportunity is to stop treating these successes as isolated miracles and start treating them as templates—to ask, in every ministry, agency, and state, which of these principles could be applied next. ## Looking Ahead Nigeria’s own successes show what is possible at home. Other nations offer a second source of evidence: societies that faced challenges similar to Nigeria’s and built stronger institutions over time. The next chapter examines what they did—and what Nigeria should, and should not, borrow. ## Institutional Mirror Think of one Nigerian institution that works well in your own experience—a school, a clinic, a bank, an agency, a market association, a community group. Ask why it works. **Who is responsible for it?** **What rewards good performance there, and what punishes failure?** **What can be seen, and by whom?** **Has it survived a change of leadership?** The answers will look familiar by now. They are the same answers this book has been searching for since its first page.

sections.markdown:
> “Every nation must build its own institutions. No nation has to build them without learning from others.” ## The Temptation of the Model Every few years, a new country becomes Nigeria’s favourite example. At one time, it was Singapore: a small island that rose from poverty to wealth within a generation. At another, it was South Korea, or Malaysia, or China. More recently, Rwanda has been held up as proof that an African state can be clean, orderly, and effective. The comparisons are understandable. They are also dangerous. They are dangerous because they often reduce a country’s story to a single leader—Lee Kuan Yew, Park Chung-hee, Paul Kagame—and conclude that what Nigeria needs is a leader like them. That is precisely the conclusion this book has argued against. And they are dangerous because they skip over the price some of those countries paid, in political freedom, for their order. This chapter takes a different approach. It looks at five countries named in this book’s original research plan—Singapore, Botswana, Indonesia, South Korea, and Rwanda—and asks not “Which country should Nigeria copy?” but “Which institutional principles have travelled, and under what conditions?” The answer, as Chapter Twenty-Three will put it, lies in adaptation rather than imitation. ![Figure 22.1. Corruption Perceptions Index scores, 2025, for Nigeria and the countries discussed in this chapter, with Ghana for regional comparison. Source: Transparency International, Corruption Perceptions Index 2025, results table as published by Transparency International Nepal.](/static/book/fig-224-43.jpg)

Figure 22.1. Corruption Perceptions Index scores, 2025, for Nigeria and the countries discussed in this chapter, with Ghana for regional comparison. Source: Transparency International, Corruption Perceptions Index 2025, results table as published by Transparency International Nepal.

## Singapore: Making Corruption a Losing Bet **What happened.** In 1951, three police detectives were among the robbers in a hijacking of opium worth a large sum in colonial Singapore. The existing anti- corruption unit, housed within the police, could not gather enough evidence to prosecute most of those involved. In 1952, the colonial government created a separate body, the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau.1 After self- government, the Prevention of Corruption Act of 1960 strengthened its hand. Under the Act, any gratification received by a public employee is presumed to have been received corruptly unless the person proves otherwise, and the identities of informers are protected.2 **What it teaches.** Singapore did not rely on the honesty of officials. It changed the odds facing dishonest ones. An investigator independent of the police; a law that shifted the burden of proof; protection for those who report: each made corruption more likely to be detected and more costly when it was. The bureau has since investigated sitting ministers—most recently the transport minister, arrested in 2023.3 No office was placed beyond its reach. **The caution.** Singapore is a city-state of a few million people, governed by one party since independence, with limited political competition. Its methods operate within a political system very different from Nigeria’s federal, multi-party democracy. What travels is not the political system but the principle: make the investigator independent, make the law hard to evade, and protect the people who speak up. ## Botswana: Treating a Windfall as a Trust **What happened.** At independence in 1966, Botswana was among the poorest countries in the world, with, by one widely cited account, barely twelve kilometres of paved road and twenty-two university graduates.4 Then came diamonds. Botswana could have suffered the fate often called the resource curse: a windfall captured by a few, an economy that neglects everything else, and governments that no longer need their citizens’ taxes. Instead, Botswana negotiated an equal partnership with the mining company De Beers in Debswana, its diamond-mining joint venture, so that the state owns half of the enterprise.5 It saved part of its revenue abroad, creating the Pula Fund in 1993 to invest surplus earnings from diamond exports, managed by the central bank under law.6 Between 1966 and 1999 its income per person grew by an average of about 7 per cent a year—one of the fastest rates in the world— and in 1994 it became the first country to graduate from the United Nations’ list of least developed countries.7 In 2024, after almost six decades of rule by one party, voters elected the opposition—and power changed hands peacefully.8 ![The central business district of Gaborone, Botswana, 2019. Photo: Jota / Wikimedia Commons, public domain.](/static/book/fig-226-44.jpg)

The central business district of Gaborone, Botswana, 2019. Photo: Jota / Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

**What it teaches.** The contrast with Nigeria’s experience of oil is uncomfortable but instructive. Chapter Three described how Nigeria’s Excess Crude Account held more than $20 billion in 2008 and less than $400,000 by 2022. Botswana’s savings were protected by rules and institutions—a fund held by the central bank under law—rather than by the restraint of each successive government. **The caution.** Botswana is not a finished success. Diamonds still make up about 90 per cent of its goods exports and about a third of government revenue. As global demand for natural diamonds weakened, its economy contracted in 2024 and 2025, and unemployment stood at about 21 per cent.9 Good institutions managed the windfall well. They have not yet diversified the economy beyond it. ## Indonesia: A Powerful Agency—and Its Vulnerability **What happened.** After the fall of the Suharto regime in 1998, Indonesia faced corruption on a scale comparable to Nigeria’s. In 2002, a law created the Corruption Eradication Commission, known as the KPK, which began operating at the end of 2003. It was given unusual powers, including the authority to wiretap without prior approval, and it pursued governors, legislators, and ministers. One foreign observer reported that in its early years it achieved a conviction in every one of its first 86 bribery and graft cases.10 **What happened next.** Its success made it enemies. In September 2019, after only twelve days of deliberation, Indonesia’s parliament amended the KPK law: an oversight council was created that must approve wiretaps in advance, the commission’s investigative and prosecutorial powers were reduced, and its staff were converted into civil servants. Dozens of investigators were later dismissed after failing a controversial test. Student-led protests involving hundreds of universities followed.11 In 2025, Indonesia scored 34 on the Corruption Perceptions Index.12 **What it teaches.** An anti-corruption agency is only as strong as the institutions that protect it. The KPK’s independence existed in an ordinary statute, and an ordinary statute could take it away. For Nigeria, whose own anti-corruption agencies depend heavily on political goodwill, the lesson is pointed: reforms that threaten powerful interests need protection that is harder to reverse—constitutional safeguards, secure funding, transparent appointment, and an engaged public willing to defend them. ## South Korea: No One Above the Institution **What happened.** South Korea’s development is often attributed to strong leadership, and its early decades were marked by authoritarian rule. But its more recent history offers a different lesson. In 2017, the Constitutional Court upheld the impeachment of President Park Geun-hye, removing her from office. On 3 December 2024, President Yoon Suk Yeol declared martial law; parliament overturned the declaration, impeached him, and on 4 April 2025 the Constitutional Court unanimously removed him from office.13 **What it teaches.** In both cases, the most powerful person in the country was removed not by a coup, a mob, or a rival’s private army, but by a legislature and a court following constitutional procedures. That is what it means for institutions to be stronger than individuals. It is also a reminder that strong institutions are not a guarantee against bad decisions by leaders. They are a guarantee that bad decisions can be corrected. **The caution.** South Korea’s rapid growth took place under governments that were often repressive. The country’s democratic institutions were won through decades of struggle by its citizens, not handed down by its rulers. ## Rwanda: Performance Contracts—and Their Price **What happened.** Since 2006, Rwanda’s districts have signed annual performance contracts known as *imihigo*, setting out targets for the year. Their performance is evaluated, and the results are published as rankings. Leaders who repeatedly fail can be removed. After a pause, the national statistics institute resumed publishing results in March 2026: the national average score for 2024/2025 was 69 per cent.14 Rwanda scored 58 on the 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, among the highest in Africa.15 **What it teaches.** Publicly ranking subnational governments on their results creates a powerful incentive to deliver. Nigeria, whose states and local governments are rarely measured against one another in public, could adapt the principle—for example, through independently verified, published scorecards of state performance in health, education, and revenue, of the kind civic groups such as BudgIT already attempt (Chapter Nineteen). **The caution.** Rwanda’s performance system operates within a political order that tolerates little dissent. In Freedom House’s 2025 assessment, Rwanda scored 21 out of 100 and was rated “Not Free.” The incumbent president won 99.2 per cent of the vote in 2024, leading opposition figures were barred from standing, and journalists widely self-censor.16 Rwanda’s own evaluators have also found that districts now track around 140 indicators each, diluting attention from results that matter.17 Nigeria can borrow the idea of measured, published performance. It should not—and under its Constitution could not—borrow the political conditions in which Rwanda applies it. ## What Travels Set these five cases beside Nigeria’s own successes in Chapter Twenty-One, and the transferable principles become clear. **Independence for those who investigate.** Singapore’s bureau and Indonesia’s commission show that investigators must be insulated from those they investigate—and that this insulation must be protected in law that is hard to change. **Rules that protect windfalls.** Botswana shows that national wealth is protected by institutions that bind every government, not by the restraint of any one of them. **Accountability that reaches the top.** South Korea shows that the most important test of an institution is whether it can hold the most powerful person in the country to account. **Measurement that is public.** Rwanda shows that publishing comparative performance creates pressure to deliver—though measurement must be honest, focused, and free from political fear to be trusted. **Freedom as a condition, not an obstacle.** The most durable successes—Botswana’s peaceful change of government, South Korea’s constitutional removals of two presidents—occurred in societies where citizens could speak, vote, and organize. Order purchased at the price of freedom may deliver results for a time, but it removes the citizens’ ability to correct the system when it goes wrong. ### Evidence Box: Lessons from Other Nations - **Singapore:** independent anti-corruption bureau founded in 1952; 1960 law presumes gifts to public officials are corrupt unless proven otherwise; Corruption Perceptions Index score of 84 in 2025.18 •**Botswana:** half-ownership of its main diamond venture; Pula Fund created in 1993; first country to graduate from UN least-developed status (1994); peaceful change of ruling party in 2024.19 •**Indonesia:** anti-corruption commission created in 2002; independence curtailed by law in 2019.20 •**South Korea:** two presidents removed through constitutional procedures, in 2017 and 2025.21 •**Rwanda:** published district performance contracts since 2006; rated “Not Free” by Freedom House in 2025.22 *Other nations offer Nigeria principles, not templates—and cautions as valuable as* *their successes.* ## The Nigerian Opportunity Nigeria does not need to become Singapore, Botswana, Indonesia, South Korea, or Rwanda. It could not, and it should not try. But it can learn from each of them. It can give its investigators real independence, protected by law. It can bind its governments to rules that protect national wealth from short-term temptation. It can strengthen the institutions that hold even the highest offices to account. And it can measure and publish the performance of every tier of government—within, rather than at the expense of, a free and democratic society. Above all, it can stop looking abroad for a saviour, and start looking abroad for principles. ## Looking Ahead Nigeria’s own successes and other nations’ experience point in the same direction. What remains is the question toward which this entire book has been moving: How do societies build stronger institutions over time—and sustain them? The next chapter examines reform itself. ## Institutional Mirror When someone next says that Nigeria needs its own Lee Kuan Yew or its own Kagame, ask: **What, exactly, did that country build that outlasted its leader?** **What did its citizens give up along the way?** **And which of its principles could work in a free, federal, and diverse country like Nigeria?** The answers will rarely be a person. They will usually be an institution.

sections.markdown:
> “Institutions rarely transform overnight. They improve through deliberate choices, consistent leadership, public participation, and sustained commitment across generations.” ## The Old House Imagine a family living in an old house. The roof leaks during the rainy season. The electrical wiring is outdated. The plumbing no longer functions properly. Some rooms remain useful. Others require urgent attention. The family faces a choice. They could abandon the house entirely. They could pretend nothing is wrong. Or they could renovate it—carefully, systematically, and patiently. Meaningful reform resembles renovation more than demolition. Strong foundations should be preserved. Weak structures should be repaired. Unsafe designs should be replaced. Useful features should be strengthened. Nations improve in much the same way. Institutional reform is rarely about beginning again. It is about improving what already exists. ![Bricklayers at work on a building site, Kwara State, 2017. Photo: Eyibeauty Oyelowo / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.](/static/book/fig-232-45.jpg)

Bricklayers at work on a building site, Kwara State, 2017. Photo: Eyibeauty Oyelowo / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

## Reform Begins with Honest Diagnosis No effective reform begins with assumptions. It begins with evidence. What is working? What is not? Why? Which institutions consistently achieve their objectives? Which struggle? What incentives encourage current behaviour? Which incentives produce unintended consequences? Diagnosis requires intellectual humility. It asks societies to confront reality without despair and to recognize progress without complacency. Reform built on accurate diagnosis has a greater chance of lasting success than reform driven by slogans or frustration. This book has tried to practise that discipline. Each chapter has looked for evidence rather than assuming the answer—and the evidence has often been uncomfortable. Two in three people held in Nigeria’s custodial centres have not been convicted of any offence (Chapter Fourteen). Only about a quarter of households that experience crime report it to the police (Chapter Sixteen). Only two of thirty-six states raise enough of their own revenue to cover the cost of running their governments (Chapter Nineteen). None of these figures names a villain. Each describes a pattern that has survived many changes of personnel. That is what a diagnosis looks like. ## Institutions Change Through Incentives Throughout this book we have returned to one recurring principle: People respond to incentives. Institutions shape those incentives. Reforming institutions therefore means redesigning the environment within which decisions are made. Merit should be rewarded. Integrity should be protected. Innovation should be encouraged. Transparency should become routine. Accountability should be predictable. Professional excellence should create opportunity. When institutional incentives change consistently, behaviour gradually changes with them. Reform is therefore not merely about replacing individuals. It is about changing the rules that influence everyone. Nigeria’s own experience shows the difference. When the federal government linked salary payments to biometric identity, more than 43,000 names that had drawn salaries without corresponding employees were removed from the payroll (Chapter Eight). No sermon against ghost workers had achieved that. A changed system did. When the Nigerian Communications Commission replaced a discredited licensing process with a transparent, published auction in 2001, it did not ask investors to trust individuals; it gave them rules they could rely on—and mobile telephony grew from a few hundred thousand lines to well over a hundred million subscriptions (Chapter Four). ## Leadership Matters—But It Is Not Enough Visionary leaders can inspire reform. They can introduce new ideas. Mobilize public support. Challenge complacency. Accelerate change. Yet lasting reform depends upon institutions capable of sustaining progress after leadership changes. History offers many examples of reforms that flourished briefly before fading because they depended almost entirely on particular individuals. Enduring reform becomes embedded in procedures, professional standards, laws, organizational culture, and public expectations. Successful leaders therefore build institutions that eventually become stronger than their own personal influence. The timeline of reform makes the point unavoidable. Of the Nigerian reforms examined in this book, few produced their central result within a single four-year term. Polio eradication took a quarter of a century from the continental pledge to certification. The report on rationalizing federal agencies waited twelve years for approval. Lagos waited forty years between its first urban rail plan and its first passengers. The fastest reform shown here—the bank consolidation of 2004 and 2005—was completed within about a year, yet the sector needed rescue within a few years and a new recapitalization in 2024 (Chapter Four). ![Figure 23.1. Years from the start of selected Nigerian reforms to a key result. Sources: as cited in the chapters indicated.](/static/book/fig-235-46.jpg)

Figure 23.1. Years from the start of selected Nigerian reforms to a key result. Sources: as cited in the chapters indicated.

Speed is not the measure of reform. Continuity is. A reform that depends on one leader’s attention will usually last about as long as that attention does. A reform that has been written into law, built into procedures, funded in budgets, and adopted by the professionals who carry it out can survive changes of government—and, in time, become simply the way things are done. ## Learning from Others Without Copying Them Every nation possesses a unique history. Its own culture. Its own constitutional arrangements. Its own social realities. Institutional reform should therefore avoid imitation for its own sake. Yet nations can learn from one another. Comparative experience reveals principles rather than templates. Transparent procurement. Professional civil services. Independent judiciaries. Strong primary healthcare. Quality education. Digital public administration. Fiscal responsibility. Merit-based recruitment. These ideas have succeeded in different forms across many societies because they strengthen institutional effectiveness rather than reflect any single national culture. Wisdom often lies in adaptation rather than imitation. Georgia offers an instructive example—both of what reform can achieve and of what should not be copied uncritically. In 2004, after a change of government, the country abolished its traffic police, which had become notorious for extracting bribes from motorists, and replaced them with a newly recruited patrol police force. Thousands of officers were dismissed. The new force was better paid, more visible, and equipped to serve the public directly. Georgia rose from joint 124th of 133 countries in Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index in 2003 to 48th of 168 in 2015.1 The World Bank later documented the reforms as a case study in reducing corruption in public services.2 Yet the same reform was carried out with sweeping executive discretion and little external oversight, by a government whose later record drew serious criticism.3 Its lesson for Nigeria is therefore not the method—mass dismissal by executive decision—but the principles beneath it: recruit on merit, pay adequately, make officers visible and accountable to the public, use technology to reduce opportunities for bribery, and measure the results. Those principles can be pursued through Nigeria’s own constitutional institutions. The method would be neither wise nor lawful to imitate. ## Reform Requires Citizens Governments initiate many reforms. Institutions implement them. Citizens sustain them. Communities monitor them. Journalists examine them. Universities evaluate them. Professional associations strengthen standards. Businesses invest within them. Civil society contributes to accountability. Institutional reform therefore belongs to society as a whole. No single institution possesses a monopoly on national renewal. Progress emerges through cooperation. The Not Too Young To Run amendment (Chapter Twenty) showed citizens and civil society changing the Constitution through lawful advocacy. Community monitors from groups such as BudgIT’s Tracka visit federally funded projects to check whether they exist at all (Chapter Two). Each is a reminder that reform does not need to wait for permission from the top. It can also be demanded, monitored, and sustained from below. ### Evidence Box: What Reform Looks Like - **Changed systems change behaviour:** more than 43,000 ghost workers removed after biometric payroll verification (Chapter Eight). •**Transparent rules attract investment:** a published licence auction in 2001 opened the way to nearly 190 million mobile subscriptions by 2026 (Chapter Four). •**Reform takes time:** most reforms documented in this book took longer than one four-year term to produce their central result (Figure 23.1). •**Speed without continuity fades:** banks consolidated in 2004–05 needed rescue within a few years and a new recapitalization in 2024 (Chapter Four). •**Learning without copying:** Georgia’s police reform reduced petty corruption but relied on methods Nigeria should not imitate.4 *The question is never only whether reform can begin. It is whether it can survive* *the people who began it.* ## The Nigerian Opportunity Nigeria has repeatedly demonstrated its capacity for adaptation. Across different sectors, reforms have expanded digital services, strengthened financial systems, improved public administration, supported entrepreneurship, increased transparency, and encouraged innovation. These experiences demonstrate an important lesson. Institutional improvement is possible. The challenge is not discovering whether reform can occur. It is sustaining reform consistently across institutions, governments, and generations. The future therefore depends less upon dramatic moments than upon disciplined continuity. ## Looking Ahead This book began with a provocative statement: Nobody is the problem. After examining history, constitutions, institutions, incentives, education, healthcare, justice, security, public finance, infrastructure, enterprise, federalism, and citizenship, we are now prepared to understand what that statement truly means. The final chapter returns to the beginning. Not to repeat it. But to understand it completely. ## Institutional Mirror Imagine Nigeria twenty-five years from now. Not transformed by a single leader. Not rescued by a single policy. Not changed by a single election. Instead, imagine thousands of institutional improvements accumulating over time. Better schools. Stronger courts. More capable civil servants. Safer communities. More transparent budgets. Healthier citizens. More productive businesses. Greater public trust. Would that nation appear suddenly? Or would it emerge gradually from countless decisions to strengthen institutions year after year? Institutional reform is rarely dramatic. Its greatest achievement is that future generations often inherit its benefits without remembering how difficult the journey once was.

The source gives inconsistent figures for the number of officers dismissed; the text therefore does not state one.

sections.markdown:
> “Hope without evidence becomes wishful thinking. Evidence without hope becomes resignation. Nations need both.” ## The Morning, Again Every morning, millions of Nigerians still wake before sunrise. The farmer still steps into the field before the heat of the day. The trader still arranges her stall. The teacher still prepares the lesson. The nurse still begins her shift. The civil servant still reports to the office. The young graduate still searches for work. Nothing about them has changed since the first page of this book. What has changed is how we see the morning. At the beginning, we noticed the people. Now we can also see what surrounds them. We can see the power line that may or may not carry electricity to the trader’s freezer, and the diesel generator she bought because it often does not. We can see the classroom where the teacher stands—one of about 230,000 schools, many of which did not even submit their annual returns. We can see the primary health centre where the nurse works, which, like most such centres, probably has no doctor. We can see the road the farmer’s produce must travel, maintained by an agency describing a “maintenance debt” it cannot pay. We can see the payroll that pays the civil servant, and the budget that has already committed most of the nation’s revenue before a single new road is built. The people were never the puzzle. The puzzle was the system in which their effort takes place. ## What the Phrase Never Meant This book began with a provocative statement: *Nobody is the problem.* It is time to say plainly what that statement means—and what it has never meant. It has never meant that no one is responsible. Chapter One stated the objection in its strongest form: specific people have stolen specific money, taken specific bribes, and abandoned specific projects. Those people are responsible for what they did. A society that stops holding individuals to account does not become wiser; it becomes defenceless. Nor has it meant that leadership does not matter. Leaders can open doors that institutions then keep open, or close them for a generation. Chapter after chapter has shown leaders who made a difference: a regulator that designed a clean auction, a state government that rebuilt its revenue service, an administration that completed a reform its predecessor began. What the statement means is narrower, and more demanding. It means that no single person—no president, no governor, no minister, no party, no ethnic group, no generation—is *the* problem, in the sense that removing them would solve it. The problems that matter most in Nigeria have survived every change of personnel the country has tried. They outlived civilian governments and military ones, parties of every kind, and leaders of every region and faith. Problems that survive every change of person are not, at bottom, problems of persons. They are problems of the arrangements those persons inherit, operate within, and pass on: the rules, the incentives, the procedures, the habits, and the institutions of national life. That is why the search for the right individual has so often ended in disappointment. Each new leader enters the same house, with the same leaking roof and the same faulty wiring. Some fix a room. Few rewire the building. And the next occupant inherits the same problems. ## What the Evidence Showed This book promised to replace blame with diagnosis. Diagnosis requires evidence, and every chapter has tried to supply it. Taken together, the findings form a pattern that no single villain could explain. ![The next generation: graduating students of the American University of Nigeria, 2022. Chapters Four, Five, and Six,* *which examine change, history, and the Constitution, are summarized in the text* *below.* Read the right-hand column again. Not one of those findings names a person. Each describes a pattern: an incentive, a procedure, a missing link between authority and accountability, a break in continuity. Change the minister, the governor, or the president, and most of those findings would remain. Many already have. ## The Pattern Beneath the Patterns Look across the chapters, and three deeper features recur. **The first is misaligned incentives.** Where honesty is costly and misconduct is cheap, misconduct spreads—whoever holds office. Where creating an agency rewards its creators and closing one punishes them, agencies multiply. Where a state government receives most of its money from a monthly transfer rather than from its own citizens, its attention is drawn upward to Abuja rather than outward to the people. In each case, the outcome follows the incentive more reliably than it follows anyone’s intentions. **The second is accountability that does not hold.** Nigeria rarely lacks rules. It has an Administration of Criminal Justice Act that limits remand, a Fiscal Responsibility Act that limits borrowing, a Public Procurement Act, an Auditor-General who finds irregularities year after year, and a Supreme Court judgment ordering that local governments be paid directly. What it often lacks is the chain that turns a rule into a consequence: the finding that is acted upon, the judgment that is obeyed, the audit query that is answered, the detainee whose waiting time someone is responsible for counting. **The third is broken continuity.** The most successful Nigerian reforms in this book—mobile telephony, polio eradication, the Treasury Single Account, the Bank Verification Number, the rebuilding of Lagos State’s revenue service—share one quality: they survived changes of government. The most frustrating failures share the opposite. A rail project cancelled in one decade and restarted four decades later. A report on rationalizing agencies shelved by one government and revived by another. A bank reform celebrated in one year, followed by rescues, and repeated twenty years later. None of these three features is a person. All three are institutional. And all three can be changed. ## What Has Already Worked It would be easy, at the end of a long diagnosis, to conclude that the patient cannot recover. The evidence in this book does not support that conclusion. Nigeria built one of Africa’s largest mobile telephone markets after creating a regulator and running a transparent auction. It eliminated wild poliovirus after years of patient, community-based effort, and then turned the same emergency structures against Ebola within days. It removed tens of thousands of ghost workers from the federal payroll by changing a system rather than preaching a sermon. It consolidated government cash into a single account across a change of ruling party. It built payment infrastructure on which an entire generation of financial companies now stands. Lagos opened Africa’s first court-connected centre for dispute resolution, and other states followed. Young Nigerians, through lawful advocacy, changed the Constitution. States have begun regulating their own electricity markets. None of these successes depended on a saviour. Each depended on an institution: a rule, a system, an agency, a procedure, or a coalition that kept working after the people who began it had moved on. That is the most hopeful finding in this book. Nigeria does not need to discover whether institutional reform is possible. It has done it, repeatedly. The task is to do it consistently. ## Who, Then, Is Responsible? If nobody is the problem, a reader may fairly ask: who, then, is responsible for the solution? The answer is not “nobody.” It is “everyone, in their place.” **Leaders** are responsible for building institutions that will outlast them, rather than for being indispensable. The measure of a reforming president, governor, or minister is not what happens while they are in office, but what continues to work after they have gone. **Public servants** are responsible for the professional standards of their institutions—for the file that is not lost, the procurement that is not rigged, the patient who is not turned away, and the detainee whose case is not forgotten. **Legislators and judges** are responsible for turning rules into consequences: for passing laws that can be implemented, overseeing their implementation, and ensuring that judgments are obeyed. **Journalists, researchers, and civil society organizations** are responsible for evidence: for counting what others prefer to leave uncounted, and for telling the public what they find. **Businesses** are responsible for competing on value rather than on access, and for supporting the institutions—courts, regulators, payment systems—on which their own success depends. **Citizens** are responsible for the expectations they hold and the habits they practise: for paying what they owe, reporting what they see, voting with judgment rather than inducement, and demanding not only that individuals be punished, but that the systems which enabled them be repaired. No one in this list can succeed alone. That is precisely the point. ## The Architect’s Question, Answered Chapter One asked readers to imagine being asked not to govern Nigeria for four years, but to design its institutions for the next fifty. Having followed the evidence through every chapter, we can now suggest what such an architect might do. **Design for the incentive, not the intention.** Assume that most people, most of the time, will respond to the costs and rewards in front of them. Make honesty cheaper, misconduct costlier, and good performance visible. **Close the chain of accountability.** Every rule should have someone responsible for applying it and a consequence when it is ignored. A finding without a follow-up is not accountability. It is documentation. **Protect continuity.** Write successful reforms into law, budgets, and procedures, so that they survive changes of government. Before cancelling an inherited project, ask what the cancellation will cost the next generation. **Match responsibility with resources and authority.** Whether at federal, state, or local level, no institution should be blamed for failing at a task it was never given the means to perform. **Count what matters, and publish it.** Most of the evidence in this book exists because someone decided to measure: a statistical survey, a project monitor, an audit, a census of schools. A nation that measures honestly can improve deliberately. **Invite citizens in.** Institutions that ordinary people can see, use, monitor, and trust become stronger with every interaction. Institutions that hide from the public become weaker, however well they are designed on paper. None of these principles belongs to a party, a region, or an ideology. Each has been tested somewhere in Nigeria already. ## The Inheritance Every generation inherits institutions it did not design. The graduates in the photograph earlier in this chapter did not choose the electricity system, the courts, the budget, or the schools they grew up with. They inherited them—just as their parents did, and as their own children will. The question each generation faces is what it will hand on. It can hand on the same arrangements, along with the same habit of looking for someone to blame when those arrangements fail. Or it can hand on institutions that are a little stronger than those it received: a court that hears cases a little faster, a budget that is a little more honest, a school where a few more children learn to read, a police station that a few more citizens trust enough to enter. No single improvement will transform the nation. Thousands of them will. ## Institutional Mirror Return, one last time, to the question at the heart of this book. When the same outcome survives different leaders, different governments, and different generations, what endures? The answer, as we have seen, is the system: the rules, incentives, and institutions within which every leader governs and every citizen lives. Nobody is the problem. The problem is what we have built together, and what we have tolerated together. And for exactly that reason, it is also something we can rebuild together.

sections.markdown:
Somewhere in Nigeria tonight, a decision is being made that no one will ever read about.

A clerk is deciding whether to file a document properly or let it disappear. A nurse is deciding whether to stay for the night shift. A teacher is deciding whether to mark the scripts honestly. A police officer at a checkpoint is deciding whether to wave a driver through or ask for something. A procurement officer is deciding whether to follow the rules or the instructions of someone more powerful. A voter is deciding whether to accept the money being offered outside the polling unit.

None of these people will appear in the history books. Yet the history of Nigeria will be written, in large part, by the sum of their decisions.

And each of them is deciding inside a system.

The clerk decides differently when every file is tracked and someone will ask where it went. The nurse decides differently when the health centre has power, water, and colleagues. The teacher decides differently when results are published and good teaching is noticed. The police officer decides differently when a camera is running and a complaint will be investigated. The procurement officer decides differently when the contract will be published for anyone to read. The voter decides differently when the vote will be counted where everyone can see it, and when the candidates have something to offer other than cash.

This book began with a question: if so many Nigerians are hardworking, talented, and determined, why do national outcomes so often fall short?

The answer it has offered is not that Nigerians are the problem. Nor is it that their leaders are, or that any single group, generation, or government is. The answer is that the systems within which Nigerians live and work too often reward the wrong things, punish the right ones, hide what should be seen, and forget what should be remembered.

That is what it means to say that nobody is the problem.

But the sentence has a second half, and it matters just as much.

**Nobody alone is the solution.**

No president can fix the systems of a nation of more than two hundred million people by force of personality. No governor can do it for a state. No minister can do it for a ministry, no judge for the courts, no activist for civil society, no citizen for a community. Every one of them, acting alone, will meet the same resistance that has defeated so many before them: the incentives, procedures, and habits that persist after good intentions have been exhausted.

What none of them can do alone, all of them can do together—slowly, and only if they persist.

That is not a slogan. It is what the evidence in this book shows. The mobile network, the polio campaign, the pension fund, the payment system, the bus lane, the citizens’ count of the vote: none was the work of a single saviour. Each was built by many people, inside institutions designed to make their efforts add up rather than cancel out, over periods longer than any one government’s term.

The future of Nigeria will not be decided by the next election alone, or by the next leader, however good or bad. It will be decided by whether, over the next twenty- five years, the country builds systems capable of producing good outcomes regardless of who occupies office.

Such systems are not built in a day. They are built one rule, one procedure, one published figure, one enforced consequence, and one honest decision at a time.

The clerk, the nurse, the teacher, the officer, the procurement officer, and the voter are all, in their way, builders of that system—or of the one that already exists.

So is every reader of this book.

Nobody is the problem.

Nobody alone is the solution.

Together, we are the system—and the system can be rebuilt.

sections.markdown:
This book rests on the work of many people I have never met.

I am grateful to the researchers, statisticians, journalists and civic organisations whose published work made its evidence possible: the National Bureau of Statistics; BudgIT and its Tracka monitors, who visit project sites so that the rest of us can know what was built; Yiaga Africa; Africa Check; Dataphyte; and the many Nigerian newspapers and reporters cited in the notes, who keep a public record that governments would often rather forget.

I thank the photographers who released their work under free licences, allowing this book to show as well as tell, and the scholars at home and abroad whose studies of institutions, federalism, corruption and reform shaped my thinking.

I am grateful to my colleagues at Zeeb Healthcare Development Initiative, whose daily work in communities and health facilities is a reminder that institutions are made of people—and that ordinary people, organised well, can change what institutions do.

To the friends and family who stood with me through the years described in the Preface: thank you. You are part of this book even where your names are not.

And to every reader who chooses to support this work: you are proof of its argument. Institutions are built by many hands, slowly, and only if they persist.

— Lincoln Matthew
